Uniform Title: Dīkṣottara Main Title: Dīkṣottara of the Niśvāsakārikā Manuscript: IFP Transcript T0017B, pages 795 to end
Description: IFP Transcript T0017B, from folio 795 to the end. The *Dīkṣottara*, the fifth section of the *Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā*. An important early Āgama of the Śaivasiddhānta.
Notes: Revision 0: December 16, 2013.
Publication Country: India (p. 795):
The supreme reality is proclaimed to be partless and composed of three limbs.
O Śambhu, how is this to be understood? This I wish to know.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret which you have inquired about;
I shall fully declare it for your benefit, O lady of virtuous conduct. 1.1–2a.

O fair-faced one, I shall describe in due order the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of the kalās (kalādhvan), the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), and the paths of the phonemes, mantras, and words (varṇa-mantra-pada-adhvan).
O Goddess, it should indeed be understood by the teachers that all these are established within the vital breath (prāṇa),
O lady of excellent vows, regarding that path of the worlds which was previously described by me.
It should be understood with effort that [the universe] is projected by twenty-six principles (tattvas);
furthermore, it is established again by eighteen principles through the divisions of the Kalās. (4)
Furthermore, O beautiful goddess, it was taught by means of nine principles;
yet all of that is again subsumed within eight divisions.
In some [traditions], one should carry that single reality joined with the principles;
this movement of thirty-six finger-breadths which I have described to you. (6)
O Goddess, one should diligently understand the limit starting from the heart-lotus;
O lady of beautiful countenance, one should endeavor to traverse the path down to the soles of the feet.
O lady of excellent hips, that path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is to be understood by the high-souled teacher; and the path of the principles (tattvādhvan) is situated above them.
One who stands outside [the body] and perceives the self as being darkened by the Kali age and breathing outwardly—
that indeed is what was previously described there as the path of the Kalās (kalādhvan). || 9 ||
In this same manner, O Goddess of the gods, another [measurement] should also be understood with effort;
having set aside thirty-six finger-breadths, O slender-waisted one, it should be done in due order.
He should be known as merely the size of a grain of rice when released from the body, yet partless;
however, his state as the Lord remains established at the *dvādaśānta*.
The Buddha is conjoined with power, while the Niṣkala consists of mere thirst;
for the Self residing in the body through power is indeed the partless Supreme Lord.
O Goddess, established in that reality, one who is liberated from the body becomes partless (niṣkala) and pervades it;
just as when fire is well-kindled, its flame licks the sky.
O beautiful lady, just as that [identification] plays within the state of the body,
so too should the preceptor establish such a sense of identification at the time of initiation. (14)
I alone am the supreme reality, and likewise, I am absorbed in that reality;
yet, by means of Śakti, who has become the friction-stick, I cast myself back into that very place once again.
Thus, he who knows in reality that [the Self] within the body is like fire— transcending that fire, O Śiva— he is indeed united with the Supreme.
One should be joined with power only so long as one has not found the ultimate reality;
but once the supreme reality has dawned, even while remaining there, one is no longer obstructed.
Released from bondage, they dissolve into the supreme, eternal Lord; dissolved therein, O Goddess, he becomes all-pervading and free from both merit and demerit.
From the heart-lotus up to that [supreme] lotus, which is characterized by the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra),
he abandons it in two stages as it reaches the mouth. (19)
The third [state] is abandoned when it is very slight; once freed from the three parts, it is partless (niṣkala).
That which has transcended is proclaimed as the lotus of power (śaktipadma) at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
The time he remains there is proclaimed to be merely the duration of a thirst;
awakened, he stays there within the lotus of Śakti as the partless (niṣkala) one.
But when, O Dear One, the one who has awakened to the past attains the state beyond mind (unmanatva),
there is no time, no movement of the digits (kalā), no ontological principles (tattvas), and no deities.
Perfect nirvāṇa is supreme and pure, established within the mouth of the Guru;
having attained it, they do not return to the bondage of the fearful cycle of existence. 23.
But for that which abides as partless (niṣkala), the name "chāmara" does not apply.
This reality of the partless (niṣkala-tattva) has thus been explained to you in brief. (24)
O Goddess, I have explained that supreme reality as being fourfold;
however, having set aside the threefold [nature], that which ends with Śakti is known as Tṛṣṭi.
Standing indeed at the third gate, he is established in the sixteenth part;
he is the enjoyer of all principles (tattvas), who is known as Tṛṭi at the end of Śakti.
He is the enjoyer of all principles (tattvas), joined with power (śakti);
O lady of excellent hips, he transcends power and is united with the ultimate principle (tattva).
There should be a four-petaled lotus; the pervasive one (Vyāpinī) resides in the pericarp.
Therein, the quartet of powers known as Sūkṣmā and the others is proclaimed. (28)
Having heard and understood this, they are liberated; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
In all the Tantras, that which resides therein is known as the universal equinox (viṣuva). (29)
O Goddess, when the vital breath dissolves there, even one who is situated there returns;
[these are] the Sakala, the Niṣkala, and the third, the Mayana.

O Goddess of gods, having attained the state of perfect tranquility, it is known as the partless equinox (niṣkala-viṣuva); when the movement [of breath] is divided into three parts, it is known as the partless Praṇava.
The Bindu is known as the tranquil and partless aspect of the Praṇava;
it is considered the individual soul (jīva) when it is joined with Śakti within the mind.
Otherwise, the self is perceived as partless, as in deep sleep;
yet, when it is known as pure consciousness alone, it is proclaimed to be the power of cognition.
Having heard and understood this, they are liberated; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
In all tantras, one should declare that the equinox (viṣuva) resides within the tantra as a universal principle. (34)
O Goddess, by means of that which resides therein, the dissolution of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs;
thus joined, this entire [body] performs various movements. (35)
In that place, the knower dissolves into the Knowable, into the supreme dissolution—the knowledge free from conceptual construction and devoid of all ontological categories. || 36 ||
Pervading all principles (tattvas) and established through a continuous succession—this entire movement of the partless (niṣkala), I have now related to you in its entirety. (37)
O Goddess, you must not give it to one who walks the path of injustice;
nor should you cause even Śrava to receive it if he has approached with deceit. 38.
Pervasive, of the nature of space, and infinite, she is remembered as the Leader;
she is renowned as the form of the God Mūrti, the power (śakti) of Devabhū. (39)

These five are indeed known as the voids (vyoma), and the state of emptiness is the deity; O lady of excellent hips, for Brahmā and the others, the supreme body is remembered as being composed of emptiness.
This first yoga of the deity has been fully described;
those beginning with the subtle state, which have become the internal states of Śakti, have also been fully described. (41)
The gods, whose nature consists of being established therein, are proclaimed to be of the nature of sound;
however, O lady of excellent hips, the third [state] must be understood by the teacher.
O Goddess, one should contemplate the form of light within the interval between the two types;
that which is thus corresponding has been described to you as the fifth.
Likewise, in the face of Īśa, as well as in Ghoras, Vāma, and Sadyojāta—
one should diligently understand the threefold body of mantra. (44)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
likewise earth, water, fire, air, and space. || 45 ||
Likewise, empty touch, sound, and the form of light, as well as the form of mantra—these have been described by me here according to their true nature. (46)
O Goddess of the Gods, the five Brahmans should be diligently understood through entities that are coarser than the coarse, and again, subtler than the subtle. (47)
Empty touch, as well as sound, fire-form, and likewise the form of reality—these are proclaimed here as the five Brahmās. (48)
Having thus known and understood this, one is released from the bonds of the snares;
one attains union with Śiva and rejoices together with Śiva. (49)
O Goddess, these six categories of mantras have been told to you;
they should be understood with effort by those who desire the goals of spiritual accomplishment and liberation.
Thus, O beautiful one, has it been told to you regarding all mantras.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Dīkṣottara of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The God said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which brings benefit to practitioners;
by the mere knowledge of which one will certainly attain liberation from the cycle of existence.
Śiva should be known as sixfold by the great-souled yogi:
as Sound, as Space, as Light, as Form, and likewise as the World. (2)
The supreme, imperishable Śiva is indeed sixfold as the Mantra-form;
by knowing the Mantra-form, one shall attain the perfection of mantra.
One whose mind is unattached to worldly existence attains the status of Bhuvaneśa;
for the sake of accomplishing the goals of Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, one should meditate upon their forms.
For the sake of attaining mastery over yogins, one should practice yoga while established in the light;
merged in the supreme reality of sound, with the mind absorbed within that sound.
Through this sound, one attains the supreme liberation for the sake of accomplishing all goals;
beyond that, O Goddess, is what is proclaimed as the Space of Power (Śaktivyoman).
Through meditation upon that, accomplishment and liberation will surely arise; there is no doubt.
807) [These are] the form, the world, the light, and likewise the sound and the shadow.
These [others] are illuminated by another, whereas Śiva is intent on the meditation of Śiva;
having thus known Śiva to be of such a nature, the practitioner, being composed, [attains success]. || 8 ||
One attains various accomplishments and even liberation, there is no doubt;
having known the mantra as the supreme form, one shall obtain accomplishment and liberation.
Through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and meditation, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained according to reality;
likewise, the world, in its cosmic form, beginning with the Brahmāṇḍa, [is realized] in due order.
It was composed of various jewels, endowed with divine and incomparable qualities,
and adorned with sapphire, great sapphire, and silver.
It was adorned with pillars made of rubies and embellished with various jewels;
it was rich in divine food, perfumes, and garments, and endowed with divine sovereignty. (12)
Having understood the world of the God of gods, one should attain absorption into it;
[one should know] the body, which has the form of a body and is characterized by the letters of Śiva and so forth. (13)
He holds the crescent moon and the trident, wears a snake as a sacred thread,
has empty hands, is mounted upon a bull, and is joined with half the body of Umā.
The form of the God of gods, white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns, is the means for accomplishing all desires and goals. (15)
One should always remember the practice for the sake of the ground of all mantras;
through constant meditation on the light, the yogi shall attain the perfection of yoga. || 16 ||
The yogin possesses the sovereign power of qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth, characterized by play and the like;
he is the supreme Śiva, pervading space, both having the form of a serpent and being formless. (17)
By meditating upon the all-pervading Lord Īśāna,
who is beyond qualities, transcends all attributes, and is devoid of houses and constellations, one shall attain Śiva.
One should contemplate the supreme ether, resembling pure crystal;
with the mind completely dissolved in the ether, established in the ether, and consisting of the ether. (19)
One attains supreme liberation when one has dissolved into sound;
through meditation on sound, there is liberation and the supernatural powers (siddhis), of this there is no doubt. (20)
Therefore, with every effort, one should take recourse in the meditation on sound (śabdādhyāna).
On its left side is the iḍā, which possesses the supreme sound of ciñciṇī.
For this is indeed called the Prākṛta, and it is proclaimed to be gross;
to the south of it, the Suṣumnā is remembered as having a long manifestation. (22)
And that which is called "human" (pauruṣa) is proclaimed as the subtle [state];
it is remembered as the supreme, situated between the end and the middle, at the cessation of the resonance of a bell. || 23 ||
Without support and without foundation—that indeed is the supreme state;
at the end of the sound of the *ciñciṇī* [vīṇā], one is without support and without refuge. || 24 ||

At the conclusion of the cessation of the sound of the bell, the wise one, realizing "I am Śiva, who is without support," should place the collection of mantras residing in the heart into the [divine] form. 25.
It is remembered as the bestower of all accomplishments through its constituent parts, beginning with Brahmā and the [other] principles;
he constantly meditates there upon the Lord Bindu situated therein. (26)
The Lord residing in the painting is Sound (nāda), who is remembered as Śiva himself in person.
He is indeed called Haṃsa, as well as Bindu, Nāda, and Nādānta. (27) p. 811)
Knowing this, the practitioner of mantra becomes Śiva himself, directly untainted.
This is that supreme secret; this is that supreme auspiciousness.
This is that supreme secret; this is that supreme state;
this is that supreme knowledge; this is that supreme syllable. || 29 ||
There is no object of meditation higher than this, and nothing more auspicious than this;
for when this is correctly understood, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
This is the procedure for the practitioner, which bestows the accomplishment of all desires and goals;
beyond these, O God, is the Lord who is devoid of sound and form.
I have previously declared that [the Self] is the pervader of all principles;
by knowing it, people are liberated and attain perfection—of this there is no doubt. (32)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Dīkṣottara of the Niśvāsakārikā. The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the unsurpassed classification of the void."
How is it known, O Śambhu, that this is the supreme, most secret of delights? || 1 ||
Īśvara said:
O beautiful goddess, it is proclaimed that among all principles (tattvas) there is emptiness;
O goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall fully explain its characteristic to you.
That path joined with the pervasive [wind] is proclaimed;
it should be understood with effort as being in the middle of day and night. (3)
Neither night nor day, nor likewise the digits of the moon—
having abandoned these fivefold [divisions], that which is utterly tranquil is called the Void.
The third, however, which transcends the body, is realized as the "niṣkala" (partless).
That which transcends the nose is the third, the void. || 15 ||
The circle of its face, up to the limit of a single *ghaṭikā*, is called the "void" (*śūnya*) transit; thus has the supreme knowledge been declared. (6)
Having established the flavors in emptiness, consciousness arises;
but having abandoned them from below, O Supreme Goddess, it becomes fivefold.
That which is utterly tranquil is said to be empty; one should not touch upon anything beyond it.
Having realized this tranquil emptiness, one is liberated from bondage. (8)
The third is proclaimed through the yoga of going and coming;
O lady of excellent hips, that which is known is remembered as this "liberation from the body."
Thus it has been told, O Goddess, that the void (śūnya) is described in the Śiva-āgama:
the upper void, the lower void, and the middle void as the third.
The fourth, indeed free from affliction, has been described in due order;
thus have these been told by me, and the fourth is indeed free from affliction.
O Goddess of gods, even that illusion exists in the state of reality;
therefore, they lead to no fault, for the remainder is characterized by great excellence.
That which is the fourth, the great emptiness, is proclaimed to be representation-only (*vijñapti*).
O Goddess, there is no conceptualization of it; it exists as a continuous succession. (13)
Having known that, it is called the "knowable"; the knower is spoken of in relation to the remaining [categories].
But that reality which transcends action is sung of as being everywhere auspicious, O virtuous one.
Its arrival is its attainment, and he with whom it is pleased is that very one.
Thus, O virtuous lady, the division of the three voids has been explained to you. (15)
That which is the fourth, the great emptiness, is proclaimed to be representation-only (vijñapti).
O Goddess, there is no conceptualization of it, as it is established through a continuous succession.
Having known that, it is called the "knowable"; the knower is spoken of in relation to what remains.
But that reality which transcends action is sung of as being everywhere auspicious, O blessed one.
Its arrival is its attainment, and he with whom it is pleased is that very one.
Thus, O lady of good vows, the division of the three voids has been explained to you. (18)
The fourth is the Great Void (mahāśūnya), which awakens everything;
by knowing that, one becomes a teacher of initiation who bestows grace upon those to be known.
Otherwise, he is not to be known as a guru, nor does initiation grant liberation.
The five voids were previously mentioned by you; they have been understood by you, O auspicious one. (20)
They are not liberated by mere knowledge within their respective diverse spheres of activity, beginning from Brahmā down to the god Sadāśiva. (21)
O fair-faced one, the five voids have been fully described by way of their withdrawal;
O Goddess, each one of them should be understood with effort as being fivefold.
The supreme distinction of emptiness among them has been described as their state;
O Goddess, it is to be known according to its nature and color, just as it is understood. (23)
I shall tell you that; listen as I speak it.
The triad of atoms is said to reside in the heart, the ears, and the palate.
O lady of excellent hips, the color [of the self] is eternally like that of a mirror;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are remembered as being like threads [woven through it]. (25)
The fourth, however, is the peaceful Lord; it should be understood with effort that the word "tat" is called *nāda*, and that has been described to you as the *jīva*.
But in this regard, O Goddess of gods, that [power] is proclaimed as *sparśa* (contact);
by its cessation, nothing would remain, which is rightly called the mouth of the Guru. (27)
O beautiful one, the conjunction has been explained to you in this very manner;
likewise, the mantras must be understood by the high-souled preceptor. (28)
The Nāda, the Bindu, and likewise the God who consists of speech and all that is moving and unmoving—this is heard and spoken as the activity of Śiva and Śakti. (29)
Having thus known and understood this, the mantras shall come under his control;
he will attain success, there is no doubt about this, for he is empowered by the Śiva-śakti. || 30 ||
But without knowing, O lady of beautiful hips, the activity of Śiva and Śakti, his mantras do not succeed, nor does he attain the supreme state. (31)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*, in the *Dīkṣottara*.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, in the past you spoke of the true nature [of reality] through the distinction between creation and dissolution; that has been understood by me, O Lord. (1)
Furthermore, O Blessed One, I wish to hear; you should deign to tell me:
which gods and dānavas were initiated directly from their own homes, and in what [state] were they so? || 2 ||
O Lord, the ṛṣis, vidyādharas, siddhas, gandharvas, and apsarases;
as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, uragas, and kinnaras.
O Mahādeva, even the Guhyakas and the cruel Vināyakas will certainly grant success to one who has been initiated by their own heart.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I desire to hear this; please tell it to me, O Śaṅkara: how many millions of divisions and branches of the scriptures have been proclaimed?
"O Lord of Gods, tell me all this, including the divisions of Śiva. Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed classification of the tantras.
The number of mantras and mandalas, as well as the compendium of the scriptures,
and those who have been initiated by me therein— none of these are subject to doubt, just as in the past.
O Goddess, this [teaching] was revealed in the past by my Supreme Preceptor (Parameṣṭhin), who is the personification of mantra, for all the Śaiva mantras.
The Supreme Lord, whose form is mantra, is the creator of this entire world and its destroyer; of this there is no doubt—he is Paraśiva.
I shall proclaim the descent [of the teaching], the determination of the compendium of names,
and the application of the rules for initiation, exactly as it was previously heard. (10)
And I shall proclaim, in due order, the various divisions of mantra-yoga;
its beginning is the Blessed Lord Śiva, who indeed possesses the form of mantra.
He is the author of the mantras and tantras, and the illuminator of the mantras and tantras. || 11 1/2 ||
It was previously revealed by Śiva, who is the embodiment of bliss.
That very speech, that knowledge, was placed within my mouth;
and by me, O Goddess of Gods, it was given to the Grandfather (Brahmā) just as it was given by you.
It was also presented by Brahmā to Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods;
and by Viṣṇu it was given to Hutāśa (Fire), and by him it was given to Vāyu.
It was undoubtedly received from Vāyu by Purāṃdara (Indra), and by Sūrya as well;
furthermore, it was then told by Sūrya to Soma. (15)
O Goddess of the gods, it was indeed by means of Soma that this was imparted for the sake of Dharma;
thus, that tenfold knowledge spoken by Śiva is summarized therein. 16.
The reality established by the Lord has been set forth as being embodied in mantra;
that very Maheśvara is the embodiment of mantra for this entire world. (17)
Through His grace, O Goddess of the gods, all this supreme knowledge and realization is attained, as well as liberation, which is difficult to find on earth. (18)
"Blessed Śiva spoke thus: 'It fulfills all desires';
and it was proclaimed once again by Rudra as 'the source of the world. (19)
When the knowledge pertaining to the Goddess is proclaimed as "Ajita," the Lord Brahmā is the cause, and Janārdana is "Ajita. (20)
"Dīptābha" is like fire; "sūkṣma" is indeed wind again;
"sahasrāṃśu" is for Dharma; and "aṃśumān" is the sun. || 21 ||
Suvrata is declared to be the Moon, the illuminator of the ten Tantras;
having presided over Śiva-Śakti, he indeed remains established as distinct once again. 22.
Thus all the gods, who have reached the further shore of the knowledge of Śiva, proceed in ten ways through the distinction of names, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Furthermore, the descent of this very Śivajñāna, which is preeminent among all forms of knowledge, has been proclaimed in many ways. (24)
The division has been declared as eightfold, and likewise again as eighteenfold;
it stands there further established through those eighteen kinds of divisions. (25)
He arrived, having come by way of the worlds of Bhuva and Suva;
these are his divisions, and his designation is now proclaimed. (26)
There, the sages who were experts in the Kalpas recognized that supreme [work] among them;
first was the Vijaya, and immediately after that, the Niśvāsa. (27)
Then there is the Svāyambhuva, and after that the Vātula;
likewise the one known as Vīrabhadra, the Raurava, and the Makuṭa. || 28 ||
Vimala, Candrabhāga, Jñāna, Mukhavālaka, Prodgīta, Lalita, and Siddhisantāna. || 29 ||
The *Śarvodgīta* and the *Kiraṇa-pārameśvara* are to be known;
Īśvara is declared to be the first, and the Goddess follows immediately after that. (30)
Brahmā and Ṣaṇmukha, as well as Vīrabhadra;
Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Īśāna, and likewise Candramas. || 31 ||
Bṛhaspati is well-known, as are the goddess Vīkā and Vāsava; likewise Lalitā, Caṇḍa, and Śāntapāṇi. || 32 ||
Sanatkumāra, Viṣṇu, and the Pārameśvara [Purāṇa]. || 32 1/2 ||
The Vijaya, Īśvarajñāna, and the Niśvāsasaṃhitā of the Goddess.
In the Vātula, Brahmā Svāyambhuva and Kumāra are to be known;
by Vīra, however, Vīrabhadra, Nandin, and Raurava are [to be known]. (34)
One should worship Mahākāla with the mantra *makuṭe*, Śukra with *visannara*,
Candra with *candrabhāsa*, and likewise Jñāna with *aṅgirasa*. (35)
The *Dadhīci-mukhabhinnam* is indeed the *Prodgīta-kavaca*;
likewise, the *Lalitam*, O Goddess, and the *Lalitā*, as well as the *Daṇḍahastam*. (36)
The *Santāna* was [revealed] by Nāśapāṇi, and the *Śarva* was sung by Viṣṇu;
the *Kiraṇa* was [revealed] by Brahmā, and the *Pārameśvara* belongs to the Supreme Lord.
These Tantras were formerly masters of the knowledge of Śiva; and at the end, those highly fortunate ones, beginning with Kramārādi, [were masters], as was the Lord of Śacī.
Likewise, there were others who had attained perfection in mantras, as well as sages whose wealth was their austerity;
they were the originators of mantra divisions and the authors of mantra manuals.
By these very [means], the knowledge of Śiva was established upon the surface of the earth,
having propitiated the Supreme Lord through the enumeration of various names. (40)
It is proclaimed likewise in the Mantrakalpa and similarly in the Bhūtakalpa;
it is designated by the divisions of the Gaṇas and Guhyakas, as well as by the divisions of Rudra. (41)
Its divisions were previously declared to be tenfold;
furthermore, they have been fully described as being likewise ten types of the "lost" (naṣṭa).
In ancient times, the Blessed Lord Rudra spoke to Brahmā during the Vijaya festival;
the mantras therein have been fully declared—listen, O lady of excellent complexion! (43)
There are eight thousand mantras, as well as five hundred;
likewise fifty-one, and indeed seventy-seven.
O Goddess, this was known by the gods; therefore, something has arrived here.
It was proclaimed in Vijaya that Brahmā was initiated there. (45)
Three thousand mantras, another three hundred thousand,
and eight hundred thousand are established within the ten maṇḍalas.
In the Niśvāsa, however, it is fully described where Nandīśa was initiated,
as were Śukra, Kubera, Varuṇa, Yama, and the two Aśvins.
The highly fortunate Gaṇas and the Rudras have indeed been initiated;
this was told to you, O beautiful one, in the supreme Niśvāsa Tantra.
One thousand [mantras] are to be known as fixed, comprising sixty;
likewise, there is another hundred by way of the enumeration of mantras. (49)
Furthermore, through eleven types of divisions and again through seven types, there is the *Saptavidyādhara-tantra* as well as the *Svāyaṃbhū*. (p. 830) || 50 ||
Two names have been proclaimed for that place where Dakṣa and the others were initiated— namely,
the lords of creatures (Prajāpatis) and those who are the sons of Brahmā.
The initiated and those bound by vows, as well as the Asuras constantly, the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Kinnaras; || 52 ||
The birds, beginning with Garuḍa, and those who dwell in the worlds—
there is one thousand of these mantras, arranged in thirty maṇḍalas.
But where the Āgneya [fire] has been consecrated, it is divided into five parts;
there, the Gātarodhas, the houses, and the hosts of obstacles and the like [are present].
In this Tantra, it is called Āgneya because it arises from fire;
its extent is eleven thousand and thirty million verses in total. (55)
There are indeed one hundred mandalas situated in eightfold enclosures;
through eighteen types of divisions, there are many groups of mantras in the world. (56)
It has been enumerated in many ways, preceded by the five embryos;
it has been spread forth by the perfect awakenings through the peaks that are the manifest causes.
And here, endowed with extraordinary power, are the sages known as the Balakhilyas, perfected ones whose wealth is their austerity, born from the Guhyakas and Guhyakas. 58.
By this very established doctrine, the gods who abide in the southern solstice as well as those in the northern, and indeed the gods such as Mānava and others, are perfected.
This tantra, which is to be accomplished by him, is known here as the *Vīrabhadra*;
it consists of eleven million [verses] and twenty mandalas of mantra. (60)
It is twofold by way of names and is renowned as Raurava;
it should be known as consisting of five hundred mantras, established in four forms.
It is known as Makuta by those who discourse on the field of Nidhana;
it is always frequented by sages who are like mothers within the Nala forest.
One hundred and one [forms] are to be known, and likewise divided into such types;
they are joined with eight mandalas, according to their respective names.
Endowed with ten maṇḍalas and ten thousand mantras, it is declared to have ten divisions; this is known as Candrabhāsa.
Containing fifty mantras established as a single hero,
it is the secret of the single maṇḍala, renowned as the Nārasiṃha. (65)
Where these initiated Daityas, the thorns of the gods, are present— Nalina, Maya, and indeed Nalinādya and the others.
The chapters on the field of rasa and the ritual actions should be understood according to their many divisions;
they are joined with twelve mantras and consist of two mandalas. (67)
O Goddess of the Gods, it is known as Mukhabimba when situated in two ways;
there are two hundred and two [units] of two thousand, and seventy-three maṇḍas.
It has seven branches and divisions, and its name is proclaimed as Prodgīta;
therein proceeds the supreme classification of mantras for yogins.
For the sake of accomplishing the practice of recitation and other rites by means of mantras possessing the power of the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra),
[this is] endowed with thirty-three [deities] and characterized by the activity of the power of Vidyā. (70)
[He performed] the Mahāvrata ritual and the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā), which arises from the well-refined sciences (vidyās) headed by the Mahāmahā and others. || 71 ||
Combined with the *Kapālottara-kalpas* and the *Siddhi-kalpas*, it is joined with the movement of the channels (*nāḍī*), and is the fifth [tantra], which is graceful and mobile. (72)
The accomplishment of command (*ājñāsiddhi*) should be understood as the mastery of a hundred mantras;
that which is called the "mandala" in ten ways is designated as "accomplished" (*siddha*). || 73 ||
There are three thousand and twenty mantras, as well as twenty maṇḍalas;
two koṭis of mantras have been proclaimed in hundreds.
(835) Endowed with the five mantras and worshipped as a single maṇḍala,
it should be known as the triple maṇḍala, as proclaimed by the secret deities. 75.
Two thousand, five hundred, and one hundred mantras, as well as one hundred mandalas, are remembered as being proclaimed by Śarva. (76)
Listen to the thousands of mantras and the twenty mandalas;
for in the Kiraṇa [Tantra] it is fully described where Āditya was initiated.
Where the Sun-god was initiated, that place is known as Koṭisapta;
likewise, there are ten million and one hundred thousand mantras known as Koṭisapta.
A compendium of a thousand mandalas has been proclaimed;
the various divisions of mantras and the various branches have also been enumerated according to their true nature. (79)
The mandalas of the mantras and those which are the supreme among all tantras—
these are remembered as proclaimed by Śiva, and many such tantric kalpas are recorded. (80)

And having previously seen the impermanence of all beings in these worlds—the gods, asuras, and humans; those known as mantra-adepts; as well as the gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and ṛṣis—(82)
All of them are indeed accomplished in mantra, and their lifespan is born of mantra;
all those practitioners are considered perfected through the recitation of mantra. || 83 ||
O Maheśvarī, this is the truth: liberation comes from realizing that reality;
this is the essence, this is the essence for one who desires to know everything. (84)
Even at the end of a thousand years, one may attain the conclusion of the scripture by diligently propitiating a guru and discerning that which consists of nothing more than the syllables. (85)
O Mahādeva, one should pray to a Guru who is proficient in the principles;
through his grace, there shall be liberation from the bonds of worldly existence. 86.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, "The Introduction to the Tantra," in the *Niśvāsakārikā*, specifically the *Dīkṣottara*.
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, filled with curiosity, I wish to hear something more."
O Lord of Gods, tell me the truth, if you would be a granter of boons to me.

Likewise, O Lord of Gods, this auspicious triad of channels— Bindu, Nāda, and Śakti— is the means for achieving the perfection of the upward departure (utkrānti) and the realization of the ultimate reality.
And the elevenfold [group] is entirely dependent upon the ninefold Self;
by it all this is to be accomplished, and by it all this is pervaded. (3)
And how is the *bindu* seen when joined with the syllables of the *kādi* [alphabet]? In which and which specific locations is the Lord *bindu* to be beheld? (4)

How is it that he is the very instrument by which that is seen in its true nature? Likewise, there is the manifestation of the resonance (nāda), the power (śakti), and the heart-center (hṛllakṣya). || 5 ||
"Tell me all this according to the proper method, out of your grace.
Īśvara said: "Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret, this most excellent mystery. (6)
Therefore, O Sovereign of All, I shall fully explain that which brings benefit to practitioners; listen to how this occurs through the ninefold [mantra]. (7)
O Goddess, the eightfold phonemes are fixed; it is called the pervasive point (bindu). Its crest is said to be the resonance (nāda), while Śakti stands as the supreme.
Furthermore, there is a supreme cause consisting of eleven categories;
it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru, just as it has been instructed by him.
I shall tell you in its entirety how one performs actions through the distinctions of the letters *a*, *u*, and likewise *m*.
The supreme, subtle knowledge of all is extremely difficult to attain;
it is primordial knowledge, beginningless and supremely imperishable. || 11 ||
Likewise, you shall attain the *bindu*, the *nāda*, the *śakti*, the subtle, the supreme, and the imperishable— that *nāda* and *bindu* which are difficult to find on this earth. (12)
I have not revealed this to anyone; I shall tell it to you, O lady of excellent vows:
Maheśvara, the God of gods, is said to reside between the eyebrows.
Resembling pure crystal, it illuminates all principles;
though devoid of the principles perceived by the senses, it illuminates those very principles.
And then that splendor is seen blazing with its own radiance;
those two, the moon and the sun, are declared to be his two lamps. (15)
The state known as *ceta* remains constant, manifesting continuously;
*iḍā* is seen on the left, while *suṣumnā* is on the right.
Between those two is the supreme station where the *bindu* is situated;
just as a lamp within a jar illuminates that very jar. (17)
But for one devoid of instruction, the supreme reality is not perceived;
just as a reflection is not seen in a mirror seized by impurities. (18)
In the same way, the direct perception of one devoid of yoga is not seen;
therefore, the wise man, placing both [hands] upon the vessel, should remain steady.
Through the application of instruction, the Lord Bindu is perceived;
one should cover both the nose, the ears, and likewise the eyes. 20.
Having established the six gates, one beholds the Bindu, the Lord;
through the act of veiling, the Bindu, pure and stainless as crystal, is abandoned.
One should meditate upon the supreme Śiva as the stainless moon, that Bindu endowed with splendor, which is utterly free from sound and resonance (nāda). (22)
Having caused the mind to dissolve into the *bindu*, one should meditate while well-restrained by the *bindu*, just as the all-pervading wind, though residing within a vessel, is not perceived. (23)
Thus, the all-pervading bindu is not perceived when devoid of yoga;
it is like fire residing in the fire-drill, which, though present, is not seen. || 24 ||
Likewise, O beautiful one, the *bindu* is not seen when devoid of yoga;
however, through union, the *bindu* is then perceived directly. (25)
Just as clarified butter, though present in milk, is not seen because it is unmanifest, so too the Bindu, though omnipresent, is not seen by one devoid of yoga. (26)
Just as clarified butter and fire are obtained through application, O beautiful one, so too is the *bindu* attained by great-souled yogins. (27)
Just as a water-crystal gem, even when cast into a great lake, illuminates that water with its own playful radiance, so too does it manifest its nature. (28)
Just as a gem submerged in water is revealed when it is drawn out, so too the *bindu* is not perceived by one who is devoid of yoga. (29)
From meditation that drop is born; through union it is seen again.
Having fully described meditation and yoga, one beholds the Lord as the Drop.
For yogins, the drop (bindu) is the means of realization; through that means, the Supreme is attained. Beyond the Supreme there is nothing else; it is eternally united and ever-present. || 31 ||
O beautiful one, attainment occurs through the cause and indeed through practice;
this secret has been told, and it should always be known by yogins. (32)
Having seen the blazing drop situated in the middle of the eye, O Goddess, one should always know that the crest-lock (śikhā) is located right in its center. (33)
That supreme, subtle [reality] is seen, possessing a radiance equal to ten million points of light;
the yogi, being well-composed, should constantly perceive his absorption in that. || 34 ||
Listen attentively, O Goddess, to the Sound and the Bindu which are difficult to attain;
O Mistress of the Gods, those nine principles which were mentioned in the context of the Ninefold Self.
Among them, seven seed-syllables beginning with the letter *ya* are concentrated;
joined with the initial syllable *hūṃ*, these seven are difficult to find on earth. (36)
Joined with the syllable *phaṭ*, these are renowned for causing immediate agitation;
when applied as a single unit, they effect instantaneous transference. (37)

And the sixth, which is the supreme seed-syllable situated at the end of the group [of consonants], when contemplated through its upward progression (utkrama) in conjunction with the form of the syllable *hā*, [is the means of liberation]. 38.
Thus, the other five seed-syllables have been briefly explained: they range from the letter *a* to the letter *m*, joined with the letters *ma* and *u*. (39)
O beautiful one, these have been described to you as those that cause immediate departure [of the soul];
these seven are known as the *kṣurikās* (dagger-mantras) that take away life.
One should recite it one hundred thousand times; of this there is no doubt. O Goddess, I speak the truth: that which is declared as the seven is called the eight *oṃkāras*.
Endowed with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, the Lord can cause [the soul] to depart immediately.
The syllable *oṃ* belongs to all deities; it is the all-pervading Supreme Śiva. (42)
It consists of three syllables, pertains to three deities, and likewise possesses more than three measures (mātrās). Therein arises Śambhu, who is beyond sound and partless (niṣkala).
The God is subtler than the subtlest, the liberator from all bonds;
abiding in various paths, all-pervading, he is difficult for the entire world to attain. || 44 ||
There are three locations in this body where the Nāda is established:
in the heart, in the ears, and likewise in the middle of the eyebrows.
Where there is a subtle thread-like form with the luster of pure crystal, it is called the "Fourth Door" (turyadvāra) and is known as the "Path of the Gods" (devayāna). || 46 ||
The three paths are thus proclaimed; they are remembered as the three channels (nāḍīs).
Furthermore, the triad of deities is remembered as the triad of powers (śaktis). || 47 ||
O Supreme Goddess, these are known as the three fruits within this body;
all-pervading and omnipresent, it remains filling everything.
The syllable *A* is situated in the center of the heart, abiding as the state of wakefulness;
there, within the pericarp of the lotus, Brahmā is established.
The syllable *u* is said to reside in the ear; that is called the station of Brahman.
That which is known as the palate and the tongue is declared to be the second station. (50)
In the midst of the eye of the letter 'A', the state of deep sleep (suṣupta) is said to be;
O beautiful one, that station has been described to you as belonging to whom? 51.
Established in the state of the fourth Brahman within that word consisting of half a mora,
his supreme and subtle station at the crown of the head bestows the path to liberation. (52)
O Goddess, that which transcends the fourth state is supreme, an exceedingly subtle and imperishable station;
by knowing it, a living being is liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra. (53)
That which is beyond the fourth state (turyātīta) is thus proclaimed; having gone there, one does not grieve.
In this way, all this—the entire realm of speech, including the moving and the unmoving—is pervaded by it.
Within the center of these sounds, Śiva is established;
within the body, at the heart, a lotus is established. (55)
In the center of the lotus of the pericarp is the letter *A*;
from the very middle of that, there emerges the Nāda, which is most difficult to attain.
Having split the letter *u* and the letter *ma*, the *nāda* has emerged;
one should contemplate it as having issued forth from the door of the fourth state (*turya*), at the end of the pair.
Arising from the syllable *A* and emerging through the gate of Brahmā,
this sound is declared to be the bestower of the path to liberation.
This supreme, divine meditation should be practiced with diligent effort;
for what is the use of any other meditation or even of fierce austerity? (59)
What is the use of visiting sacred fords or even of abundant meditations,
when one does not know the true nature of Nāda and the beautiful Bindudeva?
If that single, subtle sound, which is both supreme and non-supreme, is known as one,
then the body is like a lamp, and it is like Śivā in the sky.
Just as the pervasive ether, though dissolved, is not perceived,
such is the determination of the reality of Nāda, which is exceedingly subtle. (62)
This sound is declared to be the most excellent in all tantras;
the central channel is proclaimed to possess the brilliance of a thousand sunbeams. (63)
O beautiful one, that channel (nāḍī) is conjoined with all the principles (tatvas) and united with Śakti; it is the [source] of all sounds and indeed of all principles.
Having gathered [the elements] together as a whole, one dissolves into the principle of Śiva;
having known that which is both subtle and all-pervading, the knower is liberated.
Having abandoned both the sun and the moon, he becomes all-pervading Śiva.
Within the center of the solar disc, however, the letter *a* is established. (67)
And there a sound arises within the lunar orb;
Viṣṇu himself emerges,
renowned as the syllable "Ma," and having pierced through, the resonance (nāda) remains in dissolution.
Having entered the path of Piṅgalā, which is renowned as the door of the Fourth (turya),
the knower of yoga should meditate upon the supreme sound through the door of the Fourth by means of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*).
But its dissolution occurs in that Lord of Gods, where this Supreme Śiva resides.
That very partless reality (niṣkala-tattva) is contemplated by those who discourse on liberation.
The Goddess said:
O Maheśvara, for the maṇḍalas, the deities, and the principles (tattvas), as well as for yogins, the supreme heart-aim (hṛllakṣa) is to be known in that very same way. 73.
In that [state], accomplishment proceeds and one experiences yoga...?
The Lord said: The Self is proclaimed as ninefold, through the division into "with seed" (sabīja) and "seedless" (nirbīja).
Through the division of gradual decrease, she bestows the fruits of various accomplishments.
One should know the supreme six-syllable [mantra], the auspicious supreme five-syllable [mantra],
and the four-syllable [mantra]... || 76 ||
O Parameśvarī, he alone is said to be the perfect Śiva.
Those which are each reduced by one [vowel], yet joined with the *bindu* and the letter *u*, are taught as the Heart-mantra and the others; they should be known thus, O fair-faced one. (78)
O Goddess, the vision of the heart-center arises very soon indeed.
O Goddess, I shall tell you this other supreme [teaching], as well as the [other] two in that very same way. || 80 ||
O lady of excellent hips, meditating upon the letter *ya* joined with the letter *u*, devoid of the three phonemes, one is awakened by the lamp of the seed-syllable. (81)
Within seven nights, O Supreme Goddess, one shall see the heart-center;
one sees the marks of Viṣṇu,
as well as others that are black, white, and red in color.
On the seventh day, one should withdraw [the mind] from the heart-lotus illuminated by one's own [inner light];
for the heart-lotus blazes with the excellent lamp of one's own self.
O Goddess, the heart, ignited by its own light, blazes like a flame.
Thus, that which is renowned as the "Heart-Lakṣa" should always be known by yogins;
above the navel is the *vitantuka*... [etc.]
In the center of the lotus of the pericarp, right in its middle, the Lord Bindu blazes like the upward-pointing flame of a lamp. (87)
The heart-mantra of six syllables has been obtained; it is a seed that is most difficult to attain, just as [the state of] a poet is. 88.
In this same way, others who have been mentioned should also be understood by those seeking their own welfare.
This great knowledge, the most excellent among all knowledges, has been explained to you. (89)
This is that supreme [state] which attains oneness with gold; there is no doubt in this matter. || 90 ||
O Goddess, through the accomplishment of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*), the bound soul (*paśu*) likewise attains the supreme state;
he reaches oneness with Śiva. || 91 ||
One should fast for ten days at most; one sees [the result] here, there is no doubt.
This divine [teaching], characterized by one hundred thousand [verses], should be diligently cultivated for your welfare, O beautiful one. 93.
O Goddess of the Gods, having prepared the seat endowed with the nine powers and possessed of both dharma and jñāna, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) there.
O Goddess, one should worship the entire [deity] together with the five Brahmans;
Maheśvara is to be worshipped with this single enclosure alone. 95.
The deity who grants all accomplishments is to be worshipped day by day;
having thus worshipped him according to the rule, the practitioner of the ritual application should recite [the mantra] and meditate. (96)
O Goddess of the gods, by means of ten lakhs [of recitations], whatever is desired by the mind, that the practitioner obtains without effort; there is no doubt in this matter. || 97 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, concerning the yoga of Bindu and Nāda, in the Dīkṣottara of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the ritual worship in its proper sequence."
By the mere knowledge of which, success is achieved; there is no doubt in this matter.
Īśvara:
Beginning with Prakṛti and ending with the Śiva-tattva as the last.
But those principles which are at the beginning and in the middle, I shall explain in their proper order. || 2 ||
One should first draw a lotus with filaments and a pericarp;
O fair-faced one, within that, one should perform the entire rite without exception.
One should place the deities of the maṇḍala, endowed with the three truths (tritatva),
in the center, together with the primordial nature (prakṛti) and joined with the [divine] form (mūrti).
Perform the invocation of Śiva by means of the principles (tattvas) that have been made manifest through the sakalīkaraṇa rite:
Ananta is his heart, and that which is of the nature of space (vyoma) is remembered as his head.
The pervasive [syllable] is declared to be the *śikhā*, while the leaderless is remembered as the *kavaca*. That which is not seated is the *astra*; these are proclaimed as the limbs of Śiva. (6)
The letter *ma* is declared to be the heart; the letter *u* is remembered as the head;
the letter *ī*, O Goddess, is Śivā; and they know the letter *ā* to be the armor.
The syllable *Aṃ* is said to be the weapon (*astra*); this has indeed been explained in due order.
Brahmā is the presiding deity of the weapon, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the armor (*kavaca*).
But you alone, O Goddess of the gods, are proclaimed as Śivā.
One should know Śiva as the ninefold self; all [these] have been proclaimed everywhere.
Having placed Puruṣa in the east, one should assign Niyati in the southeast.
Kāla is on the southern petal, while Māyā is indeed in the direction of Nairṛta;
Vidyā is said to be in the west, and Īśvara in the region of Vāyu. (11)
One should place Sadāśiva, the supreme principle (tattva), in the north;
one should likewise designate Śivatattva, the supremely pure, in the northeast.
O Goddess, this sacrifice of yours has been proclaimed as belonging to Prakṛti; having placed one's own true self in the center, one should perform the worship day by day.
In this manner, O Goddess, one should sacrifice to the principles beginning with Prakṛti and ending with Śiva;
those who are said to be the limbs of Śiva are established within the pericarp.
The wise should always and at all times fashion armlets with abundant ends;
this indeed is the rule, O Goddess, for the principles beginning with Prakṛti and ending with Śiva. (15)
Having thus understood this procedure once, one shall not be subject to birth again;
likewise in rising, in invisibility, and in walking on foot. (16)
Likewise, [the rites for] the sword, the sandals, the collyrium,
the emetic, the pill, the power of traveling through the sky, the tooth-stick, and the purifying thread.
In matters of inciting enmity, attracting others, as well as for rites of pacification and nourishment, a person obtains all that which was previously declared in the preceding sūtra. || 18 ||
The practitioner of mantra should recite each one with this mantra.
Listen again, O Goddess of gods; I shall now describe the ritual worship to you. (19)
Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), O Goddess of Gods, one should meditate upon Śiva as the partless (*niṣkala*) [reality], free from long-lasting veils.
Prompted by your request in the previous sūtra, I shall now describe to you the limbs of Śiva:
O Goddess, the Heart is the Sakala (with parts), and the Head is remembered as being enriched with the Sakala. (21)
*Kham* is declared to be the *śikhā*, and *kṣapaṇa* likewise the *kavaca*;
*kṣayānta* is said to be the *astra*. Thus are the limbs of Śiva proclaimed. (22)
But by means of that very emptiness, O Goddess of Gods, one should contemplate that reality;
those which were mentioned in the previous sūtra are to be known as the limbs of the Vidyā. (23)
Having placed the heart-mantra in the center, one should place the head-mantra on the eastern petal;
one should assign the crest-mantra to the south, and the armor-mantra to the west.
Having spoken thus, one should deposit the weapon-mantra in the north according to the sequence;
O Goddess, one should assign the heart, which is a limb of the Vidyā, to the southeast.
One should place the head in the northeast; in this sequential order,
one should arrange the principles of the mantra (mantratattvas) in the second enclosure.
O Goddess, one should first install [the deities] in due order according to the initial sequence; this is now being told to you regarding the worship of the principles (tattvas).
One should worship that [deity] in due order according to the divisions beginning with Prakṛti;
having thus worshipped the Tattvas, one should likewise mutter the Navātman mantra.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each [deity], and one shall attain all accomplishments;
it brings to fulfillment everything that the practitioner has conceived in the mind. (29)
However, that which is proclaimed by the Sūtra itself shall yield the fruit of accomplishment;
for this worship is declared to be a double enclosure.

Furthermore, O woman of excellent complexion, I shall describe the sacrifice of the principles (tattvas). Having worshipped the principles with three enclosures (āvaraṇas), one shall attain perfection. (31)
O beautiful goddess, this inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) must indeed be constructed, joined with the five Brahmās and endowed with the limbs of Śiva.
The second [should be performed] with the principles (tattvas), and the third with the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅgas).
Thus, O Goddess, having worshipped the groups of principles, one shall attain perfection.
She should be worshipped with the fourfold enclosure itself;
by worshipping her, the mantra is perfected and one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. || 34 ||
The principles have indeed been accomplished through action, mind, and speech;
there is no sacrifice equal to this to be found in the three worlds. (35)
For the benefit of practitioners, I have told you all of this in its entirety.
One should fashion this womb [of the mandala] by means of the five Brahmās and the limbs of Śiva. (36)
One should place those who are limbs of Śiva, beginning with Sakala, in the second enclosure;
these are the limbs that were previously mentioned in the ninefold [mandala] in the preceding sūtra.
In the third enclosure, those [deities] should be worshipped by those who are well-concentrated, according to the ninefold divisions of the Self which have been proclaimed by me. (38)
Those [deities] within the four enclosures should be worshipped by the most excellent practitioners;
having worshipped them in this manner, the mantra-reciter should then commence the yoga of recitation (japa). || 39 ||
This has been told to you, O Goddess, by means of the fourfold enclosure;
having understood and remembered it, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth. (40)
I shall speak further; listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess.
That which has not been told to anyone, I shall relate to you in its entirety. (41)
Whether brought near by the proximity of the riverbank or dismissed by being sent away, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth merely by the act of ritual placement (nyāsa). 42.
O Supreme Goddess, having performed the previously mentioned rite, the practitioner,
as a reciter of mantras, should place the supreme syllable there in the pericarp.
One should perform the placement (vinyāsa) starting from the east and proceeding in sequence through Sakala and the others;
thus has this yoga of the Supreme Syllable (Paramākṣara) been described to you.
One should place the entire [mantra] upon the pericarp in the eastern direction; furthermore, O Goddess, one should place the supreme syllable upon the eastern petal.
In the southeast is Niṣkala; there, in the south, is Śūnyatattva;
in the southwest is Kalāḍhya; and likewise in the west is Khamala. (46)
The practitioner of mantras should place Kṣapaṇa in the region of Vāyu, Kṣayānta in the north, and Kaṇṭha and Oṣṭha in the northeast, O Supreme Goddess.
The entire lotus-seat has thus been described in due order;
one should then place the partless (niṣkala) form there in the southeast, within the pericarp.
On the eastern petal, however, is the entire [syllable] of Agni; the principle of emptiness (śūnyatattva), enriched with its digits (kalā), is in the south and in the southwest.
In the west, *khamalam* is proclaimed; in the domain of the wind (*vāyu*), *kṣapaṇam*;
at the end of destruction (*kṣaya*), in the north itself; and *kaṇṭhoṣṭham* in the domain of night.
One should visualize the partless lotus-seat in the southeast;
then, one should place the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatattva*) upon the pericarp in the south. (51)
One should place the *samala* on the eastern petal, and the *niṣkala* in the southeast;
O Goddess, it is taught that one should place the *paramākṣara* on the southern [petal].
One should place *kaṇṭhoṣṭhya* in the southwest (*nair-ṛta*) and *khamala* in the west;
it is taught that one should place *kṣapaṇa* in the region of the wind (*vāyu*). 53.
The lotus seat of Śūnya has indeed been described in due order;
one should place Kalāḍhya upon the pericarp in the auspicious south-western direction.
On the eastern petal, however, one should place the Sakala [form], and the Niṣkala in the southeast; having placed the Śūnya in the south, one should place the Paramākṣara in the southwest.
In the west, Khamala is proclaimed; in the southeast, Kṣapaṇa is remembered.
At the end of destruction (Kṣayānta) is in the north alone, while Kaṇṭha and Oṣṭha are in the domain of Īśa (the northeast).
The fourth has been fully explained; now hear the fifth.
In the western [petal], within the pericarp (karṇikā), Kha-ma-la is proclaimed.
On the eastern petal, however, the Sakala is located; the Niṣkala is remembered in the southeast. On the southern [petal] is the Śūnyatattva, while Kalāḍhya is in the southwest.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the Supreme Imperishable (Paramākṣara) in the west;
likewise, Kṣapaṇa in the northwest and that which ends with Kṣaya in the north.
The fifth [deity] was told to you as being at the region of the throat and lips;
Kṣapaṇa is proclaimed to be in the northwest of the pericarp.
One should place the *sakala* [form] on the eastern petal, while the *niṣkala* should be placed in the southeast;
the *śūnya* in the south, and the *kalāḍhya* in the southwest. (61)
Kha-ma-laṃ is in the west; Paramākṣara is in the northwest;
Kṣayānta is in the north; and Kaṇṭhoṣṭhya is in the domain of Īśa (the northeast).
This sixth seat (pīṭha) has been fully described; it is proclaimed as yours.
One should deposit the principles (tattvas) ending with Kṣaya upon the pericarp-seat (karṇikā-pīṭha) in the north.
O Goddess, the Sakala is in the east, while the supreme Niṣkala is in the southeast;
the Śūnya is said to be in the south, and the Kalāḍhya is in the southwest.
In the west, one should place *kha* and *la*, and in the northwest, *kṣapaṇa* is prescribed;
O Goddess of gods, one should install *paramākṣara* in the north.
One should contemplate the supreme reality consisting of the throat and lips in the northeast;
this seventh reality has been fully explained to you, O Goddess worshipped by those who delight in bliss. (66)
In the northeast, upon the pericarp-seat, one should arrange the labio-dental [phonemes];
on the eastern petal, however, is the *sakala* (with parts), and in the southeast is the supreme *niṣkala* (without parts).
The letter Śū (śūnya) is on the southern petal, while Kalāḍhya is in the southwest;
Khamala is in the west, and Kṣapaṇa is in the domain of the wind (the northwest).
At the end of Kṣaya is Uttara, and in the northeast is Paramākṣara;
this eighth Pīṭha has been described to you, which is most difficult to attain.
The sacrifice consisting of nine parts is remembered as the most excellent among all sacrifices;
this sacrifice, which is very difficult to obtain, has not been revealed by me to anyone.
Having achieved his purpose through this sacrifice and having severed all doubt,
he— purified and free from the fever of affliction— attains union with Śiva. (71)
The disciple to be purified should be cleansed with ten oblations for each [syllable], or with one hundred and twenty-five;
the preceptor should perform the initiation with exactly five percent of a hundred [oblations].
Having performed the illumination of the three powers (triśakti) during rites for pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), and libation (tarpaṇa),
the preeminent teacher (deśikendra) should carry out the fire-offering (homa) rite according to the proper sequence.
One should perform the ritual in detail, without practicing stinginess regarding wealth;
one should commence the sacrifice according to the inclination of one's own mind. (74)
O beautiful one, I have explained to you the division into eighty-one parts, which is common to all compendiums and supreme among all tantras.
Joined with the instruments in the sequence beginning with earth,
one should always worship with a single enclosure alone, remaining concentrated. (76)
O lady of excellent vows, the nature of time should be understood along with its true essence;
thus have the sacrifices been described in their proper sequence. (77)
In this way, O Goddess, the practitioner, being composed in meditation, unites with it;
by him, the entire earth, together with its kingdoms and oceans, is joined. (78)
O lady of beautiful hips, by him a sacrifice has been performed; there is no doubt about this.
He is eternally a man of knowledge on this earth, and that practitioner shall lead [others] to Śiva. (79)
By this, as soon as they have been initiated, the bound souls (paśus) proceed face-to-face toward Śiva;
there is no doubt in this matter, for their bonds have been severed by knowledge.
Sadāśiva, Śiva, as well as Nāda and Śakti—
these four, O fair-faced one, are indeed the great sacrifices that are not to be spoken of. (81)
Therefore, I shall explain that; listen with a one-pointed mind.
On a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or even in a mandala, [one should contemplate] air and space itself. 82.
O Goddess of the gods, one should commence the sacrifice and oblation in the fire within the waters, by means of the mind, the eye, and speech; of this there is no doubt. (83)
Through the yoga of action, dhāraṇā shall liberate one; there is no doubt in this.
From these [elements] everything proceeds, and all this is remembered as being within them. 84.
O auspicious one, from these [mantras] both spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti) are obtained when requested;
O Maheśvarī, one should perform the previously mentioned rite within the pericarp (karṇikā).
Having placed the image right there, one should then perform the ritual of Sakalīkaraṇa,
endowed with the five Brahma-kalas and the limbs of Śiva. (86)
One should perform the ritual in its entirety, joined with the invocation and the conclusion, endowed with meditative concentration and yoga, and accompanied by the five Brahmans.
Endowed with the four enclosures, one should worship with a well-concentrated mind;
one should place Īśāna in the center and install Tatpuruṣa in the east.
O Goddess of gods, one should place Aghora in the south, Vāmadeva in the north,
and Sadyojāta in the west.
Having placed the heart-mantra in the southeast, the head in the domain of Īśāna, the crest-lock (śikhā) in the southwest, O Goddess, one should place the armor (kavaca) in the northwest. (90)
O beautiful one, this indeed has been described to you as the enclosure of the womb (garbhāvaraṇa). O Goddess, listen as I describe the second enclosure. (91)
Having placed Ghoṣa in the east, one should place Rāva in the direction of Agni (the southeast);
having placed Svana in the south, one should place Śabda in the direction of Nairṛta (the southwest).
One should offer the *sphoṭa* sound to the west, the word *dhvani* to the northwest;
the *jhaṅkāra* sound to the north, and the *dhvaṅkṛta* sound in the domain of Īśa (the northeast).
One should place the ninth, which is the Great Sound (Mahacchabda), in the center upon the pericarp;
these are remembered as beginning with the letter *u*, and they are the designators of the voiced sounds (*ghoṣa*) and so forth.
O Goddess, listen as I describe the third enclosure:
one should place the *sakala* [form] on the eastern face and the *niṣkala* [form] in the southeast.
One should place *śūnya* on the south; one should set *kalāḍhya* in the southwest (*naiṛta*).
One should place *khamala* on the west, and *kṣapaṇa* in the domain of the wind (*vāyugocara*). (96)
One should place *kṣayānta* in the north and *kaṇṭhoṣṭha* in the domain of Īśa;
O Goddess of the gods, one should place *paramākṣara* in the middle region.
The third enclosure, O beautiful goddess, has been described to you;
now, O goddess, one should arrange the fourth enclosure up to the end of Prakṛti.
One should first install [the deities] in the initial sequence according to the proper order.
O Goddess, this supreme sacrifice has indeed been described to you in its successive stages. 99.
Indeed, this entire secret has been concealed for the benefit of practitioners;
it bestows both spiritual accomplishments and liberation, and there shall be nothing equal to it.
O Goddess, listen as I speak; there are four Nindās and four Kalās.
One should visualize the Heart-mantra, which transcends peace (Śāntyatīta), in the southeast. (101)
Furthermore, the nine principles beginning with Sakala follow in due order;
this, O beautiful one, is the Sādāśiva Yoga that has been described to you.
I shall now proclaim the very nature of Nāda; listen to me as it is being told:
Iḍikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and likewise Mocikā. (103)
The womb-enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa), which is connected to the upward-moving [channel], is situated;
O Goddess of gods, one should place it in the upward-moving direction within the domain of Agni.
One should place Recikā in the direction of the Mocikeśāna [corner] on the petal in the southwest,
and one should arrange Dīpikā, O highly fortunate lady, in the northwest.
The syllable *huṃ* is its heart; the syllable *huṃ* is known as the head. The syllable *huṃ* is declared to be the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the syllable *haiṃ* shall be the armor (*kavaca*).
The syllable *haḥ* is said to be the weapon-mantra; one should place it in the four directions.
O beautiful goddess, this is indeed declared to be the inner enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*).
O Goddess of the gods, one should perform the remainder according to the sequence as before.
I shall now declare its most secret [practice], the unsurpassed Śaktiyāga.
From this the yoga is completed; from this everything proceeds.
Mortals who perform initiation and bestow grace have not been described by him [in this]. (109)
One who lacks power does not achieve success, nor does he attain the supreme state;
therefore, there is no initiation by means of the "Nākhyena" [method] for one who is superior and most excellent.
There is neither a mandala of dust nor the ritual of taking possession;
furthermore, the consecration (adhivāsana) is entirely devoid of all remaining [rituals]. || 111 ||
This has been fully explained for the benefit of practitioners;
it is common to all the Saṃhitās, great, and facing in every direction.
Devoid of invocation, the bringing near, the presence, and the dismissal, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth by mere placement [of the mantra]. (113)
The practitioner of mantra should draw a four-faced lotus, radiant with filaments and a pericarp;
he should prepare a seat there and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having worshipped Maheśvara, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rite, together with Śiva joined by the five Brahmās as his limbs, || 115 ||
One should place Īśāna in the center, and install Tatpuruṣa in the east;
likewise, Aghora in the south and Vāmadeva in the north. (116)
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the Sadyojāta mantra in the west; one should place the Heart in the southeast and the Head in the northeast. (117)
O Goddess, one should place the *śikhā* in the southwest and the *kavaca* in the northwest;
having assigned the *astra* to the cardinal directions, those [syllables] beginning with the letter *ma* are prescribed.
O Maheśvarī, one should place the supreme syllable in the center of the pericarp;
and on the southern pedestal of the pericarp, one should place the Navātman mantra.
O beautiful goddess, one should place its limbs of knowledge—the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, and the weapon—in their proper sequence. (120)
One should place Prakṛti on the southern petal, Puruṣa on the south-western;
one should assign Niyati to the western [petal] and Kalā to the north-western. (121)
To the north of the principle of Māyā is indeed Vidyā;
Īśvara is the preceding principle, while Sadāśiva is in the southeast.
In the west, in the center of the pericarp, one should place the Śāntyatīta;
in the southeast, the Heart, and in the northeast, one should place the Head.
O Goddess, one should assign the *śikhā* mantra in the southwest, the *kavaca* in the northwest,
and the *praṇava* upon the pericarp in the north.
The Heart is said to be Śāntyatīta, and Peace (Śānti) is called the Head;
Knowledge (Vidyā) is declared to be the Topknot (Śikhā), and they know Establishment (Pratiṣṭhā) as the Armor (Kavaca).
Cessation is said to be the weapon; these are proclaimed as the limbs of the crest-lock (śikhā).
Ghoṣa is in the eastern quarter, and Rava is in the south-eastern quarter. (126)
In the south, however, Svana is proclaimed; one should place Śabda in the domain of Nairṛta;
Sphoṭa is remembered in the west; and Dhvani should be placed in the north-west.
With a humming sound (*jhaṅkāra*) to the north and a shrieking sound (*dhvaṃkṛta*) within the domain of Śiva, one should place Rudra and the syllable *oṃ* in the center of the pericarp to the east.
One should place the heart in the southeast and the head in the northeast;
the crest-lock (śikhā) is said to be in the southwest, and likewise the armor (kavaca) in the northwest.
One should indeed project the short [syllable] into the region of the hand at the tip of the weapon;
one should place Peace (Śānti) in the eastern quarter and Knowledge (Vidyā) to the south.
Pratiṣṭhā is indeed by the north, while Nivṛtti is by the west;
Śāntyatīta is the supreme reality (tattva), proclaimed as the Astra-mantra of the Lord. (131)
Sūkṣmā is in the direction of the subtle wind, while Susūkṣmā is in the south-west;
Amṛtā is said to be in the direction of fire, O beautiful one who art radiant with reality. (132)
O fair-faced one, Amṛtā and Mṛtā are said to be in the northeast;
O Goddess, this is the supreme sacrifice, and there is nothing more nectar-like than it that has been taught by me. (133)
"She is my beloved, she is my devotee"—thus has she been described to you by me.
Having performed the sacrifice according to this rule, the wise man should then undergo initiation.
Having offered oblations with one hundred and twenty-five, fifty,
or ten [repetitions] into the five fires, the initiation leads to final liberation.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Section on Sacrifice, in the *Dīkṣottara* of the *Niśvāsakārikā*. (p.
885) The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the unsurpassed ritual for initiation,
as well as the teaching and the reception of mantras that are devoid of ritual procedures.
O Mahādeva, for what purpose was that boon granted, O Maheśvara?
And where, O Śaṅkara, is there a severance of those pure principles?
Tell me that very [reality] which is both with parts and without parts, as well as with-and-without-parts; tell me that which consists of the three principles and the supreme principle.

Please graciously explain the practices for the study of mantras, as well as the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), and whatever other rites there may be that are most conducive to spiritual welfare. (4)
O God, there is yet another most profound secret which has not been spoken nor even suggested;
please, out of your grace, tell us all of that within this [teaching]. (5)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess; I shall tell you everything that is the supreme secret.
It is more secret than the secret, O Goddess, and has never been told by me to anyone.
The procedure for the Sūtras and Mantras is correctly presented in their proper sequence,
beginning with Ananta and ending with the Śiva-tattva.
I shall describe in brief the extent of the path of enumeration:
below [this] is the Supreme Lord, Ananta, the Sovereign Lord.
Having offered that oblation, O Goddess of the gods, one should proceed to Kālāgni.
Your Śrotā is said to be in the south; its worlds are remembered as yours. (9)
In due order, all those [sins] were suddenly declared by the authorities to be above him [the sinner], along with hells of terrible form. || 10 ||
O Goddess of the gods, O Supreme Sovereign, one should purify all of them in sequence: one hundred and likewise forty.
But above, O Goddess of gods, there are indeed seven netherworlds (pātālas);
these, O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent complexion, must be purified in due order.
The worlds, those dependent on the worlds, and those dwelling within the worlds have thus been described in brief, in their sequence, as twenty-one.
(888) But above [the netherworlds], O Goddess, I shall first describe Bhūrloka;
it stands, in brief, at a distance of three guṇas from Pātāla. || 14 ||
The divine wombs are eightfold, those beginning with the animal realm are fivefold, and the human state is singlefold; thus should the mandala of saṃsāra be known. 15.
O Goddess, one should lift up [the lineage] starting from Brahmā as far back as the primordial Brahmā;
thus, O beautiful one, the wheel of saṃsāra has been described to you. 16.

Beginning with the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), as well as the vows dedicated to the gods (devavratas), the oblation sacrifices (haviḥ-yajñas), the cooked-food sacrifices (pākayajñas), and likewise those numbered among the Soma sacrifices; || 17 ||
Furthermore, the forty-eight formative factors (saṃskāra) should be known by the teacher in their proper sequence. || 18 ||
Having offered these oblations, the mantra-practitioner should then install the thousand sacrifices;
having attained the state and abandoned [the body], the funeral rites follow immediately thereafter.
Then, having performed the funeral rites and offered the oblations, one should elevate [the soul] and apply it;
having joined it to the stations of enjoyment, one should then separate it from that enjoyment.
Having separated them from those enjoyments while they are still joined with the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka),
one should then place them in the Bhūrloka and lead them from there to the Bhuvarloka.
In this very sequence, one should likewise join [the breath] in Brahmā’s seat,
then in Rudra’s seat, and then in the seat of the True One (Saddhi) by means of the staff-like process (daṇḍakrama).
O Goddess, having meditated upon the Pāśupata weapon, which is supremely invincible,
one should offer seven oblations with it for the sake of purification.
Having joined [the mantra] with the Śatarudra in the hundredfold place according to the sequence,
the earth is thus purified and the Śatarudra is joined. (24)
O beautiful one, beginning from Ananta down to the netherworld known as Hema,
one hundred and fifty-nine [levels] have been described to you.
Having gratified the worlds, the lords of the worlds, and those dwelling within the worlds, the wise man, having performed [the rites], proceeds through each principle (tattva) in due order.
Oṃ, salutation to Bhuvana. Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of Bhuvana. Oṃ, salutation to those dwelling within Bhuvana.
The preceptor must then perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the array of Bhuvana.
One should offer oblations with the *śikhā* mantra for those who dwell within the worlds. || 27 ||
p.
891) Thus, O Goddess, that purification of the enclosure of the earthen [mandala] was performed by the high-souled teacher in the proper sequence, beginning with Ananta. (28)
I shall describe them in brief, O fair-faced one: two hundred and sixty-nine worlds have been enumerated. (29)
The identity with Kūṣmāṇḍa has thus been briefly explained;
furthermore, the five groups of eight [deities] are to be purified again in five ways, according to the sequence of the coverings (āvaraṇas).
By whichever [method], the group of eight and beyond that, namely the eightfold yoga and the eight wrathful ones, should be known by the high-souled teacher. (31)
O Goddess, one should purify those very [elements]; thereafter, the eightfold light (tejoṣṭaka). When the eightfold light has been thoroughly purified, then again the twelvefold Śiva.
The group of eight Mahādevas and likewise Vīrabhadra,
as well as the Lord of the Maṇḍala— these have been described to you, O beautiful one. (32)
Having purified these according to the prescribed method, one should subsequently offer oblations for the primary principle;
the three qualities (guṇas) and the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) are to be purified in their proper order.

And by means of the intellect (buddhi), up to the limit of the principle of reality (tattva), the eightfold group of Krodha and Tejas within that [Pradhāna] must be purified by the yogis together with the Śivas. (34)
O Goddess, the three rows of gurus are joined with Vīrabhadra, the lord of the mandala, and likewise separated by the guru.
The state of equilibrium of the *guṇas* is declared to be that *pradhāna*;
this has been described as *pradhāna* and exists in great detail. (36)
O fair-faced one, it should be understood that this has been told in brief;
previously, the three forms of the principles were fully described by me. (37)
Having recognized those Rudras in that form by means of the object to be purified, O virtuous one, beginning with Ananta and ending with Pradhāna; 38.
Four hundred and forty-four have been declared; beyond this, I shall describe the Puruṣa to you. (39)
By the mere knowledge of which they are liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Regarding the purification of Ambha and the others therein, it proceeds according to sequence through the human [state]. (40)
O Maṇimātaramambhā, I shall describe to you in brief;
dharma is said to be tenfold, O Goddess, of this there is no doubt. (41)
The sixteen transformations have been declared; the intellect (buddhi) is remembered as being eightfold.
The ego (ahaṃkāra), however, is threefold, and the triad of qualities (guṇatraya) has been illustrated.
Know that the vital breath (prāṇa) is fivefold and likewise the eightfold knowledge;
these, conjoined with the eightfold body, must be purified with great effort.
Lust, anger, and greed, as well as birth, death, and old age;
