disease is eternal in the world, as are hunger, thirst, and sorrow. (44)
Dispute and fear, as well as the most terrible intoxication and delusion; pride, grief, and confusion, as well as intoxication and envy. (45)
Dharma and adharma, as well as craving, are always dependent in this body;
these are the bonds that constitute fetters, for one who considers himself other than the Lord of the Gaṇas. (46)

The various bonds of the principles (tattvapāśas), established within each respective principle, as well as those bonds of space (deśapāśas) which have been proclaimed by Śiva for him, [are described]. (47)
The preceptors should perform the purification using [the mantra] joined with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*,
either one hundred and fifty times or again twenty-five times.
O Goddess of the Gods, in the sacrifice to Śiva, [the impurities] are to be purified by ten or fifteen oblations, or by three, five, or two, or even by a single oblation. 49.
O lady of excellent complexion, this variety of fire-offerings has been described to you;
having meditated upon the disciple as being filled with devotion, the preceptor should perform the initiation.
Regarding the number of worlds previously declared by Śiva:
one hundred are renowned as the lords of worlds within Niyati.
(896) All [the deities] are seated upon lotus-thrones, bound by their vows, together with the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras.
Having meditated upon [the soul] situated within the division of white and black, the seeker of liberation should perform purification. 52.
Śuddha, Buddha, and Prabuddha—these ten are the lords of the worlds;
they are renowned within the principle of Time (kālatattva), possessing many millions of attendants.
In the principle of Rāga (Passion), ten lords of the worlds of great power are proclaimed:
Suhṛṣṭa, Suprahṛṣṭa, Surūpa, and Rūpavardhana; || 54 ||
In this very sequence, [the state] is to be realized by those seeking liberation.
Beyond this, the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) are proclaimed. || 55 ||
Kalyāṇa, Piṭhala, Haṃsa, and others such as these have been proclaimed;
they are to be known by the high-souled preceptor within the reality of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). || 56 ||
p.
897) But as for the Rudras who are the lords of the worlds within the principle of Time (kālatattva), they must be purified by the high-souled preceptor according to the prescribed rule. || 57 ||
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Bhīma, and others such as these are proclaimed;
they are situated at the knot-gate above Gopati.
Gopati is surrounded by incalculable millions of Rudras;
beyond him are Trikāla and Kṣemīśa.
In this very sequence, the five Rudras are proclaimed as the bestowers of security and prosperity, purified by the path of initiation (dīkṣā).
Above this, O Ananteśa, the bonds (pāśas) are situated; they are joined with intoxication and delusion within this great abode of such a nature.
Furthermore, it is taught in the family of the Ṛṣis; then Vāgīśvarī again, the *chaṅkāra* to be accomplished, the *oṃkāra*, the giver, and the lord of the forest. (62)
The wise one, having surrounded Bhasmeśa with the food of meditation (dhyānāhāra),
remains situated within the veil of illusion (māyāvaraṇa) even while established in the eight measures (pramāṇāṣṭaka).
The Rudrāṅkuśa mantra is established first within the ritual arrangement;
having thus offered these and other oblations, O Sage, the knower of the rules should perform the rites for the self.
Beginning from Niyama and ending with Māyātattva,
I shall describe in due order those Rudras who are among these.
In Niyati there are ten Rudras, and ten are situated in the principle of Kāla;
ten are also proclaimed in Rāga, but in Vidyā there are no longer ten.
In the principle of Time (kālatattva), ten [subdivisions] are proclaimed; one is declared to be at the knot (granthi).
Furthermore, above that, five are situated within the principle of Māyā. (67)
Above this, moreover, the Pāśas of Ananteśa are situated;
they are joined with intoxication, delusion, and the like, holding nooses in their hands, and possessed of great strength. (68)
In this very sequence, extending down to the end of Māyā, the total number of worlds is indeed seventy-seven. (69)
This reality of the self (ātmatattva) has been declared and proclaimed as impure,
beginning from the infinite (ananta) and ending with the final reality of illusion (māyātattva).
I shall now declare by number those Rudras who are among them;
having grouped them all together as one, I shall tell you everything in its entirety.
Six hundred and forty worlds have been specified, and seven additional ones have been told to you, O beautiful one. (72)
Having meditated thus, one should perform the ritual procedure without hesitation;
this is declared to be the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), O beautiful goddess, ending with Māyā. (73)
Listen now with diligence to what must be known regarding the Vidyā:
beginning with Ananteśa, one should offer oblations in successive order. (74)
All those established in the world should be awakened by the wise;
however, those who have abandoned the collyrium of Māyā should be purified within the Lord.
Therefore, the fourfold form should be offered in successive order;
from that, the powers beginning with Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā are proclaimed.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, the powers of knowledge and action must indeed be known once again; having understood them, the teacher becomes a destroyer of bonds. (77)
Tejīśa and Bravīśa are the supreme authority and the highest state;
these two are declared to be Rudras who bestow the fruits of yoga and liberation.
Then, O Goddess, Prāṇa is remembered, and after him, Brahmadatta;
furthermore, four Rudras are remembered, who bestow the fruits of yoga and liberation. (79)
Ekāha, Piṅgala, and Haṃsa are declared to be the three Rudras;
above them, O Goddess, is Dhruva, and then again the eleven Rudras.
Those beginning with Brahmadatta and ending with Jambhika are proclaimed;
beyond them, O Goddess, is Dhruva, who is the third.
The lords of the worlds, accompanied by a retinue of seventy million, remain there;
therefore, it is called the Stainless (nirañjana), for its number is not known.
Having transcended Nirañjana, the power of will (icchā-śakti) is established;
and above that very place are those eight Lords of the Worlds (bhuvaneśvaras).
O Goddess, they are remembered as beginning with *pra* and proclaimed to end with *pra*;
O lady of excellent hips, they are to be purified, for they bestow security and well-being. (84)
Established in a subtle form, it produces a reflection;
beyond this, it is without support and devoid of all meditation.
Pervading all, it remains established as the vehicle for the radiation of its own power;
it is neither other nor supreme, being entirely devoid of the distinction between the supreme and the non-supreme.
The supreme state is beyond all cognition, free from doubt, firmly established, existing through a continuous lineage, and stainless. (87)
It is impossible to describe that Śiva who is to be known as partless;
by him, all this [universe] is pervaded, characterized by being beyond conceptual construction. 88.

Nor is the sound (dhvani) said to be some other distinct entity because it is deposited [therein]; rather, it is woven like warp and woof, without beginning or end, and illuminates all principles (tattva). || 89 ||
This knowledge, which transcends the supreme, is held to be the true essence of knowledge.
This has been told to you, O Goddess, concerning the worlds in brief. (90)
O beautiful one, I have briefly described the path of the worlds;
O Goddess of gods, it is proclaimed that within the principle of Vidyā reside the lords of the worlds.
(904) He spoke in the same manner regarding Īśvara and likewise regarding Sadāśiva; O Goddess of excellent vows, I shall explain those [states] to you according to their true nature as qualities.
The past worlds have been described in brief within the principle of Vidyā;
having understood this, O Goddess, the preceptor who has reached the further shore of the principles performs the purification.
O fair-faced one, I shall now declare those [principles] taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, within the Śiva-tattva, having first established them as a single unity. 94.
O Goddess of the gods, one hundred and twenty worlds are indeed proclaimed; this must be known by the high-souled teacher. 95.
Those who are "without mental activity" (amanaska) are purified in the path of the worlds by a thousand [offerings];
they are also purified by even a hundred full oblations—of this there is no doubt. (96)
With the Niṣkala [form] alone, there are ten; likewise, five oblations in the Śūnya;
three are proclaimed for the Praśānta; thus, the entire path is [consumed] without remainder. || 97 ||
One should perform the oblation for the path consisting of the thirty-six principles with the *sakala* [mantra];
it is declared that this may be done with the *praṇava* or again with the *śāntyatīta*.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer oblations with the supreme syllable (paramākṣara) for the sake of the Supreme Self;
O lady of excellent hips, one should perform the homa according to the path of time (kālādhvan) and the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
Likewise, one should offer a hundred oblations for each of those conquerors among the paths of sound;
O beautiful one, the path of the digits (kalādhvan) has been described to you in the same manner here.
Thus has the path of reality been briefly explained in detail;
it should be understood with effort by the high-souled teacher. 101.
Whether he be a *samayin*, a *putraka*, a *sādhaka*, or even an *ācārya*, [he should be taught] to one who is disciplined, self-controlled, and devoted to the Guru and the deity. (102)
The high-souled teacher must show them favor,
having worshipped Maheśvara, the God of gods, according to the prescribed ritual.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rule, the wise one should perform the sacrifice with his hand;
indeed, within this vow, the sacrifice is to be performed with the left hand.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one who knows the ritual procedure should place [the deities] in order beneath the path, having worshipped them with perfumes and flowers according to the proper method. 105.
Having meditated upon the god Maheśāna and having summoned the disciple, the knower of mantras, O Supreme Goddess, brings [the disciple] under his own control within himself.
Having touched his body on all sides with the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta),
one should place the principles (tattvas), which are distinct from the body, in their respective locations, beginning with the head. || 107 ||
O Maheśvarī, having meditated upon the Lord who has the form of a digit of a garland of flames,
the knower of reality, having meditated upon the Great Lord, [should place him] in the midst of the earth.
Having meditated upon the body, he undoubtedly burns away both merit and sin;
when this is performed, O Goddess, it is therefore known as the "Hand of Śiva. (109)
By the bestowing of Śiva’s hand, he is ordained as a *samayin*;
O Goddess, by this rite one should likewise grant him grace.
One attains union with the Lord, the Supreme Reality; of this there is no doubt. [This applies] even against ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and rākṣasas, when one is fully concentrated. (111)
O lady of beautiful hips, one who has fallen [into the lower realms] cannot be killed even by the gods;
for he merely traverses the path, but does not cause harm to another. (112)
O Goddess of the Gods, he becomes a *samayin* in all tantras; of this there is no doubt.
By him, O Goddess, one is called a *putraka* by the yogis of Śiva. (113)
Therefore, I shall explain that; listen to it as it is being told by me.
Having first performed the sacrifice to the Gaṇas and having beheld the solar orbs (maṇḍalas). || 114 ||

Having offered oblations according to the rule, O Goddess, and being liberated from the bonds of the principles (tattva-pāśa), the son (putraka) is then united with the supreme principle; thus he is ordained.

He alone is one who knows the ritual manuals of mantra, who understands the procedures of the mantra-tantras, who is well-versed in the ritual manuals of mantra, and who knows the proper application of place and time. || 116 ||

One who knows the rules for the practice of recitation (*japa-yoga*), who knows reality (*tattva-jña*), and who understands the ritual procedures (*vidhi-vid*), [is qualified] for heating (*tāpana*), inflaming (*dīpana*), and likewise for cutting (*chedana*). (117)
He is skilled in the rites of delusion and paralyzing, as well as in the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) technique;
he knows how to pierce the mantras of others and is devoted to the nourishment of his own mantras.
He knows the distinctions between countries and castes, and is intent upon uniting [them];
he is capable of casting down even the Daityas, Bhūtas, Siṃhas, and Vidyādharas. (119)
He is omniscient, grateful, endowed with purity and proper conduct,
capable, renounced, and always considered devoted to the recitation of mantras.
One who possesses the four feet, is skilled in the designations, and likewise skilled in the arts; who is always energetic and dexterous—he is ordained as a practitioner. || 121 ||
The high-souled preceptor should bestow the consecration using either eighteen or fifteen water-pots. (122)
Having joined together the jar known as Vidyā, O beautiful goddess,
she should then consecrate the disciple by means of the rite seen in the ritual rules.
Having encapsulated [the disciple] starting from the earth principle (pṛthivī-tattva) up to the final Māyā-tattva, one should subsequently consecrate him with that which is called Vidyā.
And thus is the consecration of the practitioner ordained, O beautiful one, beginning with the earth and ending with nirvāṇa. 125.
Once consecrated as the Lord of Gods, he is ordained as the Ācārya;
he should indeed construct a four-cornered [altar] in the eastern portion of the maṇḍala.
It should be four cubits in width and one cubit in height,
with archways and banners in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (127)
Having thus prepared the pedestal, the teacher, being well-composed,
[should perform the rite] with jars containing "timely" and "untimely" roots, smeared with sandalwood paste.
Prepare each individual jar filled with mango sprouts, accompanied by dūrvā grass shoots, and combined with all medicinal herbs.
O Goddess, one should install the five Brahmās along with the limbs of Śiva and Śiva himself, one by one, in each pitcher according to the proper sequence.
One should place the seven oceans, exactly seven in number, into each individual jar;
one should install the elements beginning with earth into the jar in their proper sequence.
Accompanied by auspicious ceremonies and festive rites joined with the songs of women,
and with the sounds of the Vedas and shouts of victory, one should begin from the east in a beautiful manner. (132)
The wise one should perform the consecration, beginning with the earth and continuing up to the Nirvāṇa-vase; this indeed is remembered as the ritual procedure. || 133 ||
Then, one should bring the consecrated disciple into the presence of Śiva;
having honored him with the water for guest-offering (arghya) and other rites, one should bestow upon him the authority.
The *saṃhitā*, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the *karaṇī* and the *kartarī*, must always be fashioned with favor toward those belonging to the four stages of life (*āśrama*). 135.
Exegesis, bestowing grace, and the instruction of the teacher and disciple;
one should perform recitation for a short time during the day, and likewise offer oblations for a short time during the day. (136)
Indeed, one should rise from even a very brief meditation while this great sacrificial session (satra) with the Guru continues.
These qualifications which have been proclaimed are prescribed for the knowledge of Śiva. (137)
Thus, O Goddess, the preceptor who has reached the further shore of reality should cause [the disciple] to hear:
"O dear one, we shall do exactly as you have told me. (138)
"O Suvikalpa, you must carry out the command of Śiva that has been spoken by you. Having thus worshipped [him], you, the highly intelligent Ācārya," || 139 ||
Having prostrated according to the rule, one should then dismiss the deity;
once the deity has been dismissed, O Goddess, one should then commence the worship of the Guru.
Having drawn a mandala measuring one cubit while remaining composed in meditation,
one should place [the image] therein and worship it according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform worship in due order with these eleven mantras alone;
indeed, one should perform the worship of the Blessed One as that of the Preceptor. (142)
The practitioner should not practice stinginess regarding wealth toward the teacher;
O Goddess, one should worship the teacher, who has mastered the tantras, as if he were Śiva himself. 143.
Merely by being honored by him, the teacher becomes Śiva;
through his grace, both accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti), as declared by Śiva, shall come to pass. 144.
Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, one should honor there the preceptor who has reached the further shore [of knowledge],
with ear-rings, bracelets, garments, girdles, and likewise crowns.
By means of gifts of villages and regions, as well as hunting expeditions, and accompanied by elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and various kinds of gold; 146.
One should give a very beautiful cow provided with a piece of cloth;
whatever [object] by which [the recipient] is well-pleased, that indeed should be given by the son. (147)
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should offer oneself;
O Goddess, once this has been offered, one becomes free from debt to the guru. (148)
O Goddess, having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rite with a well-composed mind,
one should feed those devoted to the Guru and satisfy the poor and the helpless.
Having fed [the brahmins] according to the prescribed rule, one should give a white sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, O Goddess, it should be said: "May the Blessed Lord Śiva be pleased. (150)
O Goddess, he who acts in this manner shall partake in the fruit of accomplishment;
but he who acts otherwise is a counter-practitioner against the teacher. || 151 ||

Having abandoned the knowledge of initiation and the status of a guru, one goes to hell; therefore, one should regard the teacher as Śiva himself and know him to be a practitioner of the Lord’s wisdom. (152)
O Goddess of the Gods, they should regard one another equally—as a son, as a brother, and likewise as a peer—and being honorable and worthy of worship, they shall attain mutual affection. 153.
Thus, one who knows the various injunctions attains the eternal state;
likewise, one initiated by a knower of the injunctions through the ultimate reality shall attain the state of Śiva. 154.
Having become autonomous and all-pervading, one may wander according to one's pleasure;
his accomplishment is never thwarted as long as the god Sadāśiva exists.

The procedure for the practitioner (sādhaka), which accomplishes all desires and goals, has been proclaimed; [now follows] that for the teacher (ācārya) before the Lord of Gods, as well as for the initiate (samayin) and the spiritual son (putraka). 156.
p.

918) However, for all [these methods], it has been declared that one who knows the reality (tattvavit), even if possessing every kind of pride, may liberate the bound soul (paśu) provided he acts according to the prescribed rule. 157.
He who knows reality is Śiva himself; therefore, one should worship him.
Having assumed a human body, he bestows the knowledge of Śiva.
Therefore, one who knows the truth should always worship the teacher as if he were Śiva;
one should not practice deceit toward him, for by practicing deceit, one goes to ruin. 159.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Niśvāsakārikā*, in the section on the *Dīkṣottara*.
The Lord said: "Henceforth, O Supreme Goddess, I shall proclaim the [nature] of the mantras."
O lady of excellent vows, I have thus proclaimed to you the mantras, each one recited individually. (p. 919) || 1 ||
Indeed, the common and specific [mantras] were proclaimed by Śiva;
likewise, the five Brahmans, the Śiva-aṅgas, and the Vidyā-aṅgas as well.
Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī, as well as the Supreme Syllable (Paramākṣara), Śāntyatīta, the Praṇava, and likewise the Navātman. || 3 ||
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) are indeed to be known as common [deities];
wherever there is an individual oblation, one should perform that sacrifice with the common [mantras]. || 4 ||
O Goddess of gods, one should worship each of those very ones individually;
those which were mentioned in the context of the *praṇava* are remembered as being individual.

The [powers] beginning with Nivṛtti belong to the Kalā-tattva; they are said to reside within each of those [levels] individually, according to the division of the various stages, as thirty-eight kalās. (6)

O Goddess, in the Mātṛkā, each [letter] has been proclaimed in that manner; likewise, others have been celebrated by way of the relationship between the object to be purified and the purifier. || 7 ||
Having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, one should commence the rite of homa;
with mantras illuminated by the ten [vowels], one should perform the ritual as desired.
Mantras illuminated by the syllable Oṃ and joined with a salutation at the end,
when preceded by the syllable Huṃ and ending with Svāhā, belong to the practitioner of mantra.
The practitioners of mantra, having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and ending with *vauṣaṭ*, summon forth spirits, gods, humans, and serpents.
O beautiful one, I have explained to you the most excellent *śāntika* rite which bestows fruit;
the mantras are illuminated by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with a concluding salutation (*namaskāra*). (11)
The arcane mantras should be employed in the fire, joined with "svāhā" at the end;
for the purpose of offering flowers, one should employ them joined with "suvaḥ" and "oṣaṭ".
The consecration into immortality (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) joined with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is beneficial;
one should employ it for the purpose of attaining mastery over the mantras, beginning with "Manonmanā. (13)
It should be employed for eradication accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*;
for killing, the wise practitioner should formulate the mantra as *phaṭ phaṭ*. (14)
It is joined with the syllable *huṃ* at the beginning, endowed with the mantra in the middle,
and through the application of the *phaṭ* mantra, it is remembered as that which severs the bonds.
O beautiful one, this application of the mantra has been explained to you;
without knowing it, one will not attain success, nor will one reach the supreme state. (16)
Therefore, one should employ the piercing of the mantra-syllable itself;
for the lords of practitioners achieve success through applications joined with mantras. || 17 ||
Those [practices] which are accomplished through yoga but do not lead to the supreme state—one should always perform initiation (dīkṣā) and fire-oblation (homa), ending with the word "svāhā. || 18 ||
One should effect the severing of the bonds by means of the utterance of *huṃ phaṭ*;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should cause the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to be offered with the word *vauṣaṭ* at its end. (19)
The mantra remembered as having one syllable is the first; those with two or three syllables are superior;
those with five, six, seven, or eight syllables are still further superior; and that which consists of many syllables is the highest of all.
The single-syllable mantra shall be uttered with a protracted tone;
having pervaded [the body] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, it remains established there. (21)
In the heart, up to the point of one-quarter of a *pāda*, Brahmā is situated there;
he is proclaimed to consist of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) and the primordial natures (*prakṛti*). || 22 ||
O beautiful one, this [chapter] concerning Brahmā as the presiding deity has been explained to you;
however, the twenty-four [principles] for the sake of the world were explained by Śiva. (23)
Starting from the Puruṣa and ending with the Māyā-tattva,
that which has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity has been described, from the heart up to the pericarp.
But those Rudras who are proclaimed here in this middle region, together with their worlds,
rejoice along with Viṣṇu, possessing prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu.
The utterance has reached the middle of the palate; Rudra is proclaimed to be there, along with the Vidyās, the Vidyeśvaras, and their respective worlds. (26)
Having learned of that, the Great Queen, whose prowess is equal to Rudra’s and whose strength on earth is equal to Rudra’s, sports in the world of Rudra.
One should designate that as the Īśvara [vowel] situated in the high position at the head;
there, the god Īśvara is established in his sovereignty. || 28 ||
But that word, being distinct, [reveals] the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) above that;
there, the god named Sadāśiva is established in his lordship. || 29 ||
Having established a foundation for the three powers (śakti), which exist in two states according to the division of gross and subtle, one who understands this shall attain liberation. || 30 ||
Established in the fourth state, it is known as subtle, gross, and of a single kind;
it is likewise the illuminator of the *iḍikā*, the delighter, and the liberator. (31)
This gross sound is known as *nāda*; having realized it, one attains liberation.
Indeed, these four parts, when established in unity, [constitute the goal]. || 32 ||
O auspicious lady, I have thus described to you the gross *nādasmṛti*;
the subtle is of one kind only, renowned as the "upward-moving" (*ūrdhvagāmī*).
All the deities residing therein are established together as a collective;
indeed, those deities who destroy all sins are to be understood through their pervasive union.
Beyond that, the Power (Śakti) is further established in five ways:
the Subtle (Sūkṣmā), the Very Subtle (Susūkṣmā), the Immortal (Amṛtā), and the Mortal-Immortal (Mṛtāmṛtā). || 35 ||
O Supreme Goddess, these are indeed known as the subtle states of Śakti;
beyond even that is the one called Vyāpinī, which is more subtle still. (36)
O Goddess, that which is superior to even this has come down through the lineage of gurus;
by knowing it, men are liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra. (37)
O Goddess, I have described to you that Śakti who is the supreme cause;
one should designate her as the obstructress when she brings about dissolution into that Void, O Goddess. (38)
O Goddess, without the upward expulsion [of breath], the phonemes have gone to their own dissolution;
the sound residing in the throat ceases, and this is known as the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra). || 39 ||
That sound of that sound which, having manifested the sages, is restrained—that is designated as such; they know its dissolution to be in the forehead.
O Goddess, when this [state] is differentiated, then one should designate it as *nāda*;
when it is undifferentiated, it is called *ghāṭa*, and they know dissolution (*laya*) to be in the forehead (*lalāṭa*). (41)
O Goddess, when that [state] is differentiated, then one should designate it as *nāda*;
when undifferentiated, it is called *ghāṭa*, and situated in the forehead, it returns [to its source].
Beyond the *bindu*, the reality of *nāda* reaches dissolution;
when dissolved in the reality of *nāda*, she proceeds as the supreme state.
The power established in the state of "otherness" (paratva) is likewise all-pervasive as its remainder;
therefore, O Goddess, that which has come down through the lineage of gurus is more weighty.
It is free from time and place, its support is the upward breath (udāna), it is the truth;
it is devoid of the practice of recitation (japa) and yoga, and is liberated from the substratum of the organs of action. || 45 ||
Free from even a mere atom [of conceptualization] and devoid of causal discourse,
all the deities and sages who observe partial vows suffer [in their ignorance]. (46)
Having reached it, they do not return, nor do any other men on earth;
all this has been declared as the supreme, most excellent reality.
O Goddess, listen as I tell you of the equinox of the mantra;
O Goddess, [it is that state] while reciting the mantra until the mind becomes one-pointed.
To that extent, the self, residing within the body, recites the mantra;
then the salutation (namaskāra) is uttered, joined with the ending "svāhā. (49)
When the two drops have passed beyond, that mantra is known as the equinox (viṣuva);
in the vital breath (prāṇa), however, that fourth [state] is the most excellent woman distinguished by her divisions.
O Goddess of the gods, having attained the state of perfect tranquility, it is known as the partless equinox (*niṣkala-viṣuva*).
In the forenoon of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), the second [equinox] is the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). (51)
At the midpoint between the two, however, the equinox (viṣuva) is traditionally taught by Time;
O Goddess, the best of teachers knows these four equinoxes.
He shall quickly be liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra.
All this has been told by me to you in brief. (53)
O Supreme Goddess, having become of equal flavor with the mantra, one abides;
O Goddess, the mantra is proclaimed by Śiva to be of equal flavor [with him]. (54)

O Goddess, O beautiful one, the Self situated within the central channel is the Lord through its devotions to Śiva; this is called the "equalization of the channels" (nāḍīsamarasa) as described to you.
O Goddess of the gods, the Supreme Lord abides pervading all beings;
O Goddess, that state of equilibrium with all beings has been proclaimed by me to you. (56)
O Goddess, Śiva has briefly told me that reality which is the best among all flavors of equality and which arises from all virtues. 57.
One should condense that reality, which is difficult to attain even for the gods;
I have not revealed this auspicious reality of equal flavor to anyone.
O Goddess, I have thus described to you the four equal-flavors (samarasa);
O Mistress of Gods, I shall now explain to you in truth the union of the principles (tattvasandhāna).
Now listen to how the conjunction of mantras is performed during the sacrifice;
having performed the libation to Śiva and the others in due order, the knower of mantras [proceeds]. (60)
Then, having performed the expiation for himself, the preceptor [performs it] for the disciple as well;
likewise, there is no great fault in the severing of the thread, nor in the cutting away of the calamity. (61)
One should perform expiatory oblations for those who are emaciated, corpulent, or afflicted by passion;
having offered these, the practitioner of mantra should then perform the "kindling" (dīpana) of the mantras.
Having performed the ritual slaughter of the animal, one should offer the expiation by means of oblations;
one should employ the syllable "Huṃ" at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
The utterance of the syllable *phaṭ* with total devotion is proclaimed as the act of "giving" [the victim].
Having thus performed the rite of inflaming [the victim], O lady of beautiful countenance, one should then proceed with the sacrificial animal.
Then the preceptor, having joined the three principles in their proper order,
[unites] that which is called the Vidyā-principle with the Śiva-principle, and the Ātma-principle with the Vidyā-principle.
Having unified [the individual self] with the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) by means of the principle of the Self (ātma-tattva), the wise man,
being discerning, should then unite it with the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva). (66)
Next, listen to the conjunction of the three principles and the conjunction of the mantras:
the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) with the principle of Śiva, and the World-Lords (Lokeśas) with that known as Vidyā. (67)
O Supreme Goddess, one should unite the weapons with the reality of the Self;
having thus performed this unification, one should cause [the soul] to descend by means of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
As the modifications are being cast into the midst of the fire, he beholds that smoke,
crackling with the sound "ciṭ-ciṭ," resplendent with the marks of Viṣṇu.
Having thus recognized these characteristics, one should designate him as a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmaghna).
One who has the appearance of a dark-blue mango and emits smoke is considered to be a Śālikā.
When fire is heard [to be present], one should designate the drinker of liquor;
in this very offering and oblation, [the sin] is indeed submerged. || 71 ||
One should identify the perpetrator of theft by [the sign] that a fire is extinguished in an instant;
he shall draw upon the earth a detailed and terrible form accompanied by smoke.
Thus, one who has committed the sin of approaching the wife of a teacher,
even while being dragged away, assumes the form of all things, like fire which takes on the appearance of everything it consumes.
But that, O Goddess, is a sin arising from association; one should designate it as such for him. One should likewise recognize other minor sins (upapātaka) in the same manner.
Likewise, those with the voice of a hyena, a harsh voice, or the cry of a crow or an owl;
those with the terrible voices of a camel or a vulture, or the howling of a jackal and the cries of a monkey—[these are inauspicious]. (75)
He should once scratch the ground with his smoke-colored, smoky mass [of hair];
and there shall be the sound of "jalate," "kradhuka," and the utterance of "phaṭ" once each. (76)
Having thus understood these characteristics, one should not perform the rite of initiation upon seeing men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) or who bear these marks of transgression.

Having placed that [image] in a corner and directed his attention toward it, the master preceptor, the Lord, should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the consecrating lamp and the nine principles (navatattva).
One should recite "khaṭ khaṭ" four times and "phaṭ phaṭ" again and again; thereafter, the reality established by the [mantra] of the elements is further perfected by means of the fire-oblation.
What wonder is there that one is purified by the oblation from that sin?
For it removes even most terrible poison that has entered the seven bodily constituents. || 80 ||
In this way, the knower of reality removes the evil karma of those who have committed sins,
as well as the sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and other minor offenses (upapātaka). (81)
One should purify [the disciple] even by means of one hundred and eight [repetitions]; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having thus purified the disciple, one should commence the rite of initiation (dīkṣā). 82.
But the supreme guide should not proclaim the sins of others; by speaking of faults, he incurs blame himself; therefore, one should avoid being angry. 83.
"The true essence of mantra, the most excellent of all, has been declared.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Dīkṣottara* in the *Niśvāsakārikā*. Lord [Ishvara] said:
Henceforth I shall explain, O beautiful goddess, listen:
the application of the sūtras of ritual procedure (prakriyā), and likewise the seizing of the bonds (pāśas). (1)
If I were to tell you everything that must be done without first understanding it, then the maiden would be multiplied three times over by the thread of agency. (2)
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow or again with scented water,
the wise one should worship that thread with the eleven [verses] alone.
Having worshipped that thread, the preceptor, being well-composed,
should place the thread at the region of the big toe and hold it firmly.
Then the wise one, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon that thread with all the mantras, should extend it from the tip of the crest-lock down to where it is fixed.
O Goddess, once Śiva has been worshipped by the high-souled preceptor,
he should take up the cords and fashion them with knots according to the thread-measure.
Having encased that noose with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*,
the wise one should then bind those nooses in reality.
The most excellent of teachers should bind all the cords in sequence;
having bound the cord according to the rule, he should cause the deity to dwell therein. 8.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, he who is honored by the God of gods should then illuminate the nooses in sequence, ending with *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having offered one oblation for each bond, there is no doubt;
at the clear dawn, on a bright day, the practitioner of mantra should perform this in a well-prepared place.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, one should offer the principles (tattvas) in their proper order;
at the conclusion of the oblation, the mantra-practitioner should then effect the severing of the bonds (pāśa).
Having severed [the bonds] with that very Śiva-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with it.
Having offered the oblations, the mantra-practitioner should then cause the bonds to fall away by means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). || 12 ||
One should extract all the principles (tattvas) by means of the sequence of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
then, from their respective locations, one should unite the fetters (pāśas) with their corresponding principles.
The pure reality (śuddhatattva) is short, while the impure is joined with the long [vowel];
having meditated upon it as dissolved, one should be endowed with the integration of the sense organs.
In this manner, O observer of good vows, one should sacrifice all of them in sequence by means of the *sandhi* [mantra],
beginning with Earth and ending finally with the *śiva-tattva*.
This very procedure is declared for the severing of the bonds;
this same procedure is also remembered as the method for the reintegration of the principles (tattvas). || 16 ||
O fair-faced one, [this applies] to the path of the worlds, the path of the kalās, and the path of the principles (tattvas),
as well as to the path of the phonemes, the path of the words, and likewise the path of the mantras. (17)
One should cut the bonds there with that Śiva who has been conceived;
thereafter, one should perform [the rites] on the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan). I shall describe this in brief.
First, one should establish the reality (tattva), and then the discourse on the worlds;
having worshipped with perfumes and incense, one then performs the visualization of the womb (yoni).
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should perform the striking of the animal;
having performed the striking with the crest (śikhā) and the mudrā of withdrawal (saṃhāra-mudrā), [the rite is completed].
When the person has been struck with power, that [vital energy] proceeds upward from there;
having reached the *dvādaśānta*, the wise one should then grasp it. (21)
The mantra-practitioner should join [the breath] with the left [nostril] and thereby offer oblations;
in the case of authority (adhikāra), one should offer ten [oblations], and for enjoyment (bhoga), one should offer ten oblations. || 22 ||
The wise one should take ten [units] and then separate them from the reality (tattva);
having separated them, the wise knower of mantras should effect the severing of the bonds (pāśaccheda).
In the Jyeṣṭhā [nakṣatra], Śiva severs the bonds;
at the end of that, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and then extract the Raudra [mantra] from it.
This very procedure has been declared for the entire path without exception;
having understood this procedure even once, one shall liberate [others], of this there is no doubt. || 25 ||
O Goddess, I shall explain to you in its entirety the path of the principles (tattva-adhvā) for one who knows the mantras; one should invoke the principle and then perform the fire-oblation (homa).

Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should then perform the striking again; there, one should unite [the soul] with Śiva and offer oblations into the well-prepared fire with that very [mantra]. (27)
And once purified by the threefold sacrifice, one should cause the cutting of the topknot (śikhā) to be performed. || 28 ||

Having established the bound soul (paśu) within the self of reality (tattva), one should unite it with the supreme state. Once united with the supreme reality, one should offer laudatory oblations (staumya-āhuti).
Oṃ, for the sake of omniscience and its fulfillment; be completely satisfied, and attain nirvāṇa! || 30 ||
Just as [the Self] is all-pervading, so should the oblation be offered; the high-souled preceptor must offer it, thinking, "It pervades everything. (31)
O Goddess, that bound soul (paśu) may attain omniscience by the command of the Cause;
as it has been declared by the God of gods, so shall it be—of this there is no doubt. (32)
In the same manner, the *kalās* are to be known, as well as the *padas*;
likewise, in the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), it is declared that the preceptor must perform [the ritual] accordingly.

The phonemes (varṇas) themselves are remembered as the principles (tattvas), and likewise they are the source of the phonemes; their application within the Praṇava and their striking [with it] are also remembered as the Praṇava.
The grasping is by the *praṇava* alone, and the lifting up is likewise by the *praṇava*;
as it has been taught for the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), so it is exactly the same for the path of words (*padādhvan*).
Just as in the path of the arts (kalādhvan), so here, the great-souled teacher shall proclaim the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) in brief, but not in detail.
The Gāyatrī, however, is the source; by means of it one should purify the mantras.
One should perform the striking with the Sāvitrī, and that which is to be received should be taken by means of that very mantra. (37)
The wise one should perform the conjunction with that [mantra], as well as the disjunction; and the elevation should likewise be performed by that same Sāvitrī mantra. (38)
The cutting of the bonds must be performed by the preceptor himself through Śiva;
the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered for the sake of union with the supreme Śiva.
The wise practitioner should cause [the offering] to fall by means of the *vasordhārā* application;
O Goddess, this very procedure has indeed been explained to you in due order.
O beautiful one, that which is common to all the Saṃhitās has been told to you for the sake of uniting [the disciple] with the supreme Śiva; it must be understood by the teacher alone. 41.
O Goddess, initiation is of five kinds and must be performed by the preceptor;
I shall now fully explain that which brings benefit to practitioners. (42)
The preceptor must prepare the seat with the Praṇava alone;
it consists of infinite dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. (43)
The wise one should perform the ninefold placement of the *praṇava* by means of Śaktideva;
with that, he should fashion a lotus together with sandalwood up to the pericarp.
It should be performed ending with the *puṣkara*; one should cause it to be done ending with the *maṇḍala*.
It should be performed ending with the deity; one should indeed cause it to be done ending with the *mūrti*. || 45 ||
The five Brahmās, endowed with thirty-eight kalās, should be invoked by that very [mantra], O beautiful goddess. (46)
There is no doubt regarding Brahmā by the high-souled teacher;
Nivṛtti is his head, and they know Iḍikā to be his heart. (48)
The subtle one should be known as Śikhā, while Sadyojāta becomes Kavaca;
Pṛthivī becomes Astra—thus the limbs of Brahmā are proclaimed. (49)
One should place the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) to the east and likewise to the south;
similarly, one should place it to the west and to the north, as well as in the center, conjoined with the *praṇava*.
The heart is in the southeast, and the head is remembered as being in the northeast;
the crest-lock is in the southwestern direction, and the armor is in the region of the wind (the northwest).
O beautiful one, the Rudra-tattva should be performed with the syllable Oṃ;
the letter *i* is the crest (*śikhā*), O Goddess, and the letter *a* is remembered as the head (*śiras*).
The syllable *ga* is indeed the heart, while *sa* and *dyas* are known as the armor (*kavaca*).
The syllable *la* is said to be the weapon (*astra*); these are proclaimed as the "graspers" (*grāhaka*). (53)
O beautiful goddess, one should differentiate those perceivers by means of the [mantras] called *hanta*;
however, one should perform the oblation (*homayet*) for the elemental nature of the Brahman-principle with the *praṇava*.

Having thus performed the rite according to the injunctions, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and cause [the deity] to descend for the sake of the lord of practitioners who has attained the state of a progenitor.
Engaged in that, the minister (mantrin) shall thereafter attain union with Brahman;
for as it has been declared regarding Brahman, so too is it remembered regarding Viṣṇu. (56)
The syllable *pra* is proclaimed as the form of Śiva himself;
the syllable *ru* is said to be the heart, and the syllable *ī* is remembered as the crest-lock (*śikhā*). (57)
The syllable *vām* is declared to be the armor (*kavaca*), and the syllable *va* is proclaimed to be the weapon (*astra*).
According to the previously mentioned procedure, the wise one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). (58)
Such union (sāyujya) has been proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
O Goddess, in that beginningless state, one attains union with Viṣṇu.
O Goddess, I joined him with one who was equal to Viṣṇu in prowess,
known by the name Aṅgāra, who is celebrated as the head of all sciences.
O beautiful one, the syllable *ṛ* is said to be its heart;
O goddess, O beautiful one, Aghora is the armor of the Rudra-tattva.
Just as one would do for Brahmā and Viṣṇu, so too should the preceptor act;
O Goddess, this procedure regarding the seat has been proclaimed by me to you.
The *amṛtā* is its crest (*śikhā*), proclaimed as the letter *i*;
the letter *m* is declared by name to be the head of the *vidyā*. (63)
O Goddess, they know the letter Ā as his heart, the letter P as the person, and the letter Va as the armor; the letter Ya is said to be the weapon—these, O Sovereign, are the limbs.
The ordinances of the Rudra-tattva are likewise remembered as existing even in Īśvara;
Ananta is the Rudra-tattva, and Nirvāṇa is the supreme state.
O beautiful one, she who has the form of space is said to reside in Īśvara;
however, the rite of Nidhana should always be performed in Sadāśiva according to the ultimate truth.
Just as I have previously explained, here too that very same procedure applies:
the supreme syllable (paramākṣara) is its crest-lock (śikhā), and that which transcends peace (śāntyatīta) is remembered as its head (śiras).
They know Bindudeva to be the heart and Īśāna to be the armor;
the letter *ha*, representing the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatattva*), is proclaimed as the weapon. (68)
Sāyujya has already been explained; one should perform it exactly as described and not otherwise.
These five great sacrifices (mahāyāgas) have not been told by me to anyone else.
Those men on earth who remain steadfast in lifelong celibacy—
for their upliftment, indeed, have I spoken this to you.
O lady of virtuous vows, this procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga* has indeed been told to you;
it is declared that the extraction of the *liṅga* must be performed by those who are lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*).
Having established [the disciple] in a position corresponding to his own caste, he should then perform the initiation;
or else, the practitioner who is devoted to the knowledge of Brahman [should do so]. (72)
In that regard, initiation (dīkṣā) must be performed, as well as consecration (abhiṣeka), O beautiful one;
likewise, even in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, this has been taught here by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin). (73)
The practice for the Rudras and the hosts of Rudras has thus been proclaimed;
by means of this very practice among the mantras of the Gaṇas and Guhyakas, the practitioner [attains success]. (74)
There, one should perform the initiation for all the Vināyakas, as well as for the Ḍākinīs, the Mātṛs, and likewise for the supreme Yoginīs. (75)
In this matter, the rite for the practitioner is prescribed by one who has been initiated;
he is skilled in the liberation of those bound to the Lord according to the Pāśupata system. (76)
The procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga* must be performed by the preceptor;
it should be undertaken by one who is pure, disciplined, initiated, and desiring liberation. 77.

One should worship the Lord of the Gods, the foremost of gods, who is endowed with the fruits of all principles and from whom the arising of the fruits of all principles occurs; thus one shall obtain the fruit of all things. (78)
This is named Sarvodaya, which bestows the fruit of universal liberation;
this auspicious yoga consisting of the five voids has been declared to you. (79)
I shall now proclaim the Śivayāga, which is incomparable among all sacrifices;
this sacrifice must be performed by the preceptor with four enclosures (āvaraṇas).
This is declared to be the womb arising from the five Brahmās and the limbs of Śiva;
O Goddess, in the second enclosure, however, are the Kalās consisting of Śakti.

O Goddess, one should place the digits (kalās) of Śakti in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions; as for the single digit of Nāda, it should be placed in both the cardinal and intermediate directions.
O Goddess, [this is] the digit (*kalā*) of Ya, as well as that of Ni and Do;
this sacrifice of yours has been declared, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (84)
Indeed, this entire secret has been explained to you, O beautiful one.
These sacrifices beginning with Sarva have been described to you, O beautiful one. (85)
Having known, understood, and worshipped [it], one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having made the Praṇava the seat, the wise man should worship the Mātṛkā.
Having made the *praṇava* the means of liberation, one should join [the elements] with a well-concentrated mind;
one should apply the seed-syllable on the right and place the *yoni* on the left.
O beautiful one, this sakalīkaraṇa has indeed been described to you:
the 'a' group [of vowels] on the eastern petal, and the 'ka' group [of consonants] in the southeast.
The *ca*-group is in the south, while the *ṭa*-group is in the southwest;
the *ta*-group is in the west, and the *pa*-group is in the northwest. (89)
The *ya*-group is indeed to the north, while the *śa*-group is in the domain of Īśa.
O beautiful one, this Mātṛkā-sacrifice has thus been described to you. (90)
The letter-group *a* is known as the first principle (*tattva*), and the letter-group *ka* is remembered as the Puruṣa;
thus, by the sequence of the groups, one should understand the principles (*tattvas*) within the Mātṛkā.
The syllable Oṃ is proclaimed as the first principle of the Self;
O Goddess of the gods, one should cause the principle of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva) to be performed with the Oṃ-syllable.
The offering should be made with the Nidhana [finale] by those who are concentrated on the Śiva-tattva;
thus is this sacrifice to Mātṛkā, which is difficult to attain even for the gods.
"The secret of the gods has been told; it was not hidden from you.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the *Dīkṣottara* within the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
When the time for initiation has arrived, the preceptors who are devoted to the scriptures [should act].
And how, O Maheśvara, should the disciples be stationed in that place?
O Maheśvara, where should ascetics and Brāhmaṇas be established?
O Śaṅkara, tell me what the place for Kṣatriyas is, and [the place] for Vaiśyas.
O Maheśvara, tell us the place for the Śūdras and likewise for women; and how the household sacrifice (grahamedha) should be performed at the time of initiation.
"Tell me all this according to the proper method, O you who are kind to your devotees.
The Lord said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the supreme procedure for the ritual assignment (niyoga)."
By the mere knowledge of which one is not defiled by any faults;
955) ascetics are to be stationed in the northeast, and Brahmins are situated in the north.
Those born of the Kṣatriya caste should be stationed to the south of Śiva;
the Vaiśyas in the western direction, and the Śūdras to the southwest.
One should employ a woman for the purification rite in the northwestern direction;
having thus established her according to the rules, one should perform the act of immolation.
When a householder has his own wife, children, servants, and himself as his only [dependents],
he should perform this application of purificatory rites with great restraint.
One should employ the Praṇava for the guru who is a householder;
one should regard the householder as Śiva himself, and his wife as the body of the sacred fire.

One should take the Kumāra from among those offspring, the friend, and the leader of the mantra; having taken the *kulajas* from the world-protectors (*dikpālas*), one should place the remaining groups of weapons. (10)
For householders who strive for the single-fold sacrificial consecration,
along with their wives, children, and grandchildren, this rule of appointment (niyoga) is proclaimed.
In a sacrifice performed by a householder, one should dismiss [the deity] with the offering of flowers;
for that which is employed in this very rite, one should cause the wife to perform the concluding part.
When women offer fallen flowers to their own husbands, they incur a great fault; yet, their conduct and lifespan are preserved.
When a fault arises in one's conduct, one becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed;
the sinner who performs impure rites with a joyful mind incurs a sin equal to that of violating the Guru’s bed.
The disciple falls into hell; the daughter is a synonym for ritual action.
957) There is the fulfillment of the two rituals: that of the flower and that of the funeral pyre. 15.
One should offer a hundred oblations into the fire with ghee while reciting the Śiva-mantra;
by this procedure, O Goddess, the preceptor shall become free from defects.
The sacrifice reaches completion when the oblation brings about the fruit of liberation;
O beautiful one, this procedure for the planets has thus been told to you. (17)
O Goddess of the gods, beginning with the ascetics, the Śivasaṃhitā is to be honored; then the oblation (homa) must be performed by the high-souled preceptor (ācārya).
One becomes fit for the study of mantras through the Hand of Śiva; such a practitioner of the Śiva-mantra becomes a master of both mantra and tantra. (19)
Having received initiation from me, one becomes a follower of the great siddhas and attains accomplishments;
established in the three principles (tritatva), he becomes fit for liberation. (20)
Having received permission and been consecrated, one who abides in the *bindu* partakes in the perfections of yoga;
the signs of attainment appear correctly, such as the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*.
Abiding in sound, one attains that state which is free from fear;
devoid of sorrow, one reaches the supreme station, having gone to which one becomes immortal.
He who thus knows the definitive nature of the guru’s task according to reality is worthy to perform initiation; otherwise, he becomes a doer of evil. (23)
Having thus performed the ritual arrangement for the disciples, O Maheśvarī,
the Guru should proceed to the fire-place and carry out the rite.
One who knows the procedure for the rite of cauterization (*agnikarma*), who understands the true nature of the characteristics of the tongue,
who discerns the distinction between success and failure, and who [knows] the forms of the letters within the sacrificial fire— (25)
Agni is indeed all the deities; Maheśvara has the form of Agni.
His mantras are his supreme form, while the primordial [form] is that which originates from Soma.
One should observe the seven tongues of fire through the openings of the sacrificial fire;
one who knows the procedure for the seven tongues should then commence the rite of oblation (homa).
He who, knowing the reality of the different types of tongues, performs oblations in the sacrificial fire,
shall find that all his actions burn away [impurities] and become entirely fruitful.
Having offered oblations into his fire according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped it so that it is well-satisfied,
the Bull-bannered Lord, being pleased, becomes gratified with the sacrificer.
As wide as the joint of a thumb and accustomed to many offerings of fuel,
they remain unified by means of their own small offerings of fuel. (30)
The mouth of this fire is equal in measure to that sacrificial pit;
with thousands of garlands of flames, its face is said to extend down to the netherworld (pātāla).
Having performed the awakening of the fire, one should then observe the tongues [of flame],
as well as their deity-forms and whatever kind of fruit they yield.
The tongues of the planets are established there from east to west;
at the time of the fire-oblation, one should carefully avoid two of those tongues.
The first, Dharmajihvā, is remembered as being blue in color;
the second, whose deity is Yakṣa, has a luster equal to the appearance of copper.
The third is presided over by Soma, white in color, and born from nectar;
the fifth is presided over by Viṣṇu, resembling the *atasī* flower. (35)
The sixth is presided over by the Sun as its deity; it is remembered as being both white and red.
The seventh has many deities and shines with all forms.
The first [tongue] is fruitless; the second bestows wealth;
the third brings about everything, having established union with the source of birth. (37)
Yamajihvā is of the Jaya lineage; the fifth is Kulavardhinī.
The sixth, however, has the Sun as her deity; she bestows health. (38)
The seventh [fire], when worshipped according to the rules, bestows dharma, kāma, and artha;
therefore, with every effort, the oblation (homa) in the middle [fire] is praised. (39)
The tongue of the house and the tongue of Yama are situated to the east and west;
therefore, one should avoid both tongues with every effort. (40)
The ten [fires] described as fire-colored bring about the accomplishment of ritual acts;
they possess the luster of the rising sun and resemble smooth lapis lazuli.
Some have a color resembling clarified butter, and others likewise have a coppery hue; some possess a luster like heated iron, and others resemble the juice of the kuśumbha flower.
Some resemble yellow orpiment, others are smoke-colored; some have the hue of a rainbow, and others are like the color of a glowworm. (43)
When the sacrificial fire has been kindled with many oblations and fuel, smokeless and with its flames licking upward, one should offer the oblation for the successful accomplishment of the rite.
Radiant, with a compact crest, resembling molten gold,
smooth, and turning clockwise, it bestows the fruits of all actions. (45)
Having understood this, the preceptor must duly perform the application of purificatory rites for the practitioner according to the rule; listen as I explain that. (46)
Having fashioned nooses made of thread and consecrated them with the ninefold self-mantra,
one should utter the nine principles (tattvas) as differentiated by the syllable "A".
One should apply [the mantra] everywhere—at the crown of the head, the throat, the heart, the navel, the thighs, the hips, as well as the shanks, the ankles, and the feet. || 48 ||
One should envelop the entire body with both arms and hands,
and offer one hundred oblations of the ninefold self with the utterance of "svāhā."
But it does not exist, O Queen of Gods; afterwards, one should perform the fire-oblation with what is empty.
For the purpose of binding the presence, it becomes thus, O beautiful one. (p. 964) 50.
Having bound the cord according to the rule, the cutting is likewise described;
thereafter, the spiritual son (putraka) should be joined to Śiva by the teacher (deśika).
Having purified [the disciple] according to the previously mentioned procedure, the high-souled Guru,
having performed the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, proceeds in sequence through the forty-eight [samskāras].

Having performed the consecration rites in due order with mantras originating from Brahmā, he should likewise perform the rites of depositing, extracting, joining, and so forth, in their proper sequence. (53)
Then, by this method, there shall be the severing of the bonds:
O Goddess, it consists of the letter *na* encapsulated and joined with the letters *pa* and *u*. (54)
One should apply the head, marked by the *bindu*, to the body of the disciple;
O Goddess of the Gods, there is no need for deliberation here regarding its union with Śiva. (55)
O Goddess, this is an extreme secret that has not been told by me to anyone;
it is the knower of all rites, infinite, and the most excellent among all supreme qualities. 56.
"Thus, the entirety of the commonality of all the *saṃhitās* has been told to you.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Dīkṣottara* of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the supreme path of the Mātṛkā, which brings about freedom from doubt and is the means for attaining the fruit of Nirvāṇa. || 1 ||
Īśvara:
Listen, O Goddess; I shall tell you the entire supreme secret.
By the mere knowledge of that, one attains the supreme state. || 2 ||
In the Mātṛkā, however, one should offer the oblations of the path in due order;
one should conceive of the letter *ṣa* in the Śatarudrīya as tenfold.
In the group of eight beginning with Pa, the letter Śa is the seed-syllable; in the second group of eight, the letter Va is the womb;
in the third group of eight, the letter Ya is the union; and Suśivara is remembered as the Lord.
In the third line, there is the letter *ya*; in the twenty-fifth [line], the letter *ma*;
in the *sādhya* [mantra], the letter *bha* is joined; and in the *śivasaṅkara*, the letter *ba*.
In the case of the incurable, the letter *pha* indeed [indicates it]; the letters *va* and *ka* belong to Hari and Rudraka;
the letter *na* is for the ten-fold blow (*daśaghāta*), while *ya* is remembered for the five disciples (*pañcaśiṣya*).
In the word *mahādeva*, the letter *da* is [the seed-syllable]; in *gopati*, it is remembered as *tha*;
in the state of Śiva-Brahman, it is *ṇa*; and in *nandahemaka*, it is *ta*.
In the family of Addṛṣi, the letter Ḍha is Mahāmāyā and Dṛḍhaprabhu;
at the end of Vāgeśa is the letter Tha, while the letter Ṭa is the lord of Pratipad.

The letter *tṛ* is in the station of the virtuous (*sādhu*), while the letter *jh* resides in the stainless (*vimala*). The letter *jh* indeed exists in the nourishment of meditation (*dhyānāhāra*); this should be known by the best of practitioners.
The letter *da* is to be known as Damana, and the letter *ca* is indeed Rudraka; the letter *dha* belongs to Dhātṛ, and the letter *gha* belongs to Bhasmeśvara.
In the eight great Vidyās, the letter 'ga' is preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), and 'kha' is [the seed] for the eight forms;
the wise know that the letter 'ka', ending with the labial (au), is the form for the eight Mūrtis.
The three powers (śaktis), joined with the bindu, are proclaimed as the two vidyās;
the syllable *oṃ* is said to be the weapon (*astra*), and those who know declare the syllable *aiṃ* to be the armor (*kavaca*). (12)

The letter *e* is declared to be the crest-lock (*śikhā*), while the letter *ū* is said to be the head (*śiras*). The letter *ḷ* should be known as the heart (*hṛdaya*), and *ṛ* is proclaimed to be Sāvitrī. || 13 ||
The Gāyatrī is indeed the Ṛk ending in 'u', proclaimed as Dharma and so forth;
'u' is to be known as the seat (āsana), and 'ī' is to be understood as the pericarp (karṇikā). || 14 ||
The letter *i* is conjoined with Śakti; one should know that the letter *ā* is the fifth Lord, Sadāśiva; and the letter *a* is Paramaśiva. || 15 ||
He who finds the path by means of these fifty syllables is through knowledge Śiva himself; he is a yogi, and they know him as Śiva.
With five offerings each, and likewise with ten each,
and with twenty each, and likewise with twenty-five each. (17)

Having understood that the strength of the fettered souls (paśus) is fifty or even a hundredfold according to their capacity and power, the knower of mantras should perform the rite of initiation (dīkṣā) for them as he desires.
In the Niṣkala [rite], one should offer four oblations; in the Śūnya, three again;
with a tranquil mind, one should give two, and that indeed should be offered as a single oblation.
This very rule is prescribed for everything throughout all time without exception;
this supreme secret has been concealed and not revealed.
It should be given to one who is initiated, tranquil, consecrated, and wise; to one who is dear to his guru and devoted to the worship of Śiva. || 21 ||
Otherwise, it must never be given even to one devoted to Śiva;
otherwise, this auspicious knowledge of initiation must never be given. (22)
Having understood the knowledge and realization that is common to all compendiums and supreme among all tantras, one should liberate others and be liberated oneself. 23.
That which has been explained in detail should be offered entirely as a fire-oblation (homa) in four ways: by means of the syllable, the mantra-word, the pada, and the kalā.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā), the path of the kalās, the path of the principles (tattvādhvā), O fair-faced one,
as well as the path of knowledge (jñānādhvā), the path of words (padādhvā), and the path of phonemes (varṇādhvā) once again.
O Goddess, this path is proclaimed to be of six kinds;
among these, one part is to be purified by the high-souled teacher.
The *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) should be offered for union with the supreme Śiva;
it must be bestowed by the preceptor (*deśika*) through the application of the *vasordhārā* (stream of wealth). 27.
By means of the application of mantra and substance, the bound soul (paśu) is joined to that state;
therefore, O beautiful one, [one should know] the mantra, the reality (tattva), and its majesty. 28.
The abandonment of the deities within one's own body in due order, as well as the dissolution of the *bindu* into the *nāda*, and the supreme state that transcends dissolution. (29)
In this manner, O Goddess of the gods, one should gradually unite [the soul] with the supreme state.
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall tell you everything in brief. (30)
There is no requirement for dust, nor for a dwelling, nor for the possession of land;
rather, in whatever place one has worshipped Maheśvara, [that place is suitable]. || 31 ||
Having meditated upon the path with the mind, the teacher who has mastered the tantras [should proceed];
for that path of the worlds which was described by me to you, O virtuous one, (p. 972).
Having meditated upon that within one's own body and likewise in the region of the sacrificial animal,
the wise knower of the tantra, skilled in the path of reality, should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
The teacher should offer a thousand oblations while remaining in a state of mindlessness;
indeed, O beautiful one, he should fight with a thousand [enemies] while remaining in a state of mindlessness.
This path of the worlds was proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
one should prescribe that it lasts for as long as the time required to fill the sacrificial ladle.
O Supreme Goddess, the teacher who is united with the mindless state is said to consist of all mantras and likewise to consist of all principles (tattvas).
p.
973) It consists of all the gods and always consists of all beings;
having offered this, O beautiful one, it should be drunk with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). 37.
Having first performed the preliminary rite (yojana), one who desires union with Śiva, O Great Goddess, attains eternal Śiva by offering oblations in this manner. || 38 ||
This beautiful essence, consisting of all initiations, has been kept secret by me;
initiation performed through improper means is purified by a single oblation.
O Goddess of the gods, by even a single oblation one may be joined to the supreme state;
how much more so by many oblations? What wonder is there in its purification? (40)
One is purified by a thousand oblations; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, I shall speak again in brief; listen, O lady of noble vows. (41)
One should offer all the paths without exception into the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
By means of exactly one hundred full oblations (pūrṇāhuti), [the practitioner] is purified in the sacrifice of Śiva. 42.
O Goddess of the gods, initiation leading to liberation is of this kind;
it has been declared by me as being both partless (niṣkala) and likewise purely void (śūnya). 43.
It has been declared by the Tranquil One as it truly is, in its very essence;
this pure [teaching] is unspeakable and must be guarded with great effort.
Thus, indeed, he who does not know this does not liberate the bound soul (paśu);
he is not called a guide, nor is he to be employed in the sacrifice of Śiva. 45.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the Sacrifice to Śiva, in the Dīkṣottara section of the Niśvāsakārikā. (p.
975) Īśvara said:
Henceforth, O Supreme Goddess, I shall proclaim everything, upon which the entire three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, are established. (1)
O Goddess, he in whom the various Siddhis are established is to be known as the Lord Sakala, the Master who assumes the form of the phonemes. || 2 ||
White, red, black, and tawny, as well as the color of a lotus stalk; yellow, clear, pigeon-grey, variegated, and speckled. || 3 ||
He has four or five faces on his head, ten arms, and three eyes;
he is Śambhu, bearing all weapons and adorned with a mass of matted locks.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Gods, seated in the lotus posture, whose form is complete;
he is the God who bestows all accomplishments upon practitioners, without a doubt. || 5 ||
One should employ [these mantras] for rising up, for the left side, for foot-unguents and collyrium,
as well as for pills, for traveling through the sky, and for the protection of the tooth-stick.
O beloved, for one who recites [the mantra] correctly, everything that is desired by the mind— this god who grants all accomplishments— is perfectly attained in its entirety.
For one who meditates upon the Sakala deity, perfection is not far off;
one should worship the Sakala deity and recite the mantra of the Sakala-niṣkala.
One should meditate upon the subtle, luminous [deity] and satisfy it by means of its constituent parts;
one should worship the whole deity, complete with the head, hands, and other limbs.
One should always remember Him as united with the five heads at the time of worship;
at the time of recitation, O God, one should always perform it with the deity both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
One should meditate upon the mantra-form as having parts (*sakala*), and the partless form (*niṣkala*) as consisting of light, subtle, and red, yellow, white, or black. (11)
Having thus become intent on meditation, one shall attain the perfection of yoga;
for the satiation of all mantras, it should be accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā."
Vauṣaṭ, vaṣaṭ, and likewise suvauṣaṭ;
huṃkāra and phaṭkṛta—each of these should indeed be repeated twice. (13)
Having understood "su-vaṣaṭ," "svāhā," and "namaḥ," one should employ them in ritual action;
when [the mantra] is undivided during the utterance of "svāhā," that digit is named Pratiṣṭhā.
Having performed the oblation, the cessation of the measure (mātranivṛtti) and the installation (pratiṣṭhā) and so forth are combined;
Vidyā is conjoined with Bindu, while Śānti arises from the Visarga. || 15 ||
(978) The propitiation of all mantras has been told to you, O beautiful one;
it was previously taught by Śiva for the benefit of practitioners. 16.
The reversed *kalā*, however, is prescribed for death and eradication;
one should employ it in eradication, as well as in causing enmity and paralyzing. (17)
O Goddess of the gods, everything has been told in brief:
the Lord consists of the five principles (pañcatattva) and likewise consists of all principles (sarvatattva).
It consists of all beings and is situated everywhere;
and in whatever [form], O Goddess of Gods, it is known with perfect clarity. (19)
Therefore, I shall declare it; listen as I speak it to you, O Goddess: the reality beyond the seven principles, the eleventh Lord.
The Self consists of sixteen limbs, while the Lord consists of twenty-one;
however, that very same [Lord] should be known as the thirty-sixfold reality of the *kalās*. (21)

The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) should be known as consisting of the essence of the Mātṛkās, comprising eighty-one units; it should be known as the essence of mantra, and it is indeed that very [path].
O Supreme Lord, he is to be known as the twenty-fifth among the Sāṃkhyas;
he is to be known as the thirty-sixth, the Lord, the Supreme Lord.
The Supreme Lord is sung of by those learned in the Vedanta,
and He alone is proclaimed as the Pañcarātra by those who know the truth.
Likewise the Vaimalākārakas, as well as those who are Pāśupatas, the Buddhists, the Ārhatas, and similarly the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas; || 25 ||
O Goddess, those who know the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, who are devoted to the Dharmaśāstras, and who all understand liberation, have each set forth their own definitions. (26)
Those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas worship the Lord of the gods;
he alone, O Supreme Goddess, is declared to be the manifest Haṃsa.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, he remains there in his manifest form, joined with the Kalaśa, as well as Śakti, Nāda, Ardhacandra, and Bindudeva. (28)
The letter 'A' and the letter 'U' are traditionally held to constitute the 'sakala' (the whole);
this is declared to be the definitive determination of the sakala within the body. || 29 ||
Alternatively, the Supreme Lord may describe the entire [system] through another classification of the God of gods; understand that concisely.
The first modification is proclaimed as *a*, the second is *ā*;
*u* is the third, while *m* is the fourth. (31)
The fifth is the Bindu and Nāda, while the sixth is said to be the letter *ī*. When [the mantra] is devoid of these syllables, it is the partless (*niṣkala*) Supreme Lord.
By means of the letter *a*, the letter *bha*, and the letter *i*, O beautiful one, these [phonemes],
established together in a single place, are proclaimed as the syllable *huṃ*.
When the letter *ma* is proclaimed as being joined with that which is satisfied (*tuṣṭā*), then Śambhu, having entered the *bindu*, proceeds through the nose. (34)
One should know that which ends with the letter *ka*; it causes concealment for yogins.
When it is devoid of the colors of the navel, then one should designate it as empty (*śūnya*). || 35 ||
The letter *ā*, the letter *ha*, and the letter *ī* joined together;
O Goddess, the letter *a* is said to be situated above the *bindu* and the *nāda*. (36)
Even that [power] is proclaimed to have its power only by means of something further beyond it;
O Goddess, when there remains even the slightest trace of that which transcends power.
She is declared to be all-pervasive, just as an ant is [pervasive] by its very nature; O beautiful one, this has been told to you through the grace of the Sakala [deity]. 38.
One obtains everything from her, whatever on earth is difficult to attain;
O Goddess, she is thus fully described because she is established within the body. (39)
When joined with yoga, that is proclaimed as *uccāra*;
however, when associated with the body, O Lord of Gods, it is recited as *sakala*.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— O fair-faced one, his body is joined with a thousand *ī* sounds. (41)
When the self is indeed abandoned by this, it is recited as being partless;
this was stated in the previous sūtra and was already known by you.
The god himself emerges, having cast off his body; he is known as Māruta, and he should be understood as being partless (niṣkala), O beautiful one. (43)
He who, liberated from the five deities, realizes the Self and is endowed with self-knowledge, goes to Sadāśiva. (44)
The upward-moving *kalā* is indeed one; the *kalā-śakti* consists of four.
When joined with the *vyāpinī*, Śiva is devoid of the six phonemes. (45)
Resembling pure crystal, with a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
it possesses a splendor more exalted than the rising of countless suns. (46)
O beautiful one, this which moves upward has indeed been described to you;
for when the self is situated in that place, it appears in that very form.
That subtle power called Nāma, which is as pure as clear crystal—
within it, the Self is perceived, appearing in its very form.
The digit named Amṛtā, which possesses the radiance of many rays—by that [digit] in that place, the self then becomes identical in form to it. (49)
Listen now to the form of her who is called Amṛtāmṛtā:
she resembles the luster of moonlight and constantly flows with nectar.
She is called Amṛtāmṛtā, the fourth power of the *kalās*.
At that place, the Self, having assumed that [divine] form, manifests as being of that very nature. (51)
O lady of excellent complexion, these six syllables have been taught by me to you;
for when [the mantra] is devoid of these syllables, Śiva is deprived of his sixfold nature.
Knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, the teacher becomes a destroyer of bonds;
this knowledge of the six categories has been declared by the Supreme Lord. (53)
Having known this supreme, divine state, the Self is indeed proclaimed;
by whatever means it may be, one shall attain the existence or non-existence of those respective things.
O Goddess, the self is proclaimed to be like a crystal stone;
whatever form it comes into contact with, it appears in that very form. (55)
Freed from form and color, and devoid of the organs of action, [the Self remains]; however, through its conjunction with the organs, it is both bound and liberated. (56)
Becoming the Supreme through awakening, he attains the sacrifice of knowledge;
through knowledge, that which is to be known is dissolved, and he becomes all-pervading. || 57 ||
The Self is always both knowledge and the object of knowledge; having known it, one is liberated and can liberate others.
For the Self is defined as that which, once known, knows both knowledge and its object.
Having understood this, a living being is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence;
thus has this six-syllabled knowledge been declared to you, O Supreme Goddess. (59)
Beyond these, O Goddess, is that which is called formless (arūpa) and free from affliction;
its state, established through a lineage of transmission, cannot be fully described.
Having recognized him, O Great Queen, he shall become the initiating guru;
for he who possesses both knowledge and realization is always the liberating guru. (51)
He is the bestower of grace, the destroyer of bonds, and the supreme teacher;
those forms which have been described by me are remembered as Brahmā and the other gods.
