The supreme power (parā-śakti), however, is all-pervasive and the awakener of all principles (tattvas).
O Goddess, this most difficult-to-attain reality has been declared by me. 63.
You must not give this most secret matter to just anyone—
the whole, the partless, and likewise that which is both whole and partless.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are known as the "with-parts" (sakala) through these three; the supreme reality, the Lord Bindu, is to be known as both "with-parts" and "without-parts" (niṣkala). 65.
One should know the Great-Souled Sadāśiva as the partless Śiva.
Likewise, there are three deities in the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) and in the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). (66)
Or else, O Goddess, Sadāśiva is to be known within the principle of Śiva;
but Śakti, O Goddess, is the supreme, abiding as the highest of the three principles.
He who transcends all states of reality and is the imperishable supreme among all principles—from him, O Goddess, does all this arise; by him all this is pervaded. (68)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Sakala," in the Dīkṣottara section of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear the definitive determination regarding the Sakala."
Pervasion has been declared to be of many kinds, yet it has not been properly ascertained according to the established convention. || 1 ||
How indeed is the Lord composed of the five deities? How is He the all-encompassing Master, consisting of all principles (tattvas) and consisting of all beings? (2)
How is it that the Lord, who possesses seven principles, whose essence consists of eleven principles, and whose nature comprises sixteen constituents, is also said to consist of twenty-one? (3)
That very principle of *kalā* is said to consist of thirty-six aspects;
furthermore, that which is called the essence of *mātṛkā* consists of eighty-one words.
He is the essence of all mantras and indeed the path of the worlds;
he is to be known as the twenty-fifth and likewise as the twenty-sixth.
O God, you alone are the proponent of Vedānta;
you, the knower of the truth of the Pāñcarātra, are that very supreme state.
p.
990) Furthermore, those who are Vaimalas and likewise those who are Pāśupatas—in all of them resides the God; the Supreme Lord is with parts (sakala). || 7 ||
The Buddhists and the Ārhatas, as well as the followers of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika, those who know the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and those who are devoted to the Dharmaśāstras; || 8 ||
But those who know the path to all liberation and have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, they serve the Lord of the gods, the manifest Supreme Lord.
"O Lord, this very thing has been spoken by you, yet it was not understood by me;
tell me all of this in its entirety and in detail. (10)
"O Lord, please explain this in detail according to your own reasoning. The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the definitive conclusion regarding everything.
I shall explain them in sequence as requested by you;
O Goddess, they consist of five deities: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Īśvara is likewise proclaimed, as well as the god Sadāśiva; these five gods are indeed remembered as being situated everywhere. || 13 ||
The syllable *a* has Brahmā as its deity; the syllable *ma* has Rudra as its deity;
the syllable *ū* has Viṣṇu as its deity; and likewise, the *bindu* has Īśvara as its deity.

That which is of the nature of sound (nāda) should be known as Sadāśiva—both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), as well as enriched with the creative powers (kalā) and indeed as emptiness (śūnya). || 15 ||
Kha-ma-laṃ, kṣapaṇa, kṣaya, and kaṇṭhoṣṭhya—
these are declared to be the elements (bhūtas), together with their instruments (karaṇas). || 16 ||
The sixteen modifications have been declared, along with the seven subtle primary natures; likewise, O Goddess, this triad of qualities is remembered as being of the nature of the elements. || 17 ||
Beings come into manifestation through it; therefore, it is remembered as being of the nature of the elements (bhūtātman).
It is surrounded by the elements in that place which is beautiful in every respect due to its instruments.
All this, consisting of these elements, has been described to you, O beautiful one:
Vidyā, Īśvara, Māyā, Kāla, and Niyati.
The Puruṣa and Prakṛti—these seven have indeed been described;
one should know that Īśvara is the head and Vidyā is the right line.
The three worlds are to be known as situated on the left side of Māyā;
below that, Niyati and Kāla are to be understood in their proper sequence. (21)
The Puruṣa is in the region of the face, while below him resides Prakṛti;
this god who sustains the seven principles has thus been described to you.
"O Goddess, listen attentively; I shall tell you everything regarding that which was previously stated by me: 'The Truth consists of eleven aspects.'"
Above the seven principles (tattvas), however, the principle of Sadāśiva is to be known;
above that is the Śiva-principle, established upon the upward-pointing power (ūrdhva-śakti). || 24 ||
But the supreme [power] of that [Lord] is all-pervasive; its reality consists of eleven aspects, which indeed was previously described by me as consisting of sixteen limbs. (25)
O Goddess, these sixteen, known as the *kha-khas*, must be understood by the teacher (*deśika*).
[They are: *tṛṭi*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and *muhūrta*. (26)
Night and day, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices, as well as years, the yuga, the manvantara, the kalpa, and likewise the mahākalpa. || 27 ||
For this [body] is known to have sixteen components, while Time is said to be the seventeenth;
as for that which was called the "thirty-six-fold self," listen, and I shall explain it to you. (28)
O lady of excellent vows, beginning from the earth and ending with Pradhāna,
there are indeed twenty-four principles (tattvas), while Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth.
The twenty-sixth is Niyati, while Kāla becomes the twenty-seventh;
the twenty-eighth is recorded as Rāga, and Vidyā is likewise to be known as the next.
The thirty-first [tattva] is to be known by the high-souled teacher;
indeed, the thirty-second, the *kalā-tattva*, was taught by Śiva himself. (31)
O beautiful lady, the thirty-first is proclaimed as the principle of Māyā;
the thirty-second is known as Vidyā, and the thirty-third is Īśvara.
Sadāśiva is the thirty-fourth; Śivā is remembered as the thirty-fifth;
and Śiva is declared to be the thirty-sixth by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (33)
O beautiful one, the thirty-six-fold self has been fully explained to you as it truly is;
that fourth digit (kalā) is to be known by the high-souled teacher.
First, the five Brahmās are remembered in their sequence of thirty-eight;
Sadyojāta with eight kalās, and Vāmadeva as the thirteenth.
Aghora is known by eight [syllables], and his face by four;
O Goddess, Īśāna is fivefold, having issued forth from his body. (36)
The five beginning with Brahmā are proclaimed as the five Brahmas;
and within the deity Bindu, O Goddess, there are four Kalās—this I shall tell you.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti—these four kalās are indeed that very Supreme Lord. (38)
O Maheśvarī, the Lord of the Supreme, who is manifest with all parts (sakala), consists of the subtle and subtler states of the Nāda and Śakti that have been described.
O beautiful one, that very principle of Kalā has been explained here to you;
O lovely goddess, that which was called by me the "essence of Mātṛkā" [is this]. (40)
O Goddess of the Gods, the Mātṛkā, proclaimed as beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa', should always be understood by the wise as the body of Kāma. (41)
O fair-faced one, that which was spoken by the Supreme Lord, consisting of eighty-one words, should be known as being established within that Praṇava. 42.
This has been declared and understood by you through its division into nine parts;
the mantra-nature is said to be action, and that indeed is the Supreme Lord.
The sixteenth is called *kalā*; it is sung of in all the tantras.
From those [fifteen] come two *bindus* at the end, and from those two come the two *alikas*.
One should place one [bindu] in the middle between the two bindus;
the second is below the bindu, and that is proclaimed as the essence of the mantra. || 45 ||
O beautiful one, that *jīva* of all mantras has been described to you;
by it, O Goddess, this entire triple world with its mobile and immobile beings exists. (46)
It is pervaded by the Supreme Lord; no doubt should be entertained here.
That is proclaimed as the individual soul (jīva) of those called animals, beasts, and humans. (47)
By him all this is pervaded, just as ghee is within milk;
thus has it been told to you, O beautiful one, regarding all mantras indeed. (48)
This supreme knowledge, O Goddess, is unknown even to the gods;
it is to be recognized in all mantras and all tantras, O beautiful one. (49)
O God, O Lord of Gods, at the time of exhalation, the Haṃsa is the supreme cause;
this is the true essence of knowledge and the very essence of mantra for you. (50)
This which has been called the true essence of mantra is the supreme true essence of the living soul (jīva).
This knowledge, which is very difficult to obtain, must be guarded with great effort. (51)
O Goddess, without knowing this supreme reality of the living soul (jīva), mantras do not attain success even when recited hundreds of millions of times. (52)
This well-spoken statement is sung throughout all the worlds: "Life is extremely difficult to obtain; it is not worth even a sixteenth part [of this truth]. (53)

O Goddess, O fair-faced one, because that which is higher than the highest—the knowledge and the object of knowledge—is the very essence of all things, it has been kept secret; though known, it has not been revealed to anyone at all.
It should be given to one who is self-controlled, tranquil, devoted to the guru, knowledgeable in the procedures of all tantras, and a wise practitioner. 55.
It should be given to the consecrated, high-souled Ācārya;
however, it is not to be accepted by others who do not revere the Guru. (56)
Having understood what is to be known through knowledge, a man undergoes atonement; therefore, one should seek both knowledge and the teacher with great effort. || 57 ||
O lady of excellent countenance, one who possesses knowledge, who knows the reality, and who is indeed auspicious, should perform the ritual division as spoken by the Supreme Lord. (58)
O Goddess, this Supreme Lord, whose essence is mantra, has been described to you.
Having understood him, O Goddess, perform all rites according to your desire. (59)
O beautiful one, this has been declared as common to all tantras;
O Goddess, I tell you truly that there is no knowledge superior to this. (60)
That very Parameśvara, in his manifest form, is said to be the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
O Goddess, I shall explain that to you in brief, but not in detail. (61)
The fivefold state of the five deities is established in its entirety;
I have previously explained that to you just as it is known by you.
O Supreme Goddess, beginning from Ananta and ending with Pradhāna, Brahmā is established there as the presiding lord in that auspicious realm.
O Supreme Goddess, beginning with the principle of Puruṣa and ending with the principle of Kalā, Viṣṇu is established as the presiding lord of those principles.
Starting from the knot (granthy) and ending with the principle of Kalā, the Supreme Lord Rudra is established as the presiding deity of those principles. (65)
From the Vidyā-tattva up to Sadāśiva, the Tattva of Īśvara is established through his sovereignty; of this there is no doubt. (66)
Above that is the Śiva-tattva; there resides the god Sadāśiva, who, O Goddess, pervades the path of the worlds in its entirety in five ways.
O fair-faced one, that which was previously declared by me as the twenty-five-fold [tattvas], I shall now explain in full; listen with a one-pointed mind. (68)
I shall now briefly describe them in their proper numerical order:
earth, water, fire, air, and space. (69)
Likewise, there are five organs of action and five organs of perception; and likewise, there are five subtle elements (tanmātras). How many [in total] are they, O beautiful one? (70)

Intellect, mind, ego, and the primary matter (pradhāna), together with the [five] subtle elements, are recorded as the twenty-fourfold field (kṣetra); the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the twenty-fifth. (71)

This very one, O Goddess, is the supreme enjoyer of the field (kṣetrajña), remembered as the cause; by knowing him through the discernment of the manifest and the unmanifest, one is liberated from bondage.
The manifest is declared to be the intellect (buddhi), while the unmanifest is remembered as primordial nature (prakṛti).
The self (ātman) has the nature of the knower; it is the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa.
Established in the nature of the fourth state (turya), this is that supreme station;
by its very nature it is actionless, a non-doer, yet the master of action.
"Pradhāna is the agent," they say, "endowed with decay and possessed of the guṇas.
Thus speak those who propound the path of the Sixty Tantras, O Mistress of the Gods. (75)
By means of the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), through those terms that prescribe the elements and so forth,
as well as the objects, the senses, and the subtle elements (tanmātras), which prescribe the qualities (guṇas) and so forth. (76)
That Prakṛti is to be known through its various divisions, names, and characteristics;
the Puruṣa, however, is declared to be pure consciousness, devoid of the guṇas. || 77 ||
Those who proclaim the purpose of Sāṃkhya knowledge have declared it to consist of twenty-five principles;
they regard the All-Knowing One as being partless and facing in all directions.
That which is devoid of qualities yet joined with qualities is meditated upon by the proponents of Sāṃkhya;
this is the principle of the Puruṣa, the supreme state of the Sāṃkhyas. (79)
Listen, O Goddess, to the fault of this [view] according to our own established doctrine:
by these [factors], one is bound and enters the state of a bound soul (paśu), and ignorance arises. (80)
The state of being an enjoyer, permanence, being a non-agent, being without price, desire, and dependence— these are the six attributes pertaining to the person (puruṣa). (81)
The enjoyer of that [body] is insatiable; yet, being subject to mortality, he is impermanent.
Furthermore, because he is devoid of purchase, he is indifferent, a non-doer, and ignorant. (82)
Impartiality, supreme forbearance, and freedom from the poverty of dependence—these are remembered as his qualities, as established by the Mothers. (83)
Omniscience does not belong to him who is devoid of qualities, nor indeed is there a state of partlessness for him; for it is heard that he possesses the manifestation of the foremost of powers.
But for one who is firmly bound by the qualities (guṇas), liberation is not eternal;
liberation may last for some time due to the bondage of the primary qualities (pradhāna-guṇas). 85.
One's own body is its constituent part (kalā), endowed with consciousness;
indeed, Vidyā, which discerns the true meaning, experiences that state as the nature of bliss. (86)
O Goddess, this threefold bondage of the great-souled Puruṣa is of the nature of Māyā; it causes one to proceed toward the lower realms. 87.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, this definitive exposition of the knowledge of Sāṃkhya has been told to you; it pervades everything and remains established as the very thread [of existence]. 88.
O virtuous one, as it was previously declared by me that there are twenty-six principles, I shall now explain them; listen with a one-pointed mind. (89)
Below Kalā is proclaimed to be the Puruṣa, the Karmakalā;
within the subtle eyes of men resides the Yogin, the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
That is declared to be the final goal of both the exponents of the Vedas and the yogins;
and it is recited by them as the body free from the six waves [of affliction]. (91)
They speak without knowing at all; they speak for some other purpose.
Listen to this very point, O Goddess, as to how one is free from the six waves.
O Goddess, Śiva is devoid of Śakti—[so they say]—as are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, being likewise devoid of the six waves [of affliction]. || 93 ||
The fundamental reality has been fully explained as that which produces consciousness and bliss;
it is called "not this, not this" (neti neti), known as Haṃsa, and is the designator of the supreme Brahman. 94.
This is that supreme reality; this is that supreme state;
this is that highest liberation which is certain for those who know the Vedas.
It is proclaimed by the yogis through a threefold division:
the Self (ātman), the inner Self (antarātman), and the supreme Self (paramātman). (96)

Thus, O Goddess, some speak of the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) in these three ways; others [speak of] the intellect (buddhi), and likewise [others of] the sphere of the qualities of primordial matter (pradhāna).
Some regard the twenty-fifth as the Veda, while others regard the twenty-sixth; many sages of strict vows speak thus concerning the bound [soul]. (98)
O dwellers of heaven, that one God is the sole object of worship for the sages, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, uragas, and kinnaras. (99)
O Goddess, the Gandharvas, Asuras, Daityas, as well as the Vidyādharas and others, the Siddhas, and likewise whatever other humans exist on earth— 100.
The wise conceive of the Lord as short, long, thin, subtle, even subtler than the subtle, and likewise grosser than the gross. (101)
They conceptualize the formless god in many ways as possessing form—as green, tawny, madder-red, and even like the ocean. (102)
Babhru, piṅga, kapota, dhūmra, and likewise śabalaka; śyāma, tadula, and māntra—these are found in the bound lotus.
Some [visions] resemble the light of a firefly, others are merely like a star;
some resemble the orb of the moon, and others are like the rising sun. (104)
Resembling sapphire and likewise resembling ruby—in this way, O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, it is of many such kinds and entirely complete. (105)
It is proclaimed as the support of all sciences in their entirety;
from this everything originates, and into this very same place it returns again. (106)
From this, both supernatural power (siddhi) and liberation (mukti) are established; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having first performed the rites for rising up, as well as those for causing hatred and attraction (vidveṣa-ākarṣaṇa). || 107 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, what need has that supreme practitioner for many known mantras, who always recites that very reality? 108.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, the supreme reality is complete and faces every direction;
through every sacrifice, recitation, and oblation, yogis attain perfection. (109)
And listen, O Goddess, in brief, as to how one should perform the sacrifice:
the entire deity present at the sacrifice is characterized by a head, hands, and so forth. (110)
One should worship the Supreme Lord while thus reciting the mantra and meditating upon the God who has three eyes, ten arms, and likewise bears all weapons. (111)
There is no accomplishment without form; therefore, one should contemplate the form.
When contemplating the Lord of Devas, the destruction of all obstacles occurs. 112.
The practitioner of mantra succeeds without obstacles; this has been taught by me in its entirety.
Likewise, O Goddess, beloved, at the time of yoga, everything should be meditated upon as being with parts (sakala). 113.
First, one should utter that entire reality which has been proclaimed:
situated in the *bindu*, merged with sound, having the form of light, and endowed with a crest (*śikhā*). (114)
At the time of meditation, yogis should always meditate upon the Sakala form;
at the time of recitation, one should perform the recitation of both the Sakala and Niṣkala forms.
O Goddess, at the end of the *namaskāra*, the wise one should know there are two *bindus*; beyond the two *bindus*, O Goddess, that indeed is called the partless (*niṣkala*). (116)
At the time of the fire offering, the practitioner must perform the oblation as follows:
at the time of the oblation, he should offer it accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā. || 117 ||
O Dear One, that which is known as *pratiṣṭhā* is to be understood as the portion of the deity Bindu;
by means of it, the wise should always perform the ritual of fire-offering (*homa*). 118.
For the purpose of pacification, one should say "vauṣaṭ"; likewise, for the purpose of nourishment, "namasuvauṣaṭ."

In the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), one should perform the oblation with the syllable *vaṣaṭ*; likewise, O Goddess, the wise practitioner may employ it at will for the rites of killing (*māraṇa*) and striking (*tāḍana*). 120.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and likewise the recitation (japa) joined with the utterance "phaṭ phaṭ.
Having understood this, one should carry out the practice of recitation (japayoga) with meditative absorption (samādhi). || 121 ||
Otherwise, it would not be accomplished even in hundreds of millions of aeons;
for one who recites the *sakala* [form], the *niṣkala* [form] is effectively recited.
O Goddess, he who recites the partless [mantra] which stands above the possessed [mantra] will achieve success before long; so it was spoken by the Supreme Lord. (123)
For him there would be no merit whatsoever, nor any sin in any way;
this secret has been told to you, and it was not hidden from you by me. 124.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, you too must keep this secret without a doubt,
especially from one who asks improperly regarding the departure of the soul (utkrānti) as taught by the Guru.
O Goddess, this command must not be given to him, O Supreme Sovereign, except to one who is virtuous in character, humble, devoted to his guru, and wise. (126)
This knowledge should be bestowed upon one who observes my command; therefore, those seeking their own welfare must always worship the guru constantly. 127.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Sakala," in the Dīkṣottara section of the Niśvāsakārikā.
Īśvara said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme consecration (adhivāsana), as well as the lunar days, asterisms, and yogas, and other factors that are favorable. 1.
One should perform the acquisition of the ground with Tārā and the digit of the moon alone;
for a Brāhmaṇa one should do so in the east, but for a Kṣatriya in the north. (2)
The earth of a Vaiśya is said to be yellow, and that of a Śūdra is black;
for a Brāhmaṇa it has a sweet taste, while for a Kṣatriya it is astringent.
The six tastes are to be known as belonging to the Vaiśya, while pungency is recorded as belonging to the Śūdra.
The earth that has the fragrance of clarified butter belongs to the twice-born (Brāhmaṇa), whereas that which has a red fragrance belongs to the Kṣatriya.

The ground of a Śūdra should have the fragrance of grain and smell of alkali; having carefully examined the ground, one who is skilled and knowledgeable in the application of mantras and rituals [should proceed].
Having performed worship according to the prescribed ritual, the knower of the rules [should consider] the empty signs along with their groups of constellations,
as well as the ascendant, the decans, the degrees, the lunar mansions, and their respective strengths and weaknesses.
(1016) Both worldly and religious [practitioners] are skilled in the knowledge of time.
O Goddess, if one were merely worldly, he would not know the knowledge of time.
Then the wise and discerning one should examine the internal time;
thereafter, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, the learned one should observe the sequence.
Having observed, according to the prescribed rules, the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial omens, as well as those that are internal and external, the preceptor, being well-composed, [proceeds].
With the resounding blasts of the conch and the drum, with auspicious Vedic chants and the like,
and with the loud resonance of singing and instrumental music, accompanied by shouts of victory.
The sound of a lion’s roar and the play of young maidens—these are the terrestrial sounds; those originating in the intermediate space are now proclaimed. (11)
(1017) It had the resonance of thundering clouds, a sky filled with gathering clouds, delightful with glistening streaks of lightning, auspicious, and the bringer of all prosperity. || 12 ||
One should accept those that are peaceful and avoid those that are inauspicious, such as the cawing of crows, the cries of old birds, owls, dogs, and cats. (13)
The sounds of camels, donkeys, monkeys, bears, and boars— among these, O auspicious lady, the sound of the monkey is indeed praiseworthy.
Having performed worship at the circle of the planets, one should carefully take [the earth] during the transit;
having dug a pit knee-deep, one should fill it after removing the soil. || 15 ||
Where the soil is rich in dust, that ground grants all desires;
having recognized this, the wise man who knows the ritual procedure should perform the Vāstuyāga sacrifice.
Having worshipped the enclosure of the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅgāvaraṇa*), one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times in sequence;
this is indeed remembered as the Vāstuyāga, followed by the purification of the ground.
Then, having cleared the ground of insects, hair, and bones,
one should sprinkle that well-examined ground with the five products of the cow.
One should cause the ground—excellent, firm, and free from depressions and elevations—to be pounded with hammers made of *palāśa* and *aśvattha* wood. (19)
The sacrificial ground should be made beautiful, sloping toward the northeast;
this auspicious portion of ground should be made level everywhere.
Having performed it in this manner according to the prescribed rite, one should surround it on all sides;
however, for a male [deity], neither a brick nor an earthen [structure] should be made.
p.
1019) Only one door should be made, provided with a door-leaf and a bolt. Having done this, O Goddess, [one should perform] the demarcation of the ground for Viṣṇu. 22.
One should first perform the Gaṇayāga, and then the consecration of the ground;
having worshipped Śiva with the five limbs, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times in sequence.
In the Gaṇa-sacrifice, one should worship Gaṇeśvara upon a triangular mandala marked with a lotus, which is joined with the Pīṭha and the syllable Oṃ.
In the Vāstuyāga sacrifice, there is a square in the center adorned with a lotus;
this is declared to you, O beautiful one, as the ritual demarcation of the ground.

Then, the mantra-practitioner, having gathered the necessary requisites, should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) through the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures; thus prepared with the materials, he should begin the consecration.
One should prepare eight pitchers in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
having thus arranged them with care, one should place the pitcher named after Śiva.
One who is wise should have it made of gold, or copper, or even silver; or alternatively, he may have it made of clay.
The jars made of *akālamūla* wood were smeared with sandalwood paste, likewise adorned with fragrant perfumes and neck-threads. || 29 ||
One should prepare a seat there, located in the northeast direction, using unbroken grains, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), incense, and likewise perfumes.
He should first place the water-pot (kalaśa) together with the golden image and the [five] faces; thereafter, he should install the thirty-eight kalās of the five Brahmans.
Starting from the earth, one should conceptualize the principles (tattvas). Having thus arranged the principles, one should then place the three principles in a threefold manner. (32)
Then one should bestow the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅgas), and place the eye and so forth, as well as the Kṣurikā.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with care, perform the invocation of Śiva.
One should invoke the deity with the Sadyojāta mantra, establish him with the Vāmadeva mantra,
effect his presence with the Aghora mantra, and offer the arghya water with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
One should offer flowers to Śiva with the Īśāna mantra;
one should place the Heart [mantra] upon the heart and install the Head [mantra] upon the head. (35)
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the *śikhā* on the crest, the *kavaca* on all the limbs, and the *astra* in the region of the hands, having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*). 36.
O Goddess of gods, having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in this manner, one should meditate upon the imperishable Śiva—
the supreme deity who transcends all mantras, the supreme state that transcends all principles (tattvas). || 37 ||
Having worshipped everything according to this procedure, O Supreme Goddess,
and having recited the Astra-mantra, O Goddess, one should then scatter the offerings (vikira) in all directions.
Then, the knower of mantras should scatter the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) once again;
having purified [the area] with scented water, he should then rotate the jar.
While reciting the Astra-mantra over the Vardhanī vessel, the knower of mantras should rotate it while chanting the Astra;
he should then offer an unbroken stream of water outside.
In its center it should be square, and outside of that a mirror; one should place the *vardhanī* vessel in front and the *kalaśa* jar behind it.
O Goddess, while reciting the *śivamantra*, accompanied by the preceptor, one should then cause [the vessel] to be whirled around and place it back in that very same spot. (42)
Then, having established [the deity], the mantra-practitioner should again offer the *arghya*;
thereafter, he should go to the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and worship it according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess, having worshipped Śiva, one should then go again to the fire-mantra;
resorting to the south-eastern direction, one should cause a fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) to be constructed.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (hasta) in size, provided with three tiers (mekhalā);
each successive tier is recorded as being four finger-breadths (aṅgula) shorter than the one below.
Having performed it in this manner according to the ritual procedure, the wise one should sprinkle [the site] with the Astra-mantra;
having performed the tracing (ullekhana) with that same mantra and having lifted [the dust], he should sprinkle it again.
p.
1024) One should sprinkle [the site] with the Astra-mantra and smear it with the Gāyatrī;
once it has been smeared, one should subsequently perform the preparation of the lines. || 47 ||
Three auspicious lines should be drawn from east to west;
one should be made from north to south, extending toward the north.
This is declared to be the Vajra, the supreme means of strengthening;
one should fashion a seat for Vāgīśvarī in the middle of the sacrificial pit.
Having meditated upon her as beautiful and auspicious, with a complexion dark like the petal of a blue lotus,
the mantra-practitioner should then contemplate her as being in her menses.
One should bring the Jātavedas fire into a copper vessel or a clay bowl,
having worshipped it with the five mantras and the limbs of the Vidyā in due order.
The wise one, knowing the ritual procedure, should perform the veiling with the armor-mantra;
having rotated that pit three times with the heart-mantra.

One should cast [the seed] through the path of the womb and contemplate it as having become the causal principle; the practitioner of mantras should perform the rite of conception with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, offering oblations three times.
When [the fire] has become tranquil, the knower of mantras should offer three oblations;
then he should offer the water for honor (arghya) and the water for the feet (pādya), whereby the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) is accomplished.
On the left, the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsuvana) should be performed; the mantra-practitioner should offer three oblations.
To Rudrāṇī, however, he should offer three; thus the puṃsuvana rite is accomplished.
The wise man should offer the three [substances] for the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) with the Aghora mantra;
then, he should again offer the water for honor (arghya) and the water for the feet (pādya) with the Brahmaśiras mantra.
The knower of mantras should, in due order, perform the union with the five faces, the purification of the speaker, and the opening of the mouth. (57)
One should offer three oblations beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna;
one should perform the oblation with a single mantra alone—of this there is no doubt. (58)
O fair-faced one, one should perform the expiation for the faces with the Astra-mantra;
one should offer three oblations for each face, without a doubt. (59)
One should indeed offer three oblations with the reality-mantra for the purpose of opening [the mouth];
once the mouth has been opened, one should then perform the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) by means of *homa*.
The practitioner of mantras should offer three oblations with the Tatpuruṣa mantra,
and likewise offer three oblations with the Astra mantra, O lady of beautiful countenance.
When the oblation has been thus offered, the mantra-practitioner shall have performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*).
Once the birth-rite has been performed, the wise one should thereafter provide protection. (62)
One should place Brahmā right there in the east;
in the south, one should arrange the seat for the deity Rudra upon a grass mat (viṣṭara).
In the west, one should arrange the seat dedicated to Viṣṇu;
in the north, one should likewise arrange that for Śiva in due order.
Having done this, the wise mantra-practitioner should then perform the naming ceremony; the naming ceremony should be offered with the Īśāna [mantra]. || 65 ||
In the same manner, one should offer three oblations here with the Kavaca mantra.
Having offered them in this way, the auspicious fire of Śiva is then generated.

For the purpose of accomplishing the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should cause [the fire] to descend by means of the *pūrṇāhuti* offering. When the fire has been purified by the rite, one should offer oblations into it with a ladle (*sruva*). (67)
Those who know the mantras should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the rite prescribed by rule,
accompanied by the limbs [of the ritual] and the God of gods together with the five Brahmans.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon that vessel, one should install Śiva right there.
One should first install the three principles (tattvas), and then install Śiva beyond the principles.
Having smeared it with ghee, one should cause it to be filled with milk;
[it should be offered] with barley, wheat, nīvāra, śāli rice, and ṣaṣṭika rice grains.
Or one should prepare a sacrificial oblation (caru) from kaṅgu grain, being well-composed;
the wise practitioner should cook it until it reaches a middling degree of doneness.
When one perceives that [the patient] has sweated, then one should remove him [from the fomentation bed];
however, one should perform shaking, rubbing, and anointing with the eleventh [ingredient]. (72)
One should offer three oblations with the eleven-syllable mantra of the Lord, namely: the offering of the heated [substance], and likewise the offering of the elements. (73)
Having performed the oblation with the *saṃpāta* [remnants], the wise mantra-practitioner should divide the *caru* consecrated by mantras into portions. (74)
One portion should be prepared for the deity, a second for the rite of oblation (homa),
and a third for the practitioners, preceded by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

O Goddess, one should offer, according to the prescribed rite, cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with kuśa grass, having consecrated the mouth [of the vessel] with mantras. (76)
Having consecrated it with all the mantras and with the auspicious nectar (*amṛta*),
the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) should be prepared according to this rule, O virtuous lady. (77)
I shall now quickly describe the purification for one who possesses purity; listen, for I am speaking to you.
One should place the clarified butter on the fire, and having removed it from the heat, one should then skim it. (78)

Thereafter, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the sprinkling (saṃplāvana) and the illumination (avadyotana); then he should perform the "leading out" (nīrāyaṇa) and the purification of the clarified butter (ājyaśuddhi).
O beautiful one, one should perform all the purificatory rites for the clarified butter (ājya) with the Gāyatrī mantra;
once the clarified butter has been purified by these rites, one should offer the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) as a libation.
To the south, to the north, and likewise in the middle region:
*Oṃ agnaye namaḥ* (Homage to Agni). *Oṃ somāya namaḥ* (Homage to Soma). *Oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ namaḥ* (Homage to Agni and Soma).
Om, salutation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
O beautiful one, the distribution of the portions of clarified butter has thus been explained to you. 81.
Then, once the clarified butter is pure, one should drop a drop of the mantra into it;
this is the procedure for purifying the clarified butter, as described in due order.
O Goddess, once the clarified butter is purified, one should then perform the sprinkling of the faces;
one should offer oblations one by one, beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna. (83)
Indeed, this "sipping from the mouth" has been taught by Śiva;
all rites must be performed by the preceptors using this [mantra]. || 84 ||
At the time of placing the clarified butter on the fire, the Brahman priest should first contemplate [the deity] right there;
at the time of lifting it from the fire, however, Gāyatrī is the deity, and at the time of leaping over [the fire], Viṣṇu is the deity.
p.
1032) It has been stated that in the case of such a confluence, one should contemplate Rudra right there;
this is to be known as the Avadyota-svara by the high-souled teacher. || 86 ||
Likewise, O Goddess, the Lord Sadāśiva himself, being without self, having consecrated [the site] with mantras, should contemplate Śiva right there. || 87 ||
One should drop every single drop from the *sāvitrī* [vessel] into the clarified butter (*ājya*), accompanied by the application of ritual mantras and joined with the presiding deities. (88)
All rites shall be accomplished for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
Therein, one should prepare a seat according to the ritual procedure as prescribed.
O Goddess, one should imagine within the center of the heart the seat designated for you;
first, one should place Ananta, and likewise Dharma and Jñāna.
Likewise, O Goddess, one should place the nine powers (navaśakti) in the joints of the pericarp and petals;
O fair-faced Goddess, one should place the letter *a* in the pericarp. (91)
With a well-concentrated mind, he should meditate upon the solar disc,
joined with the short syllable Oṃ and fashioned as the lunar disc.
The short letter *u*, O Goddess of gods, is the supreme fire-maṇḍala;
the letter *ā* has Brahmā as its deity and Āditya as its presiding divinity.
The letter *i* has Viṣṇu as its deity and the lunar orb as its presiding divinity;
the letter *u* has Rudra as its deity and the fiery orb as its presiding divinity.
Having thus carefully performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then place the form (mūrti) right there;
O fair-faced one, one should perform the placement conjoined with the Lord (Īśvara). 95.
The *bindu* should be known as Īśvara, and the *ātman* is proclaimed as the *haṃsa*. O Goddess of the gods, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*), one should then install the five Brahmans.
The Sun, the Moon, and Fire are deposited within the well-composed self;
however, O Supreme Goddess, it must be stated that the Self is indeed the reality of the Self (Ātmatattva). 97.
Īśāna is indeed with Puruṣa, while Aghora is well-established; Vāmadeva and Sadyojāta are proclaimed as consisting of exactly one hundred thousand [recitations]. (98)
One should fashion the head and face with thirty-eight parts (kalās),
and it should be made complete with major and minor limbs by those who are well-composed.
One should conceive of stability by means of the *kalās* of Sadyojāta;
one should worship the five heads, beginning from the east, with the mantra of Īśāna. (100)
O Goddess, the wise should sequentially assign the *kalās* of Īśāna;
they should likewise assign the *kalās* of Tatpuruṣa to the face. (101)
O Goddess, one should first place the entire [mantra] of Aghora upon the head in the very same initial sequence; thereafter, one should assign its portions to the heart and other parts.
O knower of mantras, one should place the digits of Aghora in the heart, the neck, the two shoulders, the navel, the abdomen, the back, and the chest.
One should place [the syllables] in due order in the secret region of the left side, as well as in the anus, the penis, the two thighs, and likewise the two knees. 104.
One should place the digits of Vāmadeva upon the calves, the buttocks, the waist, and both sides of the feet, according to the sequence of the secret limbs. 105.
O Goddess, the feet, the hands, the nose, the head, and both the arms— these constitute the *sadyojāta* aspect, which is immediately present everywhere in all forms. (10.6)
Having thus performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should contemplate the principles (tattvas):
either the eighteen principles, O Goddess, or likewise the nine principles. (107)
The five principles are in the Lord of Gods, as well as the thirty-sixth;
having placed the five principles, one should place the three principles above them.
Then one should offer the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅgas) and perform the invocation of Śiva; O Goddess, once he has been invoked, one should then assign the ancillaries.
One should place the heart-mantra on the heart, and likewise place the head-mantra on the head; one should place the crest-mantra on the crest, and the armor-mantra upon all the limbs. (110)
O lady of auspicious countenance, one should place the blood in the region of the hand;
one should invoke it with the *Sadyojāta* mantra and establish it with the *Vāmadeva* mantra. (111)
With the Aghora mantra, one should perform the invocation; with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, the water offering (arghya);
and with the Īśāna mantra, the flowers, the crown, and the earrings.
One should place Īśāna in the center; one should assign Tatpuruṣa in the east; Aghora in the south, and likewise Vāmadeva in the north.
One should place the Sadyojāta mantra on the western side of the Lord of Gods;
one should place the Heart mantra in the southeast and the Head mantra in the northeast.
One should place the *śikhā* in the southwest (*naiṛtya*) and likewise the *kavaca* in the northwest (*vāyavya*); the wise practitioner should then install the *astra* at the entrance. 115.
This is the enclosure of the womb; now hear of the second enclosure.
One should place Ananta in the east and install Sūkṣma in the south. (116)
Likewise, one should install the god Śivottama in the west;
the wise man should always install Ekanetra in the north.
One should worship Ekarudra in the northeast, Trimūrti in the southeast,
Śrīkaṇṭha in the southwest, and Śikhaṇḍin in the northwest.
Thus, O beautiful one, the second enclosure has been described to you;
O Goddess, listen as I describe the third enclosure to you. (119)
Taking recourse to the eastern direction (Aindrī), one should duly place Indra and the others in their proper order;
having thus performed the placement with effort, one should then place the weapons in the fourth [direction].
Having performed such a sacrifice, O Goddess, the knower of mantras should undergo initiation;
he should carry out the detailed ritual procedure according to the previously stated injunction. (121)
On the following day, the preceptor should worship Śaṇḍeśvara before the Lord of Gods,
in the north of the city of Ardhacandra, accompanied by the five ancillaries (pañcāṅga).
Having performed the oblation consisting of three parts and having thus informed Maheśvara, [he said:
"I have performed for you this oblation regarding the fault of the eightfold transgression of the rule."
In this manner, O Goddess, the preceptor should inform the Great-Souled One;
for by the fault of violating the eightfold commitments (samaya), the practitioner alone becomes defiled.
After Caṇḍeśvara has been offered oblations, one should then cause the worship of the Guru to be performed;
the wise man should worship that Guru with extensive offerings according to his means.
One should always worship the Guru with villages, gold, cows, horses, and the like, as well as with gifts of lands, and with earrings, bracelets, and armlets. (126)
Whatever with which the disciple is satisfied, that the teacher should give;
then he should offer himself, and thereby he becomes free from debt.
O beautiful one, I have explained to you the commonality of all the Saṃhitās;
the teacher who, being well-composed, performs the sixfold sacrifice [attains this]. (128)
When he is satisfied, may all the lords of the worlds be satisfied;
O Goddess, one should worship the teacher who has reached the further shore of reality just as one would Śiva. (129)
"Just as I am, so indeed is that Guru, who is proficient in the reality.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), in the *Dīkṣottara* of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
Īśvara said:
The body of all living beings is remembered as being composed of all the gods; it should be understood with effort by practitioners who contemplate reality. (1)
O beautiful one, the principles (tattvas) have been declared by me to you at the outset;
all of them are to be known within the body by the wise.
Iḍā, Suṣumnā, and likewise Piṅgalā—this yoga of moving through the nostrils must indeed be known by those who know the reality. || 3 ||
Indeed, he is the mover of all the digits (kalās) and the channels (nāḍīs) along with the vital airs (vāyus),
as well as the enjoyer of the principles (tattvas) and likewise the object of enjoyment.
Having understood, in their entirety and without exception, the divisions of time and duration as well as the transitions, the practitioner is then duly empowered. || 5 ||
When the Suṣumṇā flows through the right [nostril] in a well-regulated manner,
the knower of reality should always understand that to be the supreme northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
O Goddess of noble conduct, when the Supreme Lord resides within the *iḍā*, that is indeed called the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
O Goddess, when [the breath] is situated in the middle, established in Piṅgalā, that should be known as the equinox (viṣuva), which is proclaimed as the time for yoga. || 8 ||
Brahmā, conjoined with the syllable 'A', resides in the Suṣumnā;
he is to be known as Āditya, and his power (śakti) is proclaimed as Jyeṣṭhā.

The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is to be known as being situated in sattva; one should designate that [state] as established in the right side, which is to be understood as the station of gathering (sāṃgraha-sthāna). || 10 ||
Viṣṇu, joined with the syllable *ī*, is established in the *iḍā* [nāḍī];
he is to be known as Soma, and his power (*śakti*) is proclaimed as Vāmā. || 11 ||
That should be known as the power of action (kriyā-śakti), characterized by the quality of passion (rajas);
it should be known as the state of dreaming, situated on the left side.
They say that the letter *U* is proclaimed as the middle Rudra;
one should know Raudrī to be the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). || 13 ||
That which is declared to be the locus of fire is proclaimed as deep sleep;
one should know it to be characterized by tamas, and it is situated in the middle.
O Goddess, knowledge concerning the three periods of time is proclaimed to proceed from these [mantras]:
one should know the past as Brahman, and the future as being in the state of Viṣṇu. (15)
For the present state, established in Rudra-hood according to all the scriptures,
O Goddess, exists as the single Bindu-deity throughout the three times.
He is said to exist at all times, and is traditionally known as the very time of knowledge;
his past is the exalted sound of existence, the God of gods, Sadāśiva.
Having known [the Self] as endowed with knowledge of the three times, the practitioner becomes [successful];
it exists pervading everything in five ways, having the five deities as its essence.
Having begun from Ananta and ending with Pradhāna, Brahmā should be diligently understood as presiding over this well-arranged [system]. (19)
p.
1045) Beginning with the principle of Puruṣa and ending with the principle of Time (Kāla), these are indeed to be known by the knowers of reality; Viṣṇu is the presiding deity therein. || 20 ||
Starting from the *granthi* and ending with the *vidyā-tattva*, these should always be known by those who know them; Rudra is the presiding deity therein.
O lady of excellent hips, one should know everything from Īśvara at the beginning up to Sadāśiva as the ultimate reality; therein, Īśa is the presiding deity.
Above that is the Śiva-tattva, wherein resides the deity Sadāśiva;
all of this must be known in its entirety by the preceptor.
Śiva abides pervading all principles without exception;
having known everything in its entirety, one is ordained as an Ācārya.
Nivṛtti is said to be Brahmā; Pratiṣṭhā is called Viṣṇu;
Vidyā is fully designated as Rudra; and Śānti is called Īśvara. || 25 ||
O Goddess of gods, I have described the deity Sadāśiva, who transcends peace, as the God of gods, according to the very sequence of Nāda. 26.
Iṇḍikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and likewise Mocikā—beginning with Brahmā, O fair-faced one, these should be known;
they have been proclaimed by me as deities according to the subtle method. || 28 ||
These arts have been fully described, as well as the deities and the channels;
O Goddess, they must be understood in their true essence by the high-souled practitioner. (29)
Having pervaded the *kalās* and the deities, he remains established;
O Goddess, that Self of the knower performs the movement. (30)
O Goddess, eight principles are traditionally taught by which the entire world is pervaded; endowed with those very principles, the Supreme Lord moves within it. (31)

Among those called animals, deer, and humans, and among all beings endowed with the sense-faculties of the true nature, he who is joined with the principles (tattvas) attains his desired goal; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Goddess, having understood the coming and going, one becomes a practitioner;
without understanding it, one will not attain success, nor will one reach the supreme state. || 33 ||
He who, endowed with the principles (tattvas), acts as the food, the eater, and the giver—the Goddess said:
O Blessed One, O Śaṅkara, I wish to hear about the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment.
Who drinks the drink there, and who again perceives its flavor? Or who casts [the seed] into the womb, and who, O Lord, receives the morsel of food? (35)
Who, moreover, can discern the various tastes?
Please explain all of this in its entirety out of your grace. (36)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain in brief for the sake of the practitioner that by the mere knowledge of which one is not tainted by the defects of food. (37)
The giver, the enjoyer, and the thinker shall attain the state called Sādākhya;
for food is Brahmā, the essence is Viṣṇu, and the enjoyer is the Lord Maheśvara. (38)
O beloved, he who understands the agent, the enjoyer, and the object of enjoyment, remains present within all bodies and both experiences and bestows [the fruits of action]. (39)

Even while eating among the outcaste dog-cookers (śvapacas), he is not stained by sin, provided he contemplates the principles (tattvas) within his own body in their proper sequence with his mind. 40.
In the ears, the eyes, the nose, and likewise in the mouth, as well as in the right ear, Kha-mala is proclaimed to reside. (41)
One should contemplate Kalāḍhya on the left ear;
one should likewise imagine both Sakala and Niṣkala upon the nose.
One should contemplate those two eyes as destruction, decay, and the end;
one should diligently understand that food is seen through emptiness. (43)
When the Lord of Gods takes a morsel of food, the Supreme Lord is the throat and lips;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are the ears, and Rudra and Īśvara are the eyes. (44)
Sadāśiva, who is eternal liberation, resides constantly in the nose and the mouth;
one should know Śakti to be in the nose and the Lord Sadāśiva to be in the mouth. (45)
O beautiful one, the six-faced [one] has taught you this single method:
having thus meditated upon Śiva, the supreme cause, who consists of reality (tattva).
Thinking "I am Śiva," one who eats is not defiled;
the Lord constantly eats by means of the six-faced sacrifice itself. (47)
He always drinks water using the threefold method;
while eating solid foods and sweets, he always takes them in the bowl. (48)
One is bound by the *sakala* [form] alone, but by the *niṣkala* one becomes free from duality.
One should know that what is cast upward into the mouth is the sky rendered pure. (49)
One who remains within [the self] is liberated from grasping; a wise person should not engage in this.
By means of emptiness alone, food and other things are constantly bound together once more.
He dwells within food and examines food itself—whether it be that which is licked, sucked, drunk, or various other kinds of edibles. (51)
The supreme lord of the throat and lips should be understood with great effort;
thus, one whose doubts have been severed by the teacher [attains] this divine reality consisting of the principles (tattva). 52.
By merely feeding [him] once, it is as if ten million have been fed;
O Dear One, those who know reality eat in this very manner.
"The Blessed Lord Śiva has stated that no numerical limit exists; for one who has awakened to that which is not the [limited] reality, the number is said to be ten million for the knower. (54)
There is no limit to the number of those who know the reality of the Knower;
the fruit that comes from feeding ten million twice-born ones learned in the Vedas— [is attained by this]. (55)
One who eats even once with a peaceful mind for the sake of a wise man obtains that same fruit;
all food is of the nature of illusion, and the Great Lord, the God, is the agent. 56.
And Śiva himself is indeed the enjoyer; thus it is, without a doubt.
He who understands this is truly a teacher who has reached the further shore of reality.
Seeing him entering the house while the medicinal herbs were playing within, [the sage] thus performed the ritual for the meal correctly, yet he did not spread it everywhere. (58)
It must not be given even to one's own son to those men who possess evil intentions. He who understands it thus is truly wise; otherwise, he would be ignorant. (59)
O Goddess, it constantly consumes food and drink; of this there is no doubt.
The prāṇa moves upward, while the apāna proceeds downward. (60)
Knowing this, one should eat; thus one is liberated from all sins.
By that which has been eaten, O Lord of Gods, the families of both the giver and the eater [are purified]. 61.
"They are swiftly liberated from the ocean of hell after a very long time.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the "Ritual for the Deity, the Reality, and the Edible Offerings," in the *Dīkṣottara* of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
The Self, conjoined with the city of eight, is joined everywhere.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I desire to hear this; you should deign to speak it. || 1 ||
Indeed, when the Self, having become like the wind, is established within the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) as the experiencer of both well-performed deeds and likewise of ill-performed deeds; || 2 ||
Even while that body still exists, his torments in the hells are seen directly and heard in manifold ways. (3)
And in heaven, O Maheśvara, the embodied self, having become subtle, enjoys various pleasures such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and other siddhis, O Śaṅkara.
"Out of your grace, please describe the torments he undergoes in hell.
Īśvara:
Listen, O Goddess; I shall tell you this entire secret in its entirety.
Whether in heaven or even in hell, one experiences the fruits of good and evil deeds; O Maheśvarī, I shall describe that honored karma.
When the gross body, which arises from the elements and pertains to the worldly realm, has been abandoned,
the Self remains established within the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body), having become like the vital wind.
O Goddess, sound, touch, form, and the serpent of objects such as smell, as well as the threefold internal organ— one would not be liberated from these even for a moment.
In every way, it follows him as he moves;
it stands when he stands and runs when he runs.
Without them, O fair-faced one, the self could not remain for even a moment;
yet, joined with them, I shall again attain a body. (10)
O beautiful one, when that embodied being has cast off his former body and is departing,
a new body suddenly arises for him in a mere instant.
Then the body, composed of the elements— earth, water, fire, air, and conjoined with space— is produced from atoms.
Then [one attains] a body consisting of enjoyment, endowed with the eight qualities such as *aṇimā*,
or one born of knowledge beginning with the stars, or even one born of primordial bodies such as Akṛta.
O beautiful lady, in bodies such as those of the Piśācas, in various elements (tattvas), and in hell, there are indeed manifold kinds of torments.
From the elements (bhūtas), the body and the two vital breaths (prāṇas) are born; of this there is no doubt.
The elements consist of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, while they consist of Rudra and Īśvara. (15)
O Goddess, O lady of excellent countenance, the objects of the senses are to be known as consisting of those very atoms which are of the nature of Sadāśiva. (16)
One who is joined with them becomes bound; one who is liberated from them is released.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon Sadāśiva, the Lord of the gods of gods.
When the yogi has thus performed this placement, he shall attain the certainty of the state of Śiva;
this is renowned as Sannyāsa by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (18)
I shall proclaim the initiation of nyāsa in its proper order,
beginning with Brahmā and accompanied by the gods.
O Goddess, the preceptor should install the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka) along with its retinue,
first according to the original sequence and then in the proper order of sound and the other [objects of the senses]. (20)
Having performed the libation for them, one should offer one hundred oblations.
When a hundred have been offered in this manner, O Goddess, one should conclude with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then one should dissolve sound and touch into the pure Brahman;
one should indeed dissolve taste into Viṣṇu, and likewise form and smell.
The high-souled preceptor should perform [the ritual] in the principle of Rudra;
likewise, he should deposit the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the intellect (buddhi) into the principle of Īśvara.
O Goddess, one should place the mind in the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva;
once the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka) has been placed there, O Goddess, one should cause it to fall by means of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
O Goddess of gods, one should offer oblations to Brahmā and Viṣṇu with the syllable *oṃ* of Brahman;
O Goddess of gods, being well-composed, one should cause [the fire] to descend with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). || 25 ||
One should offer oblations to Rudra and Īśvara with the *rudroṃkāra* mantra;
one should offer oblations to the principle (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva with the *nidhana* mantra. || 26 ||
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) must be offered by the high-souled preceptor;
those who receive it are proclaimed to follow the sequence beginning with the "entire" (sakala). || 27 ||
This initiation of the female renunciant has been described to you, O beautiful one;
thus, O Goddess, the fivefold initiation has been explained in brief. (28)
If an initiation has been improperly performed, one should establish that person in steadiness;
therein he may be purified or not purified—this distinction has been declared by me. (29)
When the body of one who has been purified by initiation reaches the state of the five elements (death),
one should perform the final rite (antyeṣṭi) for the purpose of removing the cause of any breach of the rules (samaya). (30)
O fair-faced one, whatever may be desired regarding the sixfold path,
one should perform the oblation in this manner by means of the yoga of withdrawal, according to the proper sequence.
One should offer each oblation individually and, at the end,
present the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for any fault regarding the rules of conduct and for any lapse due to negligence.
The funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) is performed with Śiva alone as an expiation for the sake of purification;
or else, in brief, the path of the Mātṛkās beginning with the letter *kṣa*.
O Goddess of gods, one should offer five oblations for each of those ending in the letter 'a';
the wise practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice with each individual syllable. (34)
The wise one, however, with the entire Mātṛkā mantra,
should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and thus perform the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi). || 35 ||
For one who has been initiated here, the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) is performed by the preceptor;
indeed, the funeral rite itself is purified, and it is purified through expiation (prāyaścitta). || 36 ||
Then the practitioner, being well-composed, should offer oblations for the final rite (antyeṣṭi) after having crossed over all commands and the pure nooses as before. || 37 ||

Endowed with both primordial wisdom (jñāna) and discerning consciousness (vijñāna), the teacher who has reached the further shore of reality and knows the ritual procedures of Kālacakra is designated as one who knows time.
"He indeed liberates the living being who knows the door; there is no doubt in this.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Dīkṣottara* of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the unsurpassed Kālacakra:
from what does time proceed, and how is time described? (1)
For what purpose does time exist? What is time, and who is its impeller? By whom, O Lord, is time impelled so that it brings about all things?
In which various regions does Kāla, the Lord, move?
And how, O Lord, is he known both in worldly and spiritual matters? (3)
Likewise, the houses, the signs, the degrees, as well as the horās, the drekkāṇas, the navāṃśas, and similarly the muhūrtas. || 4 ||
The Vāyavyas, the nāḍīs, the vowels, and likewise the kalās— these are indeed declared to be, in their proper order, the ghaṭikās and the principles (tattvas). (5)
Out of your grace, please explain the southern and northern solstices, as well as the equinox, both in their worldly and spiritual aspects.
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret which you have asked about;
I shall fully declare that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (7)
O Goddess, [I shall explain] both the worldly and the internal, according to the movement of time,
and how the supreme worldly time is indeed known.
I shall explain the internal [time] specifically according to its proper seasons;
one who knows this regulation of time attains the eternal state.
It is accomplished here; there is no doubt regarding this, O Great-minded One, for one who knows time—both worldly and spiritual—in its entirety. (10)

O Goddess, he who knows the right time is remembered as such and attains renown in the world; for the Lord of Gods knows the auspicious and inauspicious, as well as the benefit and harm for the world.
He should relate the entire account, wonderful in its many aspects;
the Kālacakra is fully explained as that which proceeds from the Sun.

The muhūrtas and the lunar days (tithis), as well as the days and nights, the solstices (ayanāni), the seasons, the months, the fortnights, the houses (gṛhas), the lunar mansions (ṛkṣas), and the zodiac signs (rāśis). || 13 ||
All this, O Great Goddess, proceeds from the Sun:
the degrees (aṃśas), the junctions (sandhyās), as well as the stars (tārās), the ascendant periods (horās), and the decans (drekkāṇas). || 14 ||
And when the sun has risen, all this proceeds;
O Supreme Goddess, this is declared to be the worldly time (kāla). (15)
But according to worldly time as it is established, I shall tell it to you; listen, O large-eyed one. (16)
When the sun has risen, the wheel of the house (gṛhacakra) begins to turn;
all the months and zodiac signs are equalized by the sun, without a doubt. (17)
Bhāskara is declared to be the first, and Ketu is situated at the end;
having established the planets upon the petals, located on the petals starting from the east.
O fair-faced one, beginning with the Moon and ending with Ketu, this is known as the House-Wheel (gṛhacakra); it must be understood by one who knows Time. 19.
O Goddess, one who is well-composed should place Soma in the eastern quarter, Bhauma in the southeastern petal, and the Prince (Rajaputra) in the south. (20)
One should place Śanaiścara in the southwest in due order;
with a well-composed mind, one should always place Bṛhaspati in the west.
Having established Rāhu in the northwest and placing Śukra to the north,
and having established Ketu in the northeast, one should then arrange the mantras.
One should place the solar [deity] there, which is said to be the abode of Brahman;
likewise, one should place both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala), as well as the principle of emptiness (śūnyatattva).
Kalāḍhya, Khamala, Kṣapaṇa, Kṣaya, Antaka, and Kaṇṭhoṣṭhya—these are proclaimed as the Gṛhas belonging to the Lord of Gods. || 24 ||
O fair-faced one, having first performed the entire [rite], he who is to recite the mantras should place the supreme syllable, the supreme deity, by means of the station of Brahman. (25)
O beautiful goddess, one who knows the proper time should always remain in the station of Brahmā and perform the placement of the deities upon the pericarp of the sun.
Having thus assigned the houses, one should practice the movement therein;
I shall explain it briefly according to the sequence beginning with the Sakala.
Two ten-thousands, one thousand, and six hundred—O Goddess, these breaths are traditionally taught; one should divide them according to their sequence. (28)
O fair-faced one, for each [of these], the knower of time should recognize exactly two thousand seven hundred [years] for each. (29)
The movement through the house has been fully described in brief, but not in detail;
for, O fair-faced one, one should establish all the houses upon each and every leaf. (30)
O Goddess, one who knows the proper time should thus investigate those sequences;
Dīptāṅgāriṇī and Dhūmā are declared to be the three locations.
The Sun situated within the pericarp should look upon the three petals;
joined with the Self, he who resides in the pericarp is known as the Lord. || 32 ||
One should understand that the oblation (homa) comes first; one should commence the gentle rite (saumya-karma).
The fierce rite (raudra) is in the region of the south-eastern direction, while the pacifying rite (śānti) is indeed in the south.
For the purpose of eradication in the southwest, for one desiring prosperity in the west, for swift destruction in the northwest, and for the acquisition of wealth in the north. (34)
In the northeast, for the sake of attaining knowledge, it has been taught by the Knower of Time;
likewise, in rites for pacification and nourishment, one should proceed according to this sequence. (35)
Those [lines] which are at the openings and sub-openings, and those situated at the edge of the leaf—
what is declared as inauspicious on one side, one should declare as auspicious on the second.
O Goddess, when a wise man perceives that the best of houses belonging to a practitioner has become an obstacle, he should daily worship that house while it remains situated within the pericarp. 37.
Then that house receives grace; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, one house for each [deity] is proclaimed to last for days and nights. (38)
The Self indeed moves within that as well; I shall describe it briefly:
in each individual hour (horā), there are nine hundred [movements]. (39)
O Goddess of the lords of gods, this must be known by one who understands Time; this movement of the vital breaths has been declared to you by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (40)
One who knows this method of calculation and understands the proper time does not come to grief;
indeed, one should declare the auspicious or inauspicious results solely by means of the strength of the house and the hour.
One should recognize a sinful intention in one who is sinful, and prescribe what is auspicious for one who is auspicious;
thus, having understood the relative strength or weakness of oneself or another.
By explaining this, one who knows the proper time attains merit; there is no doubt about this.
O Goddess, the unsurpassed movement of the hours (horā) residing within the body has been described.
Beyond this, I shall describe the supreme movement through the zodiac signs; I will explain how the Self moves from sign to sign. (44)
And it consists of the year; O beautiful one, it has twelve spokes.
O Goddess, the letter *a* is proclaimed as the first, the sign of Aries (*meṣa*). (45)
In this very sequence, it should be understood with diligence;
for the Self moves within that [body] according to its true nature—understand that as it is. (46)
O Goddess of the Gods, for each [zodiac sign] there are eighteen hundred [deities] in sequence; this movement has been fully described for every sign, without a doubt. (47)
For that master of the yoga of time, however, yoga arises;
whatever defect he perceives in a lunar day, he should declare that defect to belong to the corresponding month. (48)
One who knows the conjunctions of time declares the onset of weapons, abundance, famine, and likewise hell; as well as security, health, and the acquisition of wealth. (49)
Furthermore, for every zodiac sign, I shall briefly give the movement of all the decans;
within those nine decans of each sign, I now provide their course. (50)
In each drekkāṇa, however, six hundred [degrees] are proclaimed;
one who knows the rising of each [drekkāṇa] attains success—of this there is no doubt. (51)
For that yogi who applies foot-ointment or collyrium, yoga arises very quickly, whether he is rising up or walking. || 52 ||
For one who knows the science of the knowledge of time, there is no doubt that success is achieved;
he beholds it within the heart-lotus in a month, like an eclipse over a house.
O fair-faced one, during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, the yogi perceives everything; he should declare the auspicious and inauspicious results by means of the decans (drekkāṇas). 54.
Briefly, there are three, five, and one divisions for each [sign];
likewise, briefly, there are decans (drekkāṇas), hour-signs (horās), and so on for each. (55)

The nine factors, beginning with the planets and zodiac signs, are determined by degrees, decans, and horās; good or evil fortune arises solely from the strength of the stars and the moon—of this there is no doubt. (56)
By the power of Tārā and the Moon alone, the auspicious and inauspicious are determined; there is no doubt that the illustrious yogi declares what is beneficial and harmful for the world. (57)
The Self indeed moves within these; listen as I declare them to you:
two thousand and four hundred [yojanas] are to be known. (58)
The movement of the stars has been declared; now hear how it is for the degrees (aṃśas). As great as is the number of stars, so many are the degrees remembered to be. || 59 ||
O Goddess, this movement within the wheel consisting of the year has been explained to you;
by means of this knowledge one is liberated—there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (60)
Thus, for one who does not know this, there would be no knowledge of time;
yet the Self is said to be time, and He is called the Lord. (61)
O Goddess of the gods, by knowing that, one who understands the proper time does not come to grief.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed Kālacakra.
I shall now explain, exactly as it is, that which is joined with the vowels, the movements, and the portions of the channels and winds; listen to me. (63)
Having divided [the circle] into thirty-two parts, one should briefly draw the wheel;
one should then assign sixteen digits (kalā) to the Lord of the God of Gods.
Pūṣā, Yaśas, Sumanā, Prīti, Tuṣṭi, and Dhṛti;
likewise Cakradhṛtikarī, Saumarī, and Cicchubhā. (65)
Śaśinī, Aṅgirā, Chāyā, and Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalā—
these fifteen digits (kalās) are to be known, along with Amṛtā as the sixteenth.
These are indeed declared to be the Kalās; listen now to the [names of the] channels (nāḍīs):
Jvālinī, Śamā, Dhūmrā, Kāmadā, and likewise Vijayā. || 67 ||
Amṛtā, Yaḥ, Hulā, Pakṣitvacavāhā, Atyalambuṣā, Tālujihvā, Upajihvā, and likewise Jihvāvahā; || 68 ||
The channel of the intellect (buddhi), the channel of the vital breath (prāṇa), and likewise the channel carrying nectar—
these sixteen are fully described as being adorned by Marut and the others.
Kṛkara, Devadatta, Pauṇḍarīka, and Dhanañjaya;
as well as Vepathu, Saṃbhrama, Vibhrama, and Bhrama. (70)
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
Ṛṣi, nāga, and kūrma—these sixteen are the great vital airs (mahānilas). || 71 ||

O Goddess, the vowels beginning with 'a' were known by you in the past; having analyzed them, one should explain the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the *kalās* and other elements in their proper sequence. (72)
O fair-faced one, it is declared that there are one thousand [pulses] for each [limb];
furthermore, three hundred are to be known as the vital breaths (prāṇas), and indeed fifty [more].
Likewise, the ritual of the digits (kalādhvara), as well as the vital breaths and the channels, should be understood in brief by the high-souled teacher through a single emergence. 74.
O beautiful one, I have explained to you [the matter] together with the channels, winds, and digits;
hereafter, O Camarī, I shall explain how it is within the constellations. 75.
I shall tell you that; listen as I speak it.
Seven hundred [breaths] are to be known, and likewise the vital breaths (*prāṇas*). (76)
A single breath, as well as one *nimeṣa* and one *lava*, should be known by the high-souled one who understands time. (77)
And a third of a degree along with a seventh part of a lunar mansion has been described to you;
O woman of excellent complexion, the path of degrees for the constellations is said to be ten.
One hundred and one [veins] are to be known by the high-souled one who understands Time;
I shall now describe briefly how the Self moves through these. (79)
O beautiful lady, in each constellation four degrees are proclaimed;
listen as I tell you how the Soul of the Universe moves through them. (80)
A hundred breaths are declared to be a single *prāṇāyāma*; twelve such breaths, together with two *nimeṣas*, are to be understood as [the duration of] one [unit]. (81)
Two lava-s have been described in the same manner by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
one hundred and ninety-two [breaths] are proclaimed as the count of a prāṇa. (82)
Three *nimeṣas* are well known as one-third [of a *tṛṭi*], and two *tṛṭis* are declared to be a *śṛṅgāgra*; this should be understood by those who are well-composed.
Twenty-seven constellations, one hundred and eight [deities], and eighty-four [parts] are proclaimed everywhere. (84)
O Goddess, at midday, the Avīci [hell] is proclaimed;
this should be known by one who understands the proper time regarding the jewels beginning with Kṛttikā. (85)
The goddess Cī is proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments for that man who proceeds upon the path under an auspicious lunar mansion. || 86 ||
One who goes to Vyābhīcī attains all success and becomes wealthy; there is no doubt about this, nor shall any inauspiciousness whatsoever befall him. || 87 ||
This movement has been declared to you for those who worship the Kālacakra;
it is to be understood through a single day and night by the high-souled knower of time.
He who knows this division of the spokes and who, day by day, stabilizes this wheel through meditative concentration, attains the eternal state. (89)
He attains honor in this world and proximity to Śiva in the next;
for him there shall be neither merit nor sin in any way whatsoever. (90)
Whatever evil-doers there may be, they must perform [atonement] by beholding him;
hereafter I shall declare the enumeration of the fruits exactly as they are.
That is declared to be a *tatpara*; sixty of those are proclaimed as a *viduṣa*.
Likewise, sixty *viduṣas* they declare to be a single *bindu*. (92)
The fruit of sixty drops has been declared and explained to you, O beautiful one;
this number of fruits has been stated for what is indeed worldly time.
I shall explain it once more from the perspective of the inner self, O fair-faced one:
that [vitality] of a young and preeminent living being is indeed restrained.
The six breaths are thus fully described; one should designate them as being without pleasure.
Sixty of these [breaths] constitute one nāḍī, and that is said to be one ghaṭikā. (95)
Likewise, sixty ghaṭikās are declared to be one day and night;
those who know the day and night understand that thirty muhūrtas are proclaimed [in a day]. (96)
O beautiful goddess, thirty muhūrtas are declared to constitute one day and night for mortals; this is reckoned as a single unit of time for Māta.
Nine hundred muhūrtas should be known by the high-souled knower of time;
twelve such calculated months are here called a year.
I shall tell you how many muhūrtas there are in a year: ten thousand and eight hundred are said to be their number. (99)
O lady of beautiful hips, these Muhūrtas have indeed been described by me to you;
O Goddess, I shall likewise describe to you the Navaya-muhūrta. (100)
Seven hundred and twenty [revolutions] in the Lord of the Gods—of this there is no doubt.
This movement has been declared by me; it should be understood by those who desire their own welfare. 101.
By this sequential method, one shall attain perfection in recitation;
for that practitioner of recitation, mastery over the three periods of time arises.
In each zodiac sign, O Lord of the Five Gods, there is no doubt that there are five ghaṭikās;
it is recorded that the vowel 'a' arises during those five ghaṭikās, O Lord of the Five Gods. (103)
In this very sequence, it should be understood with diligence;
the worldly [time] and the striking [of the hour] are proclaimed as six parts. (104)
Six months are indeed fully described as the northern course; it is taught that for the southern course, the same duration should be known by the high-souled one who understands time. (105)
I shall tell you of that very zodiac sign in which Time resides;
