O Goddess, the first rising has been described to you by means of the signs. (106)
In whichever zodiac sign the soul resides, that sign initiates the month;
these are Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, and likewise Taurus. (107)
The sixth zodiac sign is said to be Gemini (Mithuna); six months are thus proclaimed.
[The subsequent signs are] Cancer (Karkata), Leo (Simha), Virgo (Kanya), Libra (Tula), and Scorpio (Vṛścika). || 108 ||
And the two bows are declared to be in the south;
listen duly, O lady of virtuous vows, as they are proclaimed month by month. 109.
Four hundred and fifteen vital breaths (prāṇas) are declared to occur month by month, exactly as it is, O beautiful one. (110)
O Goddess, when one situated in the north moves toward the south, the distance traversed at the midpoint is known as the equinox (viṣuva). || 111 ||
This transition is described as situated from south to north;
when one has abandoned the objects of the senses and becomes established in space, [this occurs]. (112)
When the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, rises upward, that should be known as the Viṣuvant by those who desire their own welfare. 113.
Thus it has been taught and spoken in all the tantras:
the night is remembered as being in the lower part, while the solstice occurs in the middle.
When the breath is held motionless above and below while expanding in the middle, it is called *hikkā* (hiccup); *cikkā* is likewise described, and these occur in eight ways in succession. (115)
A deficient night (ūnarātra) becomes hiccup (hikkā), and the intercalary month (adhimāsa) is yawning (vijṛmbhikā).
Debt (ṛṇa) becomes coughing (kassa), while exhalation (niśvāsa) is called wealth (dhana). 116.
This movement has been fully explained for those who worship the Kālacakra;
one who knows the method of this movement attains the eternal state. || 117 ||
Impelled by Śakti, O Goddess, he causes various activities to be performed; through the application of the union of spies, he sustains himself. 118.
And this has been declared as *āra* by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
it includes time and mental construction, O Supreme Goddess, along with the powers (*śakti*). (119)
It undergoes modification and is attended by its attendants;
it is called "untimely sound" (akālakala), and even the proponent's [position] is extracted in two ways. (120)
Sadāśiva, the God of gods, is himself remembered as Time manifest;
O lady of beautiful countenance, this Time is eternal even for Brahmā and the other deities.
And that very [time] is metaphorically designated through its movements by means of its transitions;
otherwise, by what could time—which is eternally present—be so metaphorically designated? (122)
By this ritual practice, time is thus worshipped;
time is known through movement, and from movement comes accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.
In movement there is both enjoyment and liberation; he who knows movement does not come to grief.
Therefore, O Goddess, this movement should be understood with great effort. (124)
He who understands both external and internal time is a knower of time;
one who merely indicates the constellations should not be considered a knower of time. (125)
O Goddess, this science of astrology has been declared by me in brief;
it should be understood with diligent effort by those who know time and are its learned practitioners.
The increase of the day occurs during the night, and the decrease of the night occurs during the day;
by this convention, worldly usage is maintained.
For him there is neither night nor day, nor the solstice, nor the equinox;
O Goddess, Maheśvara himself is eternally and constantly present there in person. (128)
O Great Goddess, his desire is served by ritual offerings;
thus is Time described, which proceeds everywhere.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Section on Kālacakra," in the *Dīkṣottara* of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear; please tell it to me out of grace.
The essence of the nectar from your mouth—the nectar of knowledge—has been drunk by me.
I have heard all this—which is difficult to obtain—through your grace: the entire account of the origin and dissolution of the world, along with its continuous succession of kalpas.
Now I wish to hear; grant me your grace, O Śaṅkara! O Maheśvara, [tell me] the measure of the lifespan and the experience of human beings. (3)
How will those deluded ones understand that consciousness is their death? For that which has arisen is subject to destruction; this is what is proclaimed as "action" (kṛti). || 4 ||
But when that [body] is destroyed, what form is it that is severed, since it follows the sequence of time?
O Lord, how is one who is near death to be recognized in this regard? (1089) 4.
"Please explain all of this in brief out of your grace.
Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent! Again, excellent! This question is very difficult to obtain."
"I have been asked by you for the sake of clarity; listen, O fair-faced one, to how death becomes imminent for another."
One may perform it for a day, or for a muhūrta, or even instantly;
now listen to me regarding the specific signs by which it is characterized.
And that [sign] is indeed twofold for men, to be observed externally and internally;
it consists of the circle of stars and the houses, with the auspicious and inauspicious results occurring through their respective reversals.
The external sign is to be known as distinct from the internal sign born of *nāda*.
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the external signs in brief.
Having fashioned a wheel consisting of nine compartments, the wise man should count them;
then, in each and every compartment therein, he should write the circle of lunar mansions.
One should observe the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī as being beneficial for the house;
likewise, the three asterisms known as the birth [asterism] signify prosperity and its opposite.
The wheel of Tārā, both auspicious and inauspicious, consists of Kṣema, Pratyara, Sādhana, Naidhana, Maitra, and Paramamaitra.
A wise person should observe that [native] at birth and other times when it is afflicted by malefic planets;
for conception, the ritual of impregnation, and birth occur through Mars, the Sun, and Saturn.
O Goddess, he in whom these malefic planets reside is slain;
indeed, that man whose planets are thus adverse is surely as good as dead. (14)
Even if alone, when conjoined with a benefic, one leads a life of hardship; but when there are two benefics, there is prosperity at every step, even if situated in the *kapāla* (the second house).

O Goddess, just as in the three births there are cruel, gentle, auspicious, and inauspicious [influences], so too a man should remain well-disposed and eternally contented even during the three gentle periods.
Others likewise speak thus: "Let there be a union with Tāra;
she is the destroyer of sins, the abode of prosperity, the bestower of boons, and the one who grants the supreme state. (17)
Those [planets] that destroy security and those that bestow security, as well as those arising from many defects, exist in opposition;
yet they bring about the attainment of knowledge and the success of the practitioner's task. (18)
Situated in the house of death (the eighth house), they cause the destruction of the body;
however, in the case of Maitra, they would produce friendliness even if there were otherwise any cruelty. (19)
For houses cause harm to their wives, yet houses that possess supreme friendliness are gentle and bestow auspiciousness, yielding results one, two, or three times greater.
When malefic planets bestow auspicious results through the sequence of their qualities, one should thus understand the planetary transits for oneself or for another. (21)
O Goddess, men awaken to their own auspicious and inauspicious [karma];
O Goddess, listen as I clearly explain the portents of bodily misfortune (aṅgāriṣṭa).
With his throat, lips, and palate parched, and with a complexion suddenly turning blood-red, even his shoulder becomes crooked; within a year, he meets his destruction.
If one sees a circle of fire in the sky day after day—
whether white, green, or black— he indeed has only half a year remaining of his life. (24)
When the sun appears devoid of rays and the moon is free from its mark,
and when the light of the stars is seen within the *suṣumṇā* [the solar channel], one's life is limited to six months.
He who sees a golden-colored person, or one who is blackish-brown in a dream,
or sees his own head-shadow, lives for three seasons.

Likewise, drinking oil, anointing the body with oil, wearing red garlands, garments, and wreaths, or riding upon or sitting in vehicles drawn by donkeys or camels, or being accompanied by vultures, crows, jackals, and the like. (27)
He shall see ghosts and piśācas, as well as a marriage and the devouring of his own limbs; and in a dream he will indeed obtain a female companion, if he lives. (28)
When the *nṛttajjoma* and *medhā* [vital breaths] reach a state of motionlessness in the *śaṅkhāvarta* of the arm and at the joints of the ankles, he will certainly meet his death. (29)
If he does not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, and the luminous orbs of the Moon and Sun, that man will certainly die.

If the tongue becomes like the Arundhatī star, one will not see a hundred-year lifespan; if it is short, one will certainly not see a long life, or it is said that there will be a knot at the tip of the nose.
If one sees the orbs of the sun and moon within the circle of light by means of the beautiful rays of the fingers, his lifespan is indeed four months. || 32 ||
The smoke that has entered the cavity of the palate is not released by him;
that deluded soul does not see [the light], and he lives for only one season. || 33 ||
He becomes stout all of a sudden and suddenly becomes thin;
he is excessively fearful and excessively [passionate]; for such a person has but a single year of life remaining. (34)
In a dream, one who has reached her fertile season sees a man facing her, with a black hand, clad in black garments, and holding an iron staff.
And the body of one whose life has reached its end after two months becomes cold. || 36 ||
If one sees lightning without clouds at night,
even in a place where it has been seen before, there will be a conflagration of the quarters, and the lifespan remaining is no more than three months.
One does not hear sounds clearly; both eyes seem to hear at once;
and one smells odors while being blind—these are signs of one whose life-force has departed.
Behold: the tongue becomes black, the mouth [resembles] a red lotus or a blue water-lily, various colors appear on the limbs, and one weeps all at once. (39)
If there is no trembling of the navel, he will perish within half a month;
having failed to recognize the auspicious tongue, one has inhaled the lamp with the mouth. 40.
And the crow-like [sound] was produced; for a man whose life lasts four months, the vital air (marut) constantly follows the cavity of the mouth, causing hiccupping. 41.
One with drooping ears may see [the sun] within half a month when his life has departed;
thus, by many such signs impelled by death, one should recognize [the approaching end]. 42.
Now, O Goddess, listen to that which arises from *nāda* and resides within yogis;
this has been proclaimed by the Three-eyed One at the rising of the sun for the yogi. (43)
At that time, he should contemplate his own death and life;
then the yogi, having become pure and steadfast, shall remain in the yogic posture. (44)
The wise one, awakening to and emerging from the sound within the *suṣumnā*, should remain ever vigilant, disciplined, and absorbed in oneness with that sound. (45)
One should always calculate that for each individual channel, nine hundred breaths flow; these are the nine powers at the time of the transition (saṅkrānti). 46.
Abiding in the state of the channels, the Lord Ātman flows by his own nature;
however, when the vital breaths are in transition, he flows while stationed in the Suṣumnā.
O Lord, having understood the time at the equinox during the downward flow, the yogi desires to live for one year with each day and night. (48)
By living for exactly two days and nights, one shall live for two years;
for one whose [life] departs after five days, death shall occur within five years.
When six, seven, or eight days have elapsed, he lives for that many years.
The Lord of Time measures time by means of day and night;
sometimes the Lord of the Śakala [universe] experiences the passing of seven watches.
O Goddess, [the lifespan] would be six months; for three months it lasts for six praharas;
for five [months] it is half [of that]; with four [months], they live for four months. 52.
If the practitioner of mantras has a lifespan of half a month,
he lives for eight days once three watches have passed and two watches have likewise elapsed.
If [the breath] is displaced for only one watch (*prahara*), one may live for four [watches]; he in whom it flows for half a watch lives for two days. (54)
One whose [breath] has gone to two or three paths meets immediate death;
or, having ascended that time, it flows forth toward Yama.
One should observe for half a month or half a day; at that time, certainty will arise.
This has been told to you, O beautiful one, regarding the period born of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa). 56.
Or else, O Goddess of the Gods, another man as well—by yogis always having his two thumbs placed upon the path of the ears—does not hear any sound. (57)
O Goddess, within six months, one should predict his death; [this occurs] in the midst of the terrible [state], and not by means of a mere ritual act. 58.
If one does not hear [the teaching] constantly, even having attained it, he would die;
likewise, having produced [the realization] and heard it, he would likewise meet with the conjunction of death. (59)
The yogi who is constantly engaged and reflects upon this should perceive the collection within the mouth and the five transitions of time.
If one should lead [the breath] elsewhere while it is being generated, it would cause the loss of vital substance, mental agitation, and the increase of disease. || 61 ||

When life is sustained by the sun during its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), there occurs the breaking up of the household, the loss of friends, the waning of splendor, and the increase of suffering, occurring in the right nostril.
When the eight transitions occur, that indeed is the arising of the conjunction of the Karaṇas;
[therein] there is neither the breaking of knots nor the opening of the cavern.

Sphoṭikā, diseases of the piercing pain (śūla), disorders of the chest, and provocation [of the humors] occur when [the breath] resides within the left nostril for five and eight [ghaṭīs] during the transition. (64)
It cures fever, diseases, and headache, as well as pain, stiffness, and afflictions; it brings about freedom from disease, urinary disorders (prameha), and dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). || 65 ||
Maheśvara is situated in the middle of the phlegmatic (ślaiṣmala) disease;
at whatever time the wind flows, it flows during that same time on the following day. (66)
A living being is afflicted by diseases during the first watch of the night;
therefore, the mark of the upper touch is on the nose, while that of the lower [touch] is below the nose.
The defects of trees previously mentioned extend upwards;
if they touch [the tree] on the right side, there is ruin within a *krośa*.
In the midst [of the assembly], touching the central clarity, they achieved the overcoming of others;
through a single transition, they flow forth in many ways here and there. (69)
His [merit] is produced by the worship of the *lā* [syllable],
when he has become weak and has resorted to the state of being without seed (*nirbīja*). || 70 ||
One should effect the attainment of sovereignty over the dharmas and the reunion with loved ones when twelve [units] are in the pair. 71.

The yogin always attains [this] within a year; however, when eighty-nine [days] have passed, the destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs. This happens through the cessation of each single day until thirty years have been reached. || 73 ||
When, at the time of day on the previous day, Death issues his command... || 74 ||
One should understand the movement of time as follows: [the flow] through the *iḍā* and *suṣumṇā*.
The time born of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*)... [is to be understood].
Suṣumnā is in the right prāṇa, and she carries that very [breath] as well. || 76 ||
The Maya and the Nasmṛta;
by those two, through three exhalations, are the Viṣuva and the Ayana.
The crocodile, the water-jar, the fish, the ram, and likewise the twins—
[these are the signs] through which the Suṣumnā [flows], and that is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
O Great Goddess, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius—these zodiac signs are within the *iḍā* [nāḍī]. || 79 ||
For the transit into Capricorn and the others, Mercury is the lord of the Kaikeya [nakṣatra]. || 80 ||
In the [spheres] beginning with Āditya, there are fourteen; the emission of the vital breath (prāṇavikṣepa) should be known, and they awaken in succession. (81)
For one whose conduct is during the day, there would be a duality for that knower; [it is] the time of the intellect (*matikāla*), conceived as being near the final half. 82.
Beginning from the first rising, seventeen breaths (prāṇas) occur in succession;
sixty breaths are thus declared, and then again eleven breaths.
One *nimeṣa* is indeed one *lava*, and eleven minus one [i.e.,
ten] *tṛṭis* constitute the movement starting from Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī, as they are joyfully proclaimed. (84)
Thus has the movement born of the body in the spheres of the sky been described to you.
Having understood this, the yogi, having meditated upon the syllable "de" [or "da"] one hundred thousand times, should conquer death through recitation.
That very Lord is Time, the unconquerable, dark and tawny;
for as the Lord established within the channels and the planets, Time impels all things.
There, having composed the mind in meditative concentration, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of Time—
Śambhu, whose feet are like lotuses, the seed-syllable situated as the Lord of Time (Kāleśvara).
When the position of the nāḍī-graha is established, one should recite the mantra according to the increase;
then, his supreme knowledge of the three times proceeds.
The yogi who is disciplined speaks of the past, the future, and the present;
within six months, the knowledge of time proceeds for him. (89)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, the perfection of knowledge of the three times arises for the yogin who recites [this], whether he be the soul of time or otherwise. 90.
Time does not reckon its end, even when time itself has passed;
it transcends the pure state [of worldly existence], having overcome death and old age, and being entirely free from all diseases. (91)
For the yogin who seeks mastery over time, the cognition of hearing from afar, as well as reflection and vision, arises; of this there is no doubt. (92)
For the yogi who has attained one-pointed concentration and is focused on the nostril, all that arises is the great fear of death at any moment. (93)
The yogi should recite and meditate; he should not entertain doubt in this matter.
Or, the one of great intelligence who recites the five-syllabled mantra— (94)
Whether reciting one hundred, twenty, or even five hundred and eight times, the kings of mantras are: *Oṃ jṛṃ saḥ śivāya namaḥ*. (95)
This supreme conqueror of death is the highest remover of all suffering;
no mantra equal to this is found within the three worlds. (96)
This five-syllable mantra is saluted by all the gods;
this king of mantras, which is very difficult to obtain, is worshipped here by the thirty deities. (97)
At its beginning are three deities; the fourth is the supreme Īśvara;
the fifth is Sadāśiva, the Lord of the gods of gods, the supreme state.
O God, this deity consisting of fivefold nature has been recited by all the gods;
they have also constantly offered oblations to him. Therefore, O gods, he is the conqueror of death. (99)
In ancient times, by the grace of this mantra, death was conquered by the gods;
they became free from old age and disease and were endowed with supreme sovereignty. (100)
May they be fulfilled in all desires, acting with grace through their bonds;
free from dualities and free from ego, they shall cast off their bodies at the time of dissolution.
There is no returning for them; having reached the supreme goal, they who always recite this, having obtained this best of mantras, [attain] the Self. (102)
Those who pride themselves on the knowledge of the sacrificial animals [regard] the self as threefold and manifold;
[they hold] the self to be the principle of primordial matter (prakṛti), while the inner self (antarātman) is that of the person (puruṣa). || 103 ||
The Supreme Self is Viṣṇu, the Yogi, the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
the Self is the agent of action, while the Inner Self is the causal agent. (104)
But the Supreme Self is indifferent; those who possess the qualities are subject to them. The Supreme Self, Maheśvara, is endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. || 105 ||
Indeed, the yogis such as Sanaka and others, ever-disciplined, meditate;
they know liberation, O beautiful one—this has been explained to you for the sake of the yogis.
Thus, even for one who studies all the Vedas and practices them,
they indeed declare the knowledge of Brahman through the form of sentences beginning with the syllable *oṃ*.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Rudra—these three gods are together;
and sattva, rajas, and tamas are declared to be the triad of qualities (guṇas). || 108 ||
The three states—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—are proclaimed as the three steps;
indeed, these alone are the three Vedas: the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (109)
This indeed is the supreme syllable Om; they know it to consist of all the gods, the supreme bliss, Brahman, existing in a state of equilibrium, and composed of darkness (tamas). || 110 ||
When fire is cast into fire, it remains like water in water;
it becomes devoid of pleasure and devoid of consciousness, like a lump of clay, a staff, or a stone. 111.
Those who know the Vedas are certain that nirvāṇa is supreme bliss; now I shall explain it further—listen with respect, O virtuous one. (112)
Just as the god is worshipped in his manifest form with faces on all sides,
so too are Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and the great Saṅkarṣaṇa worshipped.
Vāsudeva is the Blessed One, the abode of all, Nara, Hari; he is named Pradyumna-kāraka, indeed Kāma, who can take any form at will. (114)
Aniruddha is proclaimed as the ego (ahaṃkāra) when it has ceased;
Saṃkarṣaṇa is the intellect (buddhi), the city consisting of prāṇa and apāna.
Vāsudeva is primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of darkness (tamas) when the qualities are in equilibrium;
for it is while abiding in that equilibrium of the qualities that he remains changeless and free from affliction.
In this manner, living beings dwell for a full day and night within the primary element (pradhāna). || 117 ||
Driven by the processes of creation and dissolution, they go forth once again;
in the springtime, the latent impressions of their own nature and qualities manifest within all beings.
p.
1112) Impression (vāsanā) and the source of impression (vāsana) alone is sung as Vāsudeva;
he is not recited as Devadeva in the Pāñcarātra. || 119 ||
Through the division of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*, the syllable *m* is the form of Māra;
it is characterized by the states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, which correspond to the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
By these forms, the wise have fully described the yoga of the Vedas;
among them, that which is named the Fourth (Turya) has its foundation in primordial nature (prakṛti).
O sinless one, I have already previously explained this very [nature] of the Puruṣa to the Sāṃkhyas;
all of this has been told to you—what more do you ask?
Likewise, there are the Vaimalas and those who are Pāśupatas;
for the Vaimalas, the Lord is Dhruva, and for the Kārakas, he is above that.
The knot of Māyā remains fixed for those who belong to the creation of Śiva;
for them, that supreme state is purified by the path of initiation (dīkṣā). (124)
Thus has been described the abode of Īśvara for the Pāśupatas;
one whose self is purified by the path of conduct goes there, of this there is no doubt. (125)
"Existence," "non-existence," "so it exists," and "the Arhat, the person"—these are certainly worshipped as the deity called the Jīva; of this there is no doubt. (126)
O Goddess, this has been fully explained together with the Śākyas and the Arhats,
as well as the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas who proclaim the state of supreme bliss.
In the Itihāsas, the Supreme Lord Puruṣa is thus celebrated as "the Ancient Person" (Purāṇapuruṣa); and in the Purāṇas, he is likewise called "the Seer" (Kavi). || 128 ||
The pure Lord, the Master of the universe, whose face is turned in every direction— the God who exists as one, as many, and likewise as a hundred thousandfold. (129)
Those who do not know the supreme reality sing of the God of gods, Maheśvara,
while he is celebrated by the sages through many different names.
Some speak thus of the "jīva," others likewise of the "puruṣa";
some call it the "prāṇin," and indeed others the "pudgala" or even the "paśu. (131)
Some wise ones [describe] the Self as subtle and all-pervading; others [call it] the unborn; and still others [distinguish] the individual self (antarātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). 132.
Beyond this very point, the netherworlds (pātālas) follow in their respective order. || 133 ||
I shall explain it in brief; understand it, O fair-faced one:
Ābhāsa, Tālasutāla, Śrītāla, and Gabhastika. (134)
The mountain-heap is declared to be Pātāla, known by the name Hema;
above these, however, the seven worlds are celebrated.
The first is declared to be the world of the earth (bhūloka), in which the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) are desired;
and within it is the fourteenfold sphere of worldly existence (saṃsāramaṇḍala).
O lady of excellent hips, I shall likewise describe to you how one should extract [the syllables], beginning with Brahmā and ending with the Piśāca, O beautiful one. (137)
The domestic animal is said to be the first, and the wild beast immediately after that;
likewise, birds are mentioned, as well as reptiles. (138)
The immobile is declared the fifth, and likewise the human;
O Goddess, this fourteen-fold sphere of transmigratory existence (saṃsāramaṇḍala) should be known. (139)

Because the self transmigrates through these [states], it is therefore remembered as "saṃsārī" (the transmigrator). Furthermore, among human beings, birth is subsequently remembered as "uddharaṇa" (deliverance). || 140 ||
The lowest-born (antyaja) is declared first, followed by the status of the Śūdra; then the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya, and finally the Brāhmaṇa caste—perform their deliverance. 141.
In the case of the office of a Brahman, however, one should likewise apply [this] during the performance of purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*),
beginning with the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending finally with the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*).
I have already stated previously that one should perform [this] in the world of mortals; once the body has been purified by sacrifices, one should indeed employ it in the mortal realm. || 143 ||

Then he should again extract them in order: the world of the earth (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), the world of heaven (svarloka), as well as Maharloka, Janarloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka. (144)
Likewise, O Goddess, the pure worlds, as well as the seats of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and the seat of Rudra within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) have been described. || 145 ||
The Nāgas and Garuḍas, as well as the Suras and Kiṃpuruṣas; the Agnikumāras, Maya, and likewise Bali. || 146 ||
O Goddess, these seven who are established in the netherworlds (pātāla) have been described:
Bala, Atibala, Balavān, and Balavikrama; || 147 ||
Bala, Balānta, and Balogra are also proclaimed;
these seven are celebrated as the lords of the worlds, possessed of great strength.
By these pure ones, these seven netherworlds (pātālas) are indeed purified:
Śarva, Rudra, Bhīma, Bhava, and likewise Ugra. (149)
Mahādeva, as well as Īśāna—these are the lords of the world of Rudra;
also Kāpālīśa, Aja, Buddha, and Vajradehapramardana. || 150 ||
Vibhūtikhyāya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa—these are declared to be the ten Rudras stationed in the eastern direction. (151)
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka. || 152 ||
In the southeastern direction, O beautiful one, the Rudras have been described to you;
they are Dhūmra-hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Karta. (153)
Kālarudra is renowned, as well as Dharma and Dharmapati;
the Uniter and the Separator—these have been described by me. (154)
In the southern direction, the ten Rudras are indeed described in successive order:
Naiṛta, Māraṇa, Hantā, Krūradṛṣṭi, and Bhayānaka. || 155 ||
Ūrdhvakeśa, Virūpākṣa, Dhūmra, Lohita, and Dṛṣṭavān—these ten Rudras in the southwest (Nairṛta) have indeed been described in their proper sequence. 156.
Balohyati, Bala, and the very powerful Pāśahasta;
Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka. || 157 ||
Baḍavāmukha and Bhīṣaṇeśa are well-worshipped by Varuṇarāja;
indeed, these ten Rudras in the western quarter are described in their proper order. (158)
Swift, light, with the speed of the wind, subtle, sharp, the ender of decay;
the destroyer of the five, the one with five tufts of hair, the one with matted locks, whose vehicle is the clouds. (159)
In the north-western direction, the ten Rudras are indeed described in successive order:
Nidhīśa, Rūpavān, Dhanya, Saumyadeha, and Jaṭādhara. || 160 ||
Lakṣmīdhṛk, Ratnadhṛk, Śrīdhṛk, Prasāda, and Prakāśana—
these ten Rudras of great power reside in the northern direction.
The lord of knowledge, the omniscient one, the enjoyer of wisdom, the master of the Vedas; the lord of the gods, the lord of all, the protector of beings, and the lover of offerings. || 162 ||
The creator of all sciences and likewise the bringer of pleasure and pain—these ten Rudras in the northeast have indeed been described in their proper sequence. (163)
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, Marutāśana,
Ugrasena, Adhivīra, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭravān. || 164 ||
Below, the ten Rudras are indeed described in their proper sequence:
Śambhu, Vibhu, Guṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, and Tridaśavandita. (165)
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, and the discerning Nabholipsu—
these ten mighty Rudras took their stand in the upward direction.
When one has reached the world of Bhūr and performs the rites of consecration,
first the immobile beings are to be purified, and after that, the crawling reptiles.
Birds, wild animals, and domestic animals—in this sequence—the divine species must likewise be purified by the wise. 168.
Having effected deliverance from saṃsāra, effect deliverance from birth!
The *antyaja* is declared first, and the *śūdra* immediately after that. (169)
One should extract [the syllables] in sequence up to Brahmā, following the order of Vaiśya and Kṣatriya;
one should purify them in due order with the faces beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Vāmadeva.

One should purify, in sequence, the Lord residing in the *antyaja* with the *Īśa-mantra*, the divine births with the *Gāyatrī*, and whatever diverse objects of meditation there may be with the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*).
Having established [the disciple] in the state of Brahman, he should perform the purificatory rites:
the impregnation (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), and the birth ceremony (jātakarman). || 172 ||
The naming ceremony, the first outing, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the initiation, and likewise the tying of the sacred thread; 173.
The girdle, the tooth-stick, the deerskin, the *triyāyuṣa* [mantra],
Bhūteśa, the *pāśupata*, and the third, the *gaṇa*.
The fourth is Gaṇeśvara, and the fifth is Uttamādhisāka. || 175 ||
Seven [types of rites] have been proclaimed as unprecedented:
those pertaining to the iṣṭi sacrifice, those pertaining to the dārṣada, those pertaining to the elements, and likewise those pertaining to Soma. || 176 ||
The four [sons] are indeed proclaimed in due order as Devavrata;
then, having performed the Godāna ceremony, he likewise performed the Patnīsaṃyojana rite.
The Śrāddha on the Aṣṭakā festival, as well as the Śrāvaṇī, Āgrayaṇī, Caitrī, and Āśvayujī, are proclaimed to be Pākayajñas. || 178 ||
The Ādhāna, the Agnihotra, and then the Darśa;
the Paurṇamāsī is to be known [next], and after that the Sautrāmaṇī. || 179 ||
For these are known as the Havis-yajñas; they should be understood in their proper order:
the Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, and the Ukthya-yajña is the third. (180)
The fourteenth is to be known as the Ṣoḍaśī; then the Vājapeya is the fifteenth. The sixteenth is said to be the Trirātra, and the Aptoryāma is the seventeenth. || 181 ||
The Soma-sacrifices are thus enumerated, seven in number in their proper sequence:
the first is Hiraṇyapāda, and after that is Hiraṇyaguhyam.
Hiraṇyameḍhra is the third, Hiraṇyapāṇi is the fourth, and Hiraṇyagarbha is declared as the fifth, O Supreme Goddess. (183)
Likewise, O Goddess, this sixth is proclaimed as Hiraṇyaśrotra;
Hiraṇyatvak is likewise declared, and Hiraṇyākṣa is the eighth. (184)
Hiraṇyajihva was the ninth, and Hiraṇyadhṛk was the tenth;
these ten sacrifices are remembered as being beyond the thousandfold sacrifice.
Surrounded by a retinue of one hundred followers,
he should perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) after ten other sacrifices.

In this manner, one becomes a householder and likewise a forest-dweller; thereafter, one should apply oneself to the life of a wandering mendicant, and finally, one should perform the funeral rite. || 187 ||
Then, having performed the funeral rites and having raised [the soul] upwards, one should unite it;
subsequently, one should unite that which is joined with the *puryaṣṭaka* into the *tattvas*.
Water, fire, wind, and space, as well as ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), intellect (buddhi), the qualities (guṇas), and the unmanifest (avyakta)— I shall describe these to you in their proper order. (189)
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkala;
Aṣaḍi, Daṇḍi, Bhārabhūti, and Lākula. || 190 ||
This group of eight secrets has been proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self; after this follow Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, and Jalpeśvara. (191)
Āmrātikeśa, Mahākāla, as well as Madhyamakeśvara, Kedāra, and Bhairava—these are known as the eight most secret [shrines]. || 192 ||
Gaya, Kurukṣetra, Khala, Nakhala, Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīma as the eighth. (193)
(1127) Indeed, this which is more secret than the secret has been told by me to you: Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, and Mahālaya. 194.
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu—this is indeed declared to be the group of eight sacred sites (pavitrāṣṭaka) in their proper sequence. || 195 ||
Phaṭala, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kālañjaravana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Sthaleśvara. || 196 ||
Likewise, Sthūleśvara is said to be situated above all;
these eight locations are to be known as established within the ego (ahaṅkāra). || 197 ||
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra; then the Saumya, Prajeśa, and the Brāhma is remembered as the eighth. || 198 ||
This group of eight divine origins (devayony-aṣṭaka), which rests within the veil of the intellect (buddhy-āvaraṇa),
consists of Saṃvarta, Ekavīra, Kṛtānta, and Jananāśana. || 199 ||
Mṛtyuhantā, Raktākṣa, Mahākrodha, and Durjaya—
these are declared to be the Lords of Wrath (Krodheśvaras) in their proper sequence and order.
I shall now speak again of the Tejōṣṭaka; listen as it is being told by me:
[it is] the overseer of the worlds, the overseer of the hosts, the destroyer of Tripura in the third heaven.
Sarvarūpa, Śānta, Nimeṣa, and Meṣaṇa—
thus the eightfold Tejas has been described by me to you in due order.
Above the eightfold fire (tejoṣṭaka), however, stands again the eightfold yoga:
Akṛta, Kṛta, Bhairava, and Brāhma. (203)
The state of being Vaiṣṇava, then Kaumārabhauma, and likewise Śraikaṇṭya— these indeed have been described for the yogins exactly and in their proper sequence. (204)
Above these, however, twelve auspicious ones are recorded:
Vāma, Bhīma, and likewise Rudra;
[then] Īśvara, Ajeśa, Ananta, and Ekaśiva. (205–206)
These twelve Suśivas have indeed been proclaimed in their proper sequence;
above Suśiva, however, Vīrabhadra is proclaimed.
The Lord of the Maṇḍala, as well as Vāmadevodbhava and likewise Bhavodbhava. || 208 ||
O Lord with the single tawny eye, these have been described in successive order;
together with the one the size of a thumb, they are known as the eight Great Gods (Mahādevas). (209)
Above these, however, the three lineages of gurus are remembered;
[the first is] Śivaprabhu, [the second is] * * * * * * *? [and the third is] Pratāpana.
Prāṇada, Śivabhīma, Karāla, Piṅgala, Mahendra, Dinakṛt, and Pradodakṣaṇa; || 211 ||
The Karevara is likewise declared, in due order and sequence:
Kaṇṭhaghaṇṭā, Bṛhantā, and Nādāśveta. || 212 ||
The teacher, who is the embodiment of Śiva, is equal to the Yajurveda; likewise, Nārāyaṇa is the eldest. || 213 ||
In the Vipragaṇḍa [section], Dara, Mayamālin, Gahaneśa, and Pīḍana are likewise desired as the line [of deities]. (214)
Śvetadāman and Sudāman, the worlds...
[and] Akṣasūtra, Ekapāda, as well as Gṛdhraśiveśvara. || 215 ||
And likewise Hustatha, as well as Ṛṣabha, Gokarṇa, and the god Guheśvara. || 216 ||
Guḥāvāsī, Śikhaṇḍī, and likewise Jaṭamāyin;
Ugra, Bhasmaśikhī, Śūlī, and indeed Sugīti as well. (217)
Suphala, Gahāsa, Kāraka, Lāṅgavistara, as well as Tridaṇḍī, Śavana, Sājya, and likewise Lakulīśa. || 218 ||
The second row is declared in successive order as follows:
Deva, Caraṇa, Dīrgha, Vā, Haribhū, and so on, according to their sequence. (219)
Ritibhūti is thus declared, and Sthāṇu follows after that;
likewise Sadyojāta, Ruṇḍī, Ṣaṇmukha, and Caturānana. (220)
Cakrapāṇi, as well as Kūrma, Ardhanārīśvara, Meṣasaṃvartaka, Bhasmeśa, and Kāmanāśana. || 221 ||
Kapālī, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and likewise Vaṣaṭkāra—these are declared to be the sense of smell through the intellect, ending with the element earth. || 222 ||
But it [perceives] the subtle element of taste as its object, and taste itself. || 223 ||
Then the organ of action is the anus; the tongue is known as the sense-organ.
However, these must be purified in succession according to their proper order. (224)
From fire arises the subtle element of form, which is designated as the object "form";
the organ of action is known as the foot, and the eye is proclaimed to be the faculty of cognition.
This obstruction of fire must be purified in due order;
in the case of air, however, the subtle element of touch is the object, known as "touch. (226)
The hand is known as the organ of action, and the skin is the sense organ of perception;
the preceptor should purify these within the element of air in successive order.
In space, the subtle element of sound is the object known as "sound";
speech is considered the organ of action, and the ear is considered the organ of perception. 228.
The knower of mantras should purify [the elements] in the ether in successive order:
the body hairs, blood, and flesh are said to be produced by the Mother. (229)
The aggregate of marrow, bone, and semen is said to be the triad derived from the father;
food, drink, and the mind are likewise proclaimed in their respective order. (230)

Within each of the principles beginning with earth, that which is to be purified should be cleansed according to the rule and in due order, as prescribed for the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest. 231.
Having performed it thus according to the rule, one should again offer the eightfold yoga;
having offered to the three rows of gurus, one should then offer to the principal deity.
O beautiful goddess, listen further to that which is even beyond this;
I shall describe the principle of Puruṣa to you in due order.
Ambhā and Salilā, as well as Tuṣāvṛṣṭi;
likewise Sutārā, Supārā, and Sunetrā. (234)
The four supreme forms of Sumārī have been proclaimed;
now I shall describe Tārā and the others as they are attained—learn from me. (235)
Tārā, Sutārā, and likewise Tarayantī;
Pramodā, Pramuditā, and likewise Modamānā. || 236 ||
That which is known as Ramyakā and that which is always joyful (Sadamuditā)—
these are declared to be the eightfold Siddhi, which must be understood by the teacher.
Atomicity, levity, and indeed magnanimity, as well as reach; and likewise the power of will, lordship, and mastery. (238)
I have described the sovereignty consisting in the fulfillment of all desires.
Above these, one should offer oblations to the channels and the eightfold Vidyā. (239)
Iḍā and Candriṇī, Gaurī and Śāntikarī, as well as Mālā and Mālinī, Svāhā and likewise Svadhā. || 240 ||
The channel (nāḍī) is declared to be knowledge; it should be understood with diligent effort.
For this very reason, the eightfold body (vigrahāṣṭaka) has been described above.
For the sake of favoring the worlds, it abides within all embodied beings as both effect and cause, as well as pleasure and pain. (242)

For these are remembered as being of the nature of the Puruṣa; they should be understood thus by the wise. O Goddess, those others which were previously mentioned by way of the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) [are not so]. || 243 ||
p.
1137) The various bonds of the body are to be understood by the teachers;
[they are] above the *puruṣa*... [end of fragment].
The noose of pleasure and the noose of pain—both of these are white and black.
Now, regarding his true nature, listen as I describe those Rudras:
Vāmadevodbhava and likewise Bhavodbhava. || 246 ||
Dhātāra, Kramaśas, and likewise Vikrama. || 247 ||
Prabheśāna is proclaimed, as well as Suprabheśāna;
these ten Rudras are indeed established within Niyati in brief. (248)
From this point upward, O Rudra, that time which is well-remembered is the imperishable syllable Rama.
Śiva, Suśiva, Dhruva, and Akṣara—these ten are declared in their proper sequence, one after another. (250)
Established in the reality of time, the Mātṛkā exists as an insertion; O Goddess, regarding those syllables which have been declared there within this triad of channels (nāḍī): || 252 ||
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā are remembered as the three;
Will, Knowledge, and Action are likewise remembered as the supreme triad of powers.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—these three constitute the nature of authority;
they are the Gārhapatya fire, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, and the Āhavanīya as the third. (254)
For these three fires are proclaimed to have the right to the sacrifice;
indeed, the three qualities are illustrated by these very three steps. || 255 ||
The three worlds were pervaded by them—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
indeed, Īśvara was the fourth, and Sadāśiva the fifth. || 256 ||
The salutation (namaskāra) is the power that awakens all mantras;
O Goddess, this mantra, which consists of everything, is most difficult to obtain. (257)
Through recitation, success is attained; one becomes victorious over time and death. Through recitation, one attains satisfaction and becomes equal to Amṛtīśa. || 258 ||
